ACCOUNTING
        8244
       Paper 1



1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

The overall standard of the learners’ work has improved and there are fewer learners who were not able to cope with
the demands of Accounting AS level.

Teachers must emphasise the importance of dates (consisting of a day, month and year), names of contra accounts,
as well as layout of Statements among others. It is also of vital importance that learners are taught to show their
calculations.

Learners have still misinterpreted some of the questions and did not answer what was asked. Teachers are requested
to encourage learners to read the questions carefully and only answer what is asked. Some learners could not apply
their knowledge to the questions asked.

Teachers need to teach learners that if a question asks the candidates to compare the difference must be shown and
they must not just state the facts.

The neatness of the learner’s work needs improvement, especially with regards to numbers. Learners must make their
digits clear and legible. Abbreviations are not allowed.

2.   COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

1    (a) Fairly well answered. Most of the learners defined fixed capital account correctly although they failed
         to give the reasons why a fixed capital account is preferred. Some learners differentiated instead of
         giving reasons and some learners stated the features of partnerships.
         Answer:
         Fixed capital accounts
         -    When the partners' current accounts and capital accounts are kept separately.
         -    Therefore, the partners’ capital account balances will remain fixed to their initial capital contributions 		
              each year. (1)

         Reasons why business may prefer fixed capital accounts
         -   If partners withdraw more than the profit share that they are entitled to, it is shown by a debit balance 		
             on the current account (1)
         -   A debit balance acts as a warning (1)
         -   Fixed capital account makes it easier to calculate interest on capital (1)
         -   Partners are able to see amount invested. Partners can differentiate between amount invested by 		
             partners and amounts due to partners by the business or a debit balance which shows how much is 		
             due by partners to a business (1)                                                  Any two               [3]

     (b) Poorly answered. Most of the learners struggled with dates, while some included drawings, Bank or
         Current account in the capital account. Only a few learners managed to find the correct balance c/d.

         Some learners wrote “delivery truck” instead of vehicles. Some learners included goodwill on the
         debit side although the question indicated that goodwill was to be maintained. Some learners failed
         to work out the amount contributed by Danny.

    -   If the partners charge interest on drawings of 12 % their residual profit would have increased (1) with

    Solly:       20 000 x 12%              = 2 400
    Claire:      80 000 x 12%              = 9 600             N$14 880
    Danny:       24 000 x 12%              = 2 880

    -       Interest on drawings is seen as a penalty/fine payable by a partner, therefore, it will relieve the 		
            conflict as each partner will have to pay the same percentage interest per annum, meaning the more 		
            each partner draws the more they pay. (1)
    -       Claire’s drawings are much higher than the other partners so paying interest will discourage her in the 		
            future and prevent the business from cash flow problems early in the financial year. (1)
    -       Solly is making the suggestion because he is the partner with the lowest rate of drawings and the 		
            highest share in the profit-sharing ratio and, therefore, will gain if the suggestion is implemented. (1)
    -       It can be debated whether the interest on drawings must be per month/year, as it would be more

(e) Fairly well answered. Although some learners knew what a debenture was, they failed to identify the
    features from the advantages.
     Answer:
     Features of debentures
     - Long-term loans evidenced by deeds which set out the rate of interest payable and the date of redemption
     - A debenture is a certificate that certifies that an amount is owed to someone
     - Instead of buying shares, some investors prefer to give these certified loans (debentures) to the company 		
       and to receive their money back after some time together with interest
     - It is considered the safest way to invest in a company since priority to repay the amount loaned is 		
       guaranteed by the certificate whether the business has made a profit or not
     - a company may issue shares as security to obtain debentures and redeem them later upon repayment
     - It is thus the easiest way to attract investment in the company and thus raise large sums of capital
     - it is treated as a liability since the company will have to repay the amount back with interest thereof
     - Interest on debenture is a financial expense to the company
     - if a company is wound up, debentures must be repaid before any capital is repaid to shareholders
     - Debenture holders are lenders: they are not members of the company and are not entitled to vote at 		
       shareholders’ meetings
     			                                                                                  Any three            [3]

3.   POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS

Teachers should coach learners to read carefully and with understanding, especially the requirements of a question and
to answer only what is asked.

Learners should show all workings and calculations as well as explain terminology in full sentences.

The correct definitions should be studied and not made up by students as they go along.

Learners must pay attention to dates, the correct account names and the correct layouts.

Learners should not only work on old examination papers, but as they tend to be threatened by questions with a different
format.

Teachers must plan enough time for revision and examination preparation. They must pay attention to terminology.

The different level questions should be practised by teachers, especially the level C and D questions.

        8244
       Paper 2



1.   GENERAL COMMENTS


The paper of 2025 was of the same standard as the paper of 2024. The difficulty level was the same as 2024, although
learners did not cope with the work in 2025, for various reasons. Many questions, especially the theory questions were
misinterpreted by learners. Learners did not always answer what was asked. Learners were supposed to first give a
specific answer and after that were supposed to elaborate on the “yes” or “no” answer, “should” or “should not” answer.

Managerial accounting counts to 25% of the total marks and 50% of the marks of Paper 2. This topic remains a big
problem for learners. That is either because the topics were not dealt with in detail or were not taught at all. This topic
is very important because of the weight it carries in the Paper 2.

          Answers
          (i) Limited liability
              Means the company coexists as a separate legal entity and the owners’ liabilities are limited to the
              amounts of capital they have invested in shares. This means that shareholders' personal possessions
              cannot be sold to settle company debts in case of insolvency. (1)
              Unlimited liability
              Means the business does not coexist as a separate legal entity and the owners’ personal possessions
              can be sold to settle business debts in case of insolvency. (1)                                      [2]

          (ii) Nominal value of shares
               The actual price that shares are listed in the company as per memorandum of association. (1)
               Authorised value of shares. (1)                                                  Any one
               Market value of shares
               The share price determined by		                                                                           [2]

          (iii) Cumulative preference shares
                These shares give the holders the right to receive/accumulate their unpaid dividends in future periods in
                case of insufficient profits. (1)
                Non-cumulative preference shares
                These shares do not give holders the right to receive/accumulate their unpaid dividends from one period
                to another period. (1)		[2]

                Dividends declared and paid from profit by directors of a company during a financial year, before the

                approval at the annual general meeting. (1) Paid after the end of the financial period.               [2]

3.   POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS

Teachers are doing well in teaching a very full syllabus in 6 months.

A suggestion is that all teachers start of with Managerial Accounting. They do not need the other topics to be able to
do Managerial Accounting. It counts 50% of Paper 2, so it is of the utmost importance that this topic MUST be dealt
with in earnest. Old examination papers, also old Higher papers are the best way to prepare learners for Managerial
Accounting.

Teachers must teach learners to read the theory questions very well and break them up into parts if they want to do well
in theory questions.

The overall commitment from the teacher’s side is there and by looking at the scripts, one can see that the syllabus has
been covered.

Teachers are recommended to stay positive and force the learners to do the theory questions by handing out old papers.
They only learn how to answer theory if they practice it. Learners tend only to do the Accounting part of revision and
write the theory questions down if the teacher provides the answers.

Algemene opmerkings
Hartlike dank aan al die taalonderwysers wat hard gewerk het om hul kandidate op standaard en gereed vir die
2025-eksamen te kry.

Dit is baie belangrik dat u, as onderwyser, elke jaar die verslag deeglik bestudeer en aan alle aspekte van die sillabus
aandag gee. Sommige kandidate se leesvaardighede was beter, soos geblyk het uit hul antwoorde, maar ongelukkig
geld dit nie vir al die sentrums nie. Onthou: LEES, LEES en LEES bly maar die sleutel tot ’n uitgebreide woordeskat
en sukses in die beantwoording van ’n vraestel! Ons wil u herinner dat u moeite moet doen om tydskrifte en koerante
vir u kandidate te gee om te lees. Kandidate is op die Gevorderde vlak, so daar word van hulle verwag om ŉ goeie
taalgebruik te hê.

Aanbevelings
Kandidate moet ook aangemoedig word om te probeer om alle vrae te beantwoord. By heelwat sentrums het kandidate
vrae net oopgelos.

AFDELING 1

Deel 1: 1 – 5
Vrae 1 – 5: Baie min kandidate het vol punte by hierdie vraag gekry. Heelwat kandidate het ten minste 3 punte in
hierdie afdeling verdien. Daar was egter ook kandidate wat slegs 1 - 2 punte gekry het. Onderwysers moet seker maak
leerlinge kry blootstelling aan hierdie soort vraagstelling.

Kandidate moet ook daarop gewys word dat vrae 1 – 5 in die tabel wat voorsien word, beantwoord moet word. Kandidate
moet geleer word dat hulle die tabel moet gebruik. Daar was vanjaar minder kandidate wat nie die tabel gebruik het nie
en eerder hul antwoorde omkring het.

Die korrekte antwoorde is soos volg:     Vraag 1: A
                                         Vraag 2: C
                                         Vraag 3: B
                                         Vraag 4: B

                                         Vraag 5: A                                                                  [5]

Deel 2: Vrae 6 – 11

Vraag 6 (a): Die korrekte antwoord is uithouvermoë. Heelwat kandidate het dit reg geantwoord.
Vraag 6 (b): Die korrekte antwoord is bose kringloop. Baie min kandidate het dit reg geantwoord.

Hulle moes slegs ŉ frase of ŉ woord aangehaal het. Heelwat kandidate het punte verloor deur die woord “kringloop”
aan te haal.
Kandidate moet leer om opdragte te lees, en ten minste probeer om die vrae te beantwoord, in plaas van om dit net
oop te laat!

Vraag 7 (a): Die vraag is nie goed beantwoord nie. Kandidate moes die figuurlike betekenis soos in die sin gebruik
word, verduidelik het. Iemand se voorbeeld volg is die korrekte antwoord.
Vraag 7 (b): Die vraag is ook nie goed beantwoord nie. (Om) resultate (te) kry / om suksesvol te wees is die korrekte
antwoord.

Vraag 8 (a): Baie min kandidate kon hierdie vraag korrek beantwoord. Dit moes die letterlike betekenis van hierdie
uitdrukking gewees het. Voorbeeldantwoord: Die kind het sy hond se voetspore gevolg en hom by die rivier
gevind.

AFDELING B – Gerigte skryfwerk

Vraag 12
Kandidate moes ŉ artikel vir hulle skoolkoerant skryf waarin hulle vir jong mense moes raad gee wat om te
doen om die regte loopbaan te kies.

Die meerderheid kandidate het daarin geslaag om hierdie vraag te beantwoord. Kandidate moes relevante feite uit die
teks asook hul eie idees in hul artikel genoem het. Heelwat kandidate het net die feite uit die teks genoem en sodoende
heelwat punte vir inhoud verloor. Daar was egter ook kandidate wat glad nie die teks gelees het nie en nét hul eie idees
gegee het, wat veroorsaak het dat hulle baie punte verbeur het.
Die meerderheid kandidate het die artikel van ŉ opskrif voorsien en hul naam en van geskryf.

Die gebruik van Engelse woorde, anglisismes het minder voorgekom, maar heelwat spelfoute was aan die orde van die
dag. Idiomatiese uitdrukkings wat verkeerdelik gebruik was, het ook voorgekom. Dit het ongelukkig die kandidate se
puntetoekenning beïnvloed.
By die taalgebruik het kandidate heelwat punte verloor omdat hulle die inhoud van die teks woordeliks oorgeskryf het.
Daar was wel nie so baie kandidate wat dit hierdie jaar gedoen het, in vergelyking met die vorige twee jaar nie. Baie
dankie aan die onderwysers wat daaraan gewerk het om dit uit te skakel!

Kandidate wat die lengtevereiste oorskry het, se ekstra woorde is geïgnoreer en dit het die inhoudspunt verlaag.

skryfstukke) oor te skryf, tesame met hul eie idees.

Sit tyd opsy en dink rustig oor jou keuses vir ŉ loopbaan.

Inleiding
Dit was duidelik hierdie jaar dat almal probeer het om so voorbereid as moontlik vir die eksamen te wees. Daar is egter
nog altyd plek vir verbetering. Hierdie jaar was daar nie een enkele kandidaat wat nie die opstelle in paragrawe geskryf
het nie. Dit is ’n prysenswaardige verbeterig op al die vorige eksamens. Baie ander aspekte het egter nog aandag
nodig, of is selfs nog kommerwekkend.

Die meeste kandidate kon die vraestel aandurf, soms met uitdaging, maar ook omdat hulle ’n keuse het in die tweede
deel.
Die onbaatsugtige harde werk van die leerkragte, in hierdie verband, word hartlik waardeer.

Spesifieke uitdagings

A Vraestel

1   Sosiale neigings
    Facebook, Instagram, Twitter en Snapchat beïnvloed die keuse van modeneigings en sosiale gedrag onder tieners.

    Bespreek hierdie stelling.
    Die meeste kandidate kon hierdie opstel, met wisselende sukses aanpak. Sommiges het een deel van die vraag
    mis gelees en toe net op die ander deel daarvan gekonsentreer. Die vaardigheid om te beredeneer was egter nog
    vir baie kandidate ’n probleem.

2   Taal en kommunikasie
    Elke mens het die reg om sy/haar storie in sy/haar moedertaal te vertel.

    Wat is jou mening?
    Baie kandidate het hierdie opstel gekies.

    Heelwat kandidate sukkel egter nog om ’n storie/verhaal te vertel.

3   Reis en Vervoer
    Ons infrastruktuur behoort ons in staat te stel om wêreldgehalte-openbare vervoer te kan geniet.

    Bespreek die rol van infrastruktuur na aanleiding van bogenoemde stelling.
    Redelik min kandidate het die onderwerp gekies. Die antwoord was met wisselende sukses omdat die vaardigheid
    om redenasie te hanteer vir van die kandidate moeilik was.

4   Die kunste
    ’n Kultuurskat van onmeetbare waarde het uit die kunsmuseum verdwyn.

    Vertel wat gebeur het.
    Heelwat van die kandidate het hierdie onderwerp gekies. Redelik baie kon die onderwerp hanteer, terwyl ander
    nog gesukkel het om storie te vertel.

5   Burgerskap
    Daardie dag het ek besef dat ek ’n Namibiër in murg en been is.

    Vertel jou storie.
    ’n Goeie aantal kandidate het besluit om die onderwerp te kies, sommiges met beter sukses as ander. Vaardigheid
    het van die kandidate se pogings in die wiele gery.

B Opdrag

1   Baie kandidate vind dit nog steeds moeilik om die opdrag binne die konteks van die tema te interpreteer
    en te verstaan.

2   Vaardighede om te vertel, argumenteer, beredeneer en te beskryf is kommerwekkend swak, of selfs
    onderontwikkel vir ’n redelik groot persentasie van die kandidate.
    Let daarop dat in die toekoms “kreatief” met “beskrywend” vervang sal word in die instruksies van
    Deel 2 op die vraestel vanaf 2027.

3   Daar word nie van kandidate verwag om in 2027 n titel te skep nie. Hulle word toegelaat om net met
    die opdrag te werk omdat dit voorkom dat hulle die opdrag misinterpreteer en sodoende die inhoud dan
    anders aanbied.

C Uitvoer van opdrag/Opstel/Antwoord

1   Die oorgrote meerderheid van die kandidate skryf die opstelle in hierdie belangrikste eksamen van hulle
    skoolloopbaan sonder enige aanduiding van ’n plan/beplanning. Bladsye 7 en 8 (op die vraestel) moet
    spesifiek vir hierdie doel aangewend word. Die afwesigheid van beplanning is duidelik sigbaar in die totale
    aanbieding van die opstel, ten opsigte van:

    (a) tema,

    (b) inleiding,

    (c) woordeskat,

    (d) winskonstruksie,

    (e) lees- en skryftekens,

    (f)   paragrafering,

    (g) inhoud en

    (h) lengte.

2   Daar is sommige kandidate wat die inleiding hanteer asof dit vir ’n ander skryfstuk, byvoorbeeld ’n
    toespraak, is. Hulle begin met, “In hierdie opstel gaan ek…”, of, “Die opstel gaan…”. Kandidate moet
    geleer word om op die opdrag te reageer, met die spesifieke vereistes wat daarmee gepaard gaan.

3   ’n Groot mate van kommer is die duidelike afwesigheid van aangeleerde/tematiese inligting, in die
    aanbieding van die inhoud, deur baie van die kandidate. Dit kom voor asof die aanleer, spelling, konteks
    en aanbieding van hierdie kennis nie ’n weg vind tot in die opstel nie. Die onrusbarende feit is dat ’n té
    groot aantal van die kandidate die verwagte standaard verwater as ’n aanbieding.

4   Sommige kandidate sukkel nog om ’n paragraaf te vorm. Dit wil voorkom asof dit moeilik is om die
    spesifieke paragraaf saam te stel. Spesifieke aandag moet deurentyd hieraan gegee word gedurende
    die onderrigtyd.

5   Spelling is ’n enorme probleem. Die redes hiervoor is dat die kandidate nie die klanke, asook die alfabet
    in Afrikaans, onder die knie het nie. As gevolg hiervan bestaan daar twyfel of die spel van woorde hier
    dan werklik in Afrikaans plaasvind.

6   Sinskonstruksie gaan gebuk onder die invloed van veral Engels. Woordorde raak dan die probleem.
    Die ander gevolg is lang, lomp sinne in ’n paragraaf, sonder die gebruik van toepaslike voegwoorde.

7   Die gebruik van sinsnedes as volsinne, buite konteks, kom gereeld voor. Spesifieke leiding is hier nodig.

8    Idiome is vaste uitdrukkings. Dit moet korrek en in die regte konteks gebruik word. Daar moet teen
     verwaterig en vertaling hiervan gewaak word. Nuwe uitdrukking of skepping moet egter korrek en in
     konteks gebruik word.

9    Interpunksie is nog uitdagend vir baie. ’n Groot frustrasie is egter die komma (,) aan die einde van ’n sin.

10 Die gebruik van voegwoorde aan die begin van sinne veroorsaak probleme. Onderrig is nodig.
   Kandidate moet ook geleer word dat hierdie opstelle is en nie toesprake of webjoernale nie.

     gebruik. Hulle moet weet dat dit ’n vertelling is en nie ’n dialoog nie.

   word ten strengste afgeraai. Die inligting moet in Afrikaans weergee word.

     (a) spelling,

Aanbevelings

     (a) Kandidate moet afgerig word om aan die vereistes van hierdie vraestel te voldoen. Aandag moet
         gegee word aan argument, redenasie, beskrywing en vertelling. Kandidate moet ten minste 20
         opstelle (4 soorte × 5 temas) skryf om genoeg ervaring op te doen ter voorbereiding van die eksamen.

     (b) Woordeskatuitbreiding en die gebruik in konteks moet deurentyd geoefen word.

     (c) Taal moet deurgaans hersien, geoefen en gebruik word.

     (d) Kandidate moet voluit in ’n reël skryf. Van hulle doen dit nie in die eksamen nie.

     (e) Kandidate moet let op handskrif en die netheid van hulle werk. Hierdie twee aspekte was nogal
         steurend hierdie jaar.

     (f)   Beplanning is ’n vereiste wat kandidate moet bemeester.

     (g) Kandidate móét die aantal woorde tussen hakies aandui aan die einde van die opstel.

     (h) Die onderwyser word aangemoedig om die vrymoedigheid te neem, om raad en hulp op
         verskillende vlakke te verkry.

GENERAL COMMENTS
The standard of the question paper was moderate, however, most questions were context oriented, therefore, most
candidates could not apply the correct answers accordingly. It was noticed that questions that had topics linked to
Grade 11 content were not as well answered by the learners as expected. Teachers are once again reminded to
refrain from presenting scientific terms casually when teaching in order to train candidates to use the correct scientific
language. For example, candidates used the term “offspring” to refer to cells in the question on differentiating between
meiosis and mitosis. Emphasis should be placed on all syllabus themes throughout the year to ensure candidates are
well prepared to answer all questions from all themes. It was noticed that the questions on theme 5 and 6 were not well
answered.

Positive suggestions to teachers
•   Teachers should ensure they revise topics with content linked to Grade 11 to assist learners in answering questions
    that contained aspects of the Grade 11 content, such as nitrogen fixation and flower structures.
•   Teachers should expose candidates to assessment objective B type of questions in order to capacitate candidates
    with critical thinking skills and understanding contextualized questions: Page 16 of the Agricultural Science syllabus.
•   Teachers should encourage candidate to read the whole stem of the question instead of answering straight away.
    This will help candidates to analyze correctly and understand the question before answering.
•   Teachers should address the questions based on comparisons to help learners score maximum marks by using a
    table of comparison as marks are awarded horizontally.
•   Teachers should emphasise on soil zone formation and not just its potential for productivity.
•   In addition, maximum time on task must also be spent on Themes 5 and 6 of the syllabus, as candidates are still
    not scoring good marks in these themes.

        8222
       Paper 2



GENERAL COMMENTS
Most centres submitted the required documents and worksheets of good standard for external moderation. A few
worksheets submitted were, however, not of acceptable standard. Most centres submitted evidence in the form of
pictures as required. Centres are encouraged to ensure that pictures submitted as evidence for practical investigations
are attached to specific investigation reports. Pictures must be clear enough, well annotated and should show all major
stages of the investigation with candidates busy carrying out the tasks. Centres that print their pictures in black and
white must ensure that the picture are clear otherwise colour pictures are more preferable than black and white pictures.
Candidates who are submitting typed reports are advised to use Arial / Times New Roman font and font size 12 with
1.5 line spacing.

Appropriateness of Assessment Tasks
Some centres selected all practical tasks from the same theme in the syllabus. Thus, centres are advised to take
practical topics from different themes of the syllabus for fairness. Some centres selected simple tasks that are not
challenging enough for candidates at this level. Candidates should not only prepare seedbeds but should also grow
some vegetables on the prepared plots and take care of them till harvesting or marketing. Similarly, for the task on seed
germination, which was selected by most centres, candidates should grow the viable seedlings and take care of them
until harvesting time. Centres should take note that testing for soil pH alone is insufficient, thus, it should be extended
to regulation of the soil pH. A food sample should be tested for at least two or more nutrients. Centres can alternatively
test various samples for one nutrient.

Some centres selected topic tasks that were more of an investigation such as tropism. Tasks should be hands-on,
allowing candidates to apply their technical skills by using tools and apparatus. Some tasks did not assess any
practical skills as they were only addressing assessment objective B, such as cash flow statement, thus, they must be
discouraged in future.

Interpretation and application of assessment criteria
Most centres were aware of the five assessment criteria that should be assessed in each practical task and there was
a great improvement in the generation of marking points per marking criteria generated from various centres. Few
centres submitted worksheets with theoretical questions. Centres are urged to develop more challenging practical-
based questions by addressing Assessment Objective C, see page 17 of the syllabus, under the written component of
the worksheets.

Suitability and relevance of practical investigations
Selection of relevant question (hypothesis) for the investigation
Many candidates were able to come up with a hypothesis for their investigation. However, some hypotheses were
not clearly formulated. Examiners should provide appropriate guidance to help candidates in developing clear and
brief hypotheses. Marks should then be awarded in accordance with the level of guidance provided by the examiner
as indicated in the marking criteria. Some candidates selected topics that were not experimental such as surveys.
Selected topics should be of investigative nature, meaning candidates should find information for themselves by direct
observation and measurement. See page 26 of Agricultural Science NSSCAS syllabus.

Planning of the investigation
It was evident that centres that did prior planning, produced investigations of an acceptable standard. Candidates at
some centres opted for topics with more than one variable but failed to attend to all the variables such as influence of
organic fertilizer on germination, growth and yield as they only collected data on growth. Some investigations required
a control such as the effect of manure on plant growth. A control plot was required for comparative reasons to make
reasonable deductions. Some candidates could not replicate their work. Replication of treatments is necessary to
increase reliability. Therefore, it is advisable for centres to guide candidates from the title selection until all the stages of
the investigations are exhausted. However, teachers guiding the candidates should not do the work for candidates but
should just guide and allow candidates to do their own work. Some methodologies were shallow. Methodology is the
backbone of the investigation and should include all aspects namely: methods used to plan, sample, measure, collect
and analyse data.

Handling of evidence
It was impressive to learn that most candidates showed understanding of how to handle data collected through completed
tables and graphs. However, some candidates failed to label and scale their graphs correctly. Results presented by
some candidates seemed unrealistic. Candidates whose reports are handwritten are encouraged to use graph paper
for plotting graphs. Thus, such centres should make graph paper available to candidates for such purposes.


                                                 NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     36
Ability to make deductions
Most candidates could interpret and analyse their data. However, interpretations were not supported by the data
collected. Deductions conclusions made by some candidates were, however, not linked to the data collected or
hypotheses. Examiners should ensure that candidates are guided to draw conclusions that are clearly linked to the
data collected and directly address the original hypothesis. In addition, centres should ensure that candidates provide
clear and well-reasoned justifications for their conclusions.

Limitations
Most candidates were able to identify 1 or 2 limitations experienced during their investigations. However, some
candidates identified challenges that what already been addressed during the investigation and therefore, cannot be
regarded as limitations. Some recommendations suggested by candidates were not addressing the identified limitations.
Some identified limitations were not having suggestions on how they could be addressed or improved in future. Centres
should guide and encourage candidates to suggest improvements that will help future researchers to overcome the
identified limitations.

Presentation, layout and originality
Many candidates were able to follow the report layout as outlined in the syllabus. However, some candidates did not
indicate the brief plan of their practical investigations. Candidates need proper guidance on how to write methodology.
Some candidates’ methodologies were not clearly describing what their investigations were all about. Methodology
should give a clear insight into what the investigation entails. Some candidates did not attach pictures or pictures
attached were insufficient. Candidates are urged to attach pictures from their own investigations showing all major
steps and active participation of candidates.

Interpretation and application of assessment criteria for practical investigations
Most centres were able to interpret and apply the assessment criteria for practical investigation with regards to the six
marking criteria. However, some centres did not adhere to the specific descriptors outlined within the marking criteria
such as maximum marks awarded for stating limitations even when no corresponding improvements were suggested.
Centres are urged to use the assessment criteria guide for practical investigations, when awarding marks for candidates’
practical investigations and to provide annotations as to how the marks were awarded. Please see page 29 and 30 of
NSSCAS Syllabus for the criteria and guide to marking practical investigations.

Administration
It is appreciated that many centres complied with all the administrative procedures that are required for moderation
purposes and that some centres put in extra effort by providing the required information in neat and well-organised files.
This made the moderation exercise much easier. Some errors in addition of marks were, however, detected. Centres’
internal moderators should not only moderate and verify marks in the Assessment Summary form but are urged also to
ensure that marks are correctly transferred from the Candidate Individual Record Cards to the Continuous Assessment
Summary Form (CASF) and later to the MS1 form.

There was an improvement by most centres in submitting evidence of candidates’ work in the form of pictures, showing all
the main stages of the practical tasks and not just the end result. It is important to verify before sealing the envelope that
all the necessary documents for external moderation are enclosed in the envelope. Centres are referred to the reverse
side of the Individual Candidate Record Cards, Coursework Assessment Summary Forms for additional information.
In conclusion, the performance demonstrated by candidates was satisfactory. We recommend that training be arranged
by Regional Offices for centres. Agricultural Science Advanced Subsidiary level teachers should seek assistance
regarding the conducting and administering of School-Based Assessment in Agricultural Science.

COMMENTS ON PAPER 1 AND PAPER 2

A: Research and record

Some noticeable improvement have been detected in some candidates’ work. Candidates should be encouraged to
do proper investigation and research on a variety of appropriate sources. In Component 2, ideas observations and
insights should always be recorded visually and in written form relevant to intentions teachers should guide candidates
to reference all sources otherwise their work might be seen as plagiarism which can lead to an irregularity. Candidates
must reflect critically on work and the progress thereof. This means thought processes must be recorded at all times.
Teachers must guide candidates to refrain from excessive annotations. Some candidates used a variety of appropriate
sources, but the latter were not always thoroughly investigated. Because of a lack of research and recording the
candidates were not able to reflect critically on work and progress.

B: Explore and select

Although some candidates did gather extensively, there was very little to no experimentations on techniques and
processes. Some candidates did not select and explored their gathered sources intentionally to realise their final
outcome. It is advisable that ideas should be reviewed and refined as the work develops.

C: Develop ideas

Some candidates lack development stages. That means they should have improved on their existing work. Skills
and techniques should also be part of the development stage. In some cases, focus was not clear throughout the
developmental process, therefore, analytical and critical thinking were not very effective. Little to no personal and
contextual referencing was done.

D: Produce

In some cases, candidates need to demonstrate a more analytical and critical understanding to produce a more personal
and meaningful response toward their final outcome, therefore, connections made between visual and other elements
must be thoroughly thought through to be executed effectively.

Thank you for the hard work and effort during this year.

General Comments
Paper 1 assessed a wide range of AS Biology knowledge and understanding, including biological classification, cell
biology, biochemistry, transport, physiology, immunity, disease, and cell division. Overall performance was satisfactory,
with strong performance on recall-based questions and variable performance on questions requiring application,
calculations, or interpretation of diagrams and graphs.

Where performance was weaker, misconceptions were often linked to:
•   confusion between similar biological terms (e.g. species concepts, diffusion pathways),
•   poor handling of magnification and unit conversions,
•   superficial recall without understanding underlying mechanisms.

Comments on specific questions
1   B    This was very well answered. Most candidates correctly identified the hierarchical order
         phylum → class → order → family → genus → species. More than 95 % of candidates gave the
         correct answer. A small minority confused the sequence of taxonomic ranks, particularly family and order.
2   D    The performance was moderate. Many candidates incorrectly chose the biological species concept,
         which depends on interbreeding and cannot be applied to fossils. Only 49% answered this question correctly.
3   B    Only 48% were able to correctly identify that a higher Simpson’s Index indicates greater biodiversity
         and therefore greater stability. Other candidates selected very low or very high numerical values
         without understanding what the index represents. Learners should understand the interpretation of
         values, not just calculations.
4   D    Only 49% got the correct answer. Many candidates omitted biotic interactions, selecting options that
         excluded feeding relationships and energy transfer, they confused habitat with niche. It should be
         noted that a niche includes abiotic conditions, resource availability, and interactions with other organisms.
5   C    50% of the candidates got the correct answer. Other candidates often confused magnification with
         resolution, leading to incorrect pairings.
6   C    52% got it correctly. Some candidates failed to convert millimetres to micrometres correctly. The
         common issue was unit conversion errors rather than conceptual misunderstanding.
7   A    More than 60% correctly applied the formula: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. Those who
         answered incorrectly typically converted millimetres to metres incorrectly.
8   B    67% of candidates understood the sequence: nucleus → ribosomes → rough ER → Golgi apparatus.
         Errors occurred when the Golgi was incorrectly placed before protein synthesis.

         ribosomes, demonstrating limited understanding that these are found in mitochondria and chloroplasts.

         but no membrane-bound organelles.

         heads. Learners should always try to link structure directly to function when revising membrane

      Paper 2



Introduction

We are living in a time where information can readily be found on the internet. This information, however, needs to be
understood and analysed for accuracy as not all information found on the internet is always correct. To be able to do
that, certain skills are taught at school and in Biology.

The following skills were tested in this examination paper:

•   Communication skills: The ability to read and understand a question and to express yourself in writing using
    whole sentences with correct punctuation and grammar.

•   Numeracy skills: The ability to work with numbers given in standard notation, such as, 650 000 000 becomes
    6,5 x 108 and to interpret numerical information provided in a table.

•   Problem-solving skills: The ability to apply learned content to new situations.

•   Work and study skills: The ability to answer a question by completing a diagram. In Biology it is very helpful to make
    use of diagrams whilst studying.

•   Critical and creative thinking skills: The ability to think logically, especially when describing processes. Learners
    must learn to answer questions using their own knowledge, rather than repeating text from the textbook or the
    internet.

The text in italics is quoted from the Namibian National Curriculum Guidelines. All these skills are needed to answer
a question paper successfully. This requires factual knowledge, but also a good understanding of the content. In
the 2025 examination, the recall questions were answered fairly well but questions requiring the application of that
knowledge were poorly answered by most candidates.

General comments
Candidates demonstrated insufficient proficiency in English to express their ideas clearly when responding to examination
questions. This should not be a problem any more after 12 years of schooling. Learners should have more opportunities
in class to answer questions orally.  Teachers should correct learners in their use of the English language and give
candidates the opportunity to also do this in their written work, which should then be marked and corrected, not only
in terms of the subject knowledge, but also with regards to the language.

General terminology issues:
•   Time increases and decreases.  Time does not get higher or lower time or greater or smaller,

•   Distance increases and decreases, or becomes longer or shorter but not bigger, greater or smaller distance.

•   Size gets bigger or smaller or increases or decreases but does not become higher, more or less.

Teachers should also concentrate more on their own choice of words when explaining subject content. If they are unsure
about how to explain certain content, they must do some research on the internet. There are very good YouTube videos
available. Teachers should watch these videos open mindedly, as not all the content is always correctly explained. Use
credible resources when doing research. Also check the content in the textbooks, which also contain some mistakes.
Teachers must encourage learners to rather work on understanding what they are learning than to learn content off by
heart.

Punctuation rules apply in all subjects! Candidates still write sentences without a capital letter at the beginning, and
they still do not use any punctuation marks, or they use punctuation wrongly, which affects the structure and meaning
of their answer.  This makes it extremely difficult to mark their work.

Many candidates still answer questions using bullet points, which is not acceptable in questions where candidates must
describe, explain, suggest, discuss, provide a reason or give an outline. Candidates still struggle with the instructions
‘describe and explain’.

Biological terminology must be used correctly and more care should be taken with spelling. Teachers, must remind
candidates to read through their answers, since errors in sentence construction, spelling or grammar are excessive and
can cost learners marks!

Handwriting is also an issue. If a candidate’s handwriting is illegible, marks cannot be awarded. Teachers must

                                             NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                  43
advise candidates accordingly, especially those whose handwriting is so small that a hand lens is needed to read it.

Candidates should be encouraged to attempt answering all questions and have good time management.

Teachers must start marking much more strictly at school for candidates to learn how they should answer questions
correctly.  Teachers should avoid giving ‘benefit of the doubt’ marks.  A fact or an application is either right, or it is wrong.

Candidates have often used the margin ‘for examiner’s only’ and they should be told not to do so as it is the space
needed by the markers.

Teachers must make use of the examiner’s report yearly as to improve their own knowledge and through doing so help
their students.

             Candidates do not understand the process.
             Look at the following explanation of the process:
             Cell signalling is a process of cellular communication.
             Cells communicate by using cell signals through signal transduction pathways. The chemical signals
             can be proteins or other molecules produced by ‘sending cells.’ The signals are secreted from the cell
             and released in the extracellular space (space around the cells.)
             The signal is released in response to a certain condition.




             The cell that receives the ‘message ‘is the target cell. The target cell must have a receptor for the signal,
             where it can bind and alter the shape or the activity of that receptor. The signalling molecules are called
             ligands (a term used for molecules that bind to other molecules.)
             Transduction pathway: Signal transduction is the process by which cells respond to ligands.   Mostly
             the receptors are outside the cell, on the cell membrane and the signal therefore must be passed to other
             molecules in the cell.

                    ligand




             https://www.labxchange.org/library/items/lb:LabXchange:d0211b15:html:1
             Once the ligand binds to the receptor, the signal is transduced i.e., the ligand changes the protein’s shape
             and stimulates a certain process within the cell.
             The signalling molecule unbinds from the receptor protein, which stops the transduction pathway and
             allows the receptor molecule to return to its original configuration.
             Cell signalling leads to the regulation of cellular activities, which is called the response.

            1 concentration of substrate decreases as substrate molecules are changed into product

		(ii)      Candidates do not understand enzyme action correctly.
            Many candidates did not read the question properly. The question was about the end of the reaction
            meaning no substates are left. Candidates explained what they thought would happen if more substrate
            or enzyme was added, meaning either one becoming a limiting factor. This was not mentioned in the
            question.  Others mentioned the use of competitors, which was also not part of this question.
            As the substrate binds to the enzyme to form an ESC, the substrate concentration decreases and the
            ESC concentration increases.
            ESC’s however are not permanent; as soon as the reaction has been catalysed, the product is released,
            therefore, the product curve starts rising as soon as the substrate curve starts going down.
            The enzymes are not used up during the reaction, but are used again and again, i.e., when the product
            has been formed and released, the free enzyme immediately forms a new ESC.  That is why the ESC
            concentration stays constant, and the free enzyme concentration stays at 0 for the time of  the reaction.  
            When the substrate concentration is lower than the original enzyme concentration, not all free enzymes will
            form ESC’s, therefore the enzyme concentration starts rising and will reach its original concentration.  The
            number of ESC’s will decrease, as there is less substrate to bind with, therefore, the ESC concentration
            decreases to 0.
            The product concentration cannot increase to be more than the original substrate concentration.
            It is very important that the necessary experiments or investigations on this topic are done in class to help
            the candidates understand the functioning of the enzymes.

			Answer




            1 product molecules increase (at the same rate as substrate molecules decrease);
            2 all substrate molecules have been changed to product molecules, therefore, reaches 0;
            3 when all substrate is used up, no new enzyme-substrate complexes are formed, therefore, decrease
            to 0;
            4 enzyme concentration returns to original concentration;
            5 concentration of product molecules equals original concentration of substrate molecules as all substrate
            has been changed into product;
            6 product concentration reaches its max when all products have been released from enzyme-substrate
            complexes;
            Product curve may not go higher than substrate curve at start.
            When enzyme concentration increases, not higher than original.
            max 2 for explanation

Key messages
Advanced Practical Skills is a laboratory-based practical paper focused on learners mastering the skills and competencies
relevant to the investigations outlined in the syllabus, rather than simply practising past examination questions. Learners
should be provided with sufficient time to engage in all practical activities within the syllabus, enabling them to develop
skills that are applicable both for the examination and for further studies or future employment.

General comments

It is advisable that AS learners demonstrate an advanced level of proficiency in the English language to
comprehend scientific concepts thoroughly and accurately interpret questions, thereby enabling them to provide appropriate
responses.

Centres are urged to complete their reports meticulously and to observe the practical activities performed by the
learners, as the information contained in the Supervisor’s report is essential for the accurate assessment of
candidate’s answers during marking.

Candidates who have engaged with materials and apparatus during practical work as part of the course are generally
better prepared for the examinations. While the examination activities may not be entirely unfamiliar, candidates who
have consistently followed instructions in a variety of practical tasks typically find it easier to organise and execute
original activities.

To ensure effective execution of a practical, candidates must carefully read the instructions, analyse the available data
required, and respond to questions based on the specific practical at hand, rather than rely on practical work completed
earlier in the academic year.

     ∆H = (sum of bond energies of reactants) – (sum of bond energies of products)
        = [6(C-H) + C=C + C-C + H-Br] – [7(C-H) + 2(C-C) + C-Br]
        = [(6 × 410 + 610 + 350 +3 66] – [7 × 410+ 2 × 350 + 280]

GENERAL COMMENTS
•   Learners demonstrated a solid grasp of fundamental chemistry concepts but showed inconsistency in applying this
    knowledge to unfamiliar situations. While most performed well on questions requiring straightforward recall, many
    struggled with higher-order tasks, such as justifying the choice of operating temperature in the Contact process and
    applying the mole concept.
•   There was clear evidence of strong preparation in fundamental areas such as atomic structure and bonding.
    Learners also demonstrated solid understanding of core topics basic organic chemistry. Nonetheless, notable
    gaps appeared in physical chemistry (especially mass spectral analysis) and in introductory inorganic chemistry,
    including explanations of periodic trends among Period 3 elements..
•   Learners are advised to pay close attention to the command words and the stem of each question. Underlining
    key terms can help in identifying exactly what the question requires. For instance, in Question 1, learners were
    asked to state the ions responsible for each peak, yet some provided formulas of neutral atoms or molecules
    despite the explicit instruction to give ions. Additionally, learners should read questions thoroughly and respond only
    to what is being asked, avoiding unnecessary detail.
•   There was frequent misuse of technical terminology, particularly in defining ionisation energy and describing
    variation in metallic bonding of period 3 metals and maximum oxidation numbers of period 3 elements. Learners
    should be encouraged to learn precisely certain definitions, trends and principles. The omission of a single key
    word or interchanging some words can lead to marks not being awarded if it is an important part of the definition.
    Learners are reminded to keep their responses to simple questions as short and as precise as possible. The
    accurate use of chemistry terminology is welcomed as it removes ambiguity from responses. Lengthier responses
    or the inclusion of more details than required by a question sometimes led to contradictions in learners answers.
•   Teachers should emphasize the importance of writing clear, step-by-step solutions to calculations and giving the
    final answer to the prescribed degree of accuracy. For example, most learners lost marks in question 1 (b)(ii) and
    3 (b) as some of the answers were not expressed to four and three significant figures respectively.
•   There was a remarkable improvement in organic chemistry with many learners showcasing clear understanding of
    the optical isomerism and infra-red spectroscopy. However teachers should emphasize more on the classification
    of alcohols, reagents and conditions for different organic reactions and systematic nomenclature of compounds
    belonging to different homologous series.
•   Teachers are encouraged to expose learners to common organic reactions (including the iodoform reaction)
    and practical aspects specified in the syllabus. Practical experiments help learners visualize and experience
    chemical reactions, making abstract concepts like stoichiometry and organic chemistry more tangible and easier to
    comprehend. It encourages learners to think critically fostering analytical and problem-solving abilities.
•   Learners should be encouraged to write their responses only in the answer spaces provided. If part of a response
    is unavoidably written elsewhere in the booklet, it should be clearly labelled so that the Examiner knows which
    question it belongs to. When boxes are provided for diagrams or structures, only the final answer should be in the
    box. When more than one structure is provided it is difficult for Examiners to decide which one is the final answer.

General Comments
•   Learners should quote numerical answers to the number of significant figures that reflects the data provided
    regarding the reactants and the errors inherent in the method.
•   Learners should be given the opportunity to discuss errors arising in the practical methods during their studies and
    identify possible improvements to ameliorate these.
•   Centres are reminded that the following documentation for each session and for each laboratory within a session
    should be included in the script packet:
    - a list of the learners present and a seating plan for the laboratory
    - a copy of the examination paper with the Supervisor’s experimental result
•   Learners should ensure they read and follow the general instructions given at the start of both the Quantitative and
    Qualitative Analysis sections.

Comments on Specific Questions

Question 1
It appears as though learners had some trouble with the setup of the experiment which took some time.

    (a) Well answered.  Majority of learners recorded a value for the final volume of gas collected.  There
        were a few learners who incorrectly gave the unit as dm3.  Some learners recorded a volume of gas
        collected exceeding 250 cm3, which is not possible as the measuring cylinder has a limit of  250 cm3.

    (b) Some learners inappropriately gave their answer to one, five or five or more significant figures in any
        of (i) to (iii).  Some learners were not able to round their answers correctly when taking the number of
        significant figures into account.

         (i)   Well answered.  Most learners knew how to calculate the number of moles of gas from its volume
               in (a).  A few learners omitted the division by 1000 to convert their answer from cm3 to dm3.

        (ii)   Moderately well answered.   A large number of learners were able to correctly calculate the
               concentration of H2SO4 by dividing their answer in (i) by 0.01.

       (iii)   Well answered.  Majority of learners were able to correctly calculate the mass of Mg by using
               their moles of H2 since it is a 1:1 ratio. Quite a few number of learners used 24 for the Ar of Mg
               instead of 24.3.  Learners are encouraged to use the relative atomic mass values as it is given
               on the AS periodic table.  They must use the values with their decimal places as this is more
               accurate than what was previously used on NSSCO.

    (c) Poorly answered.  Some learners were able to correctly explain whether they agree or disagree with
        the statements made.
         Statement 1:
         Many learners correctly recognised that the reaction would be slower; far fewer went on to state this meant
         that the experiment was more accurate because less gas would escape before the bung was fitted.
         Some learners also referred to gas loss being completely prevented, which is incorrect.  Gas loss cannot be
         prevented completely, it can only be reduced, as some gas will always be lost.
         Statement 2:
         More learners realised that, since the magnesium was already in excess, the use of twice as much would
         not affect the volume of gas and hence the determination of the concentration of sulfuric acid.  Some
         learners said that using twice as much magnesium will result in it becoming in excess, which is incorrect, as
         it was clearly stated at the beginning of the question that it already starts in excess.

    (d) Poorly answered.  Very few learners could correctly explain that the concentration of B would
        decrease because less gas would be released.  A satisfactory explanation was only given by better
        performing learners.  A significant number of learners stated that less hydrochloric acid would react;
        fewer related this to the experimentally measured volume of hydrogen produced and hence the
        reduced concentration of the acid.

Question 2
Many learners were able to complete the practical work to a high standard.  This was a straightforward titration exercise
and it was apparent that most learners were well acquainted with the method, the presentation of results and the
calculation using the titration data.  There were, however, still a few learners that it was clear have never done a titration
before. Many learners had difficulties with the sections dealing with errors.

     (a) Well answered.   Majority of learners were able to draw up a neat titration table with all required
         headings and in the correct format.
              Some mistakes made by learners included the following:
              •  Not recording the initial and final burette readings for the rough titre
              •  Not including units with the table headings
              •  Not giving accurate burette readings to two decimal places ending in 0.00 or 0.05 cm3
              •  The final accurate titre not being within a range of 0.10 cm3 of any previous accurate titre
     (b) Well answered.  The majority of learners gained credit for the mean titre.  The most common error
         was to omit working or to give an answer that was not correct to two decimal places.  Learners should
         be aware that the mean calculated, should be rounded to the nearest 0.01 cm3, and not 0.00 or 0.05
         cm3 as the readings for the burette should be given.  Some learners incorrectly included the value for
         the rough titre or used a spread of titres that was greater than 0.20 cm3.
                                                   NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025

                significant figures.  A number of learners recognised this fact and therefore wrote two or three

        (ii)    Poorly answered.   Very few learners were able to correctly calculate the number of moles of
                NaOH.  Majority of learners simply divided 1.0 by 40, but then failed to take into account that E

11   This section of the syllabus continues to pose a big challenge for most candidates. While   8
     only a few candidates managed to give impressive solutions, scoring full marks, most
     candidates failed to score more than 4 marks for this question. Candidates needed to
     be better prepared for this section.
     1 mark each correct bullet point
     MP1 initialise variable e.g sentence, WordCount, SentenceType
     MP2 prompt to enter sentence
     MP3 correct loop (., ? or !) end mark to be catered for
     MP4 split sentence into string words
     MP5 count number of words and store in WordCount
     MP6 check the last character in the sentence // determine sentence type
     MP7 display WordCount, SentnceType
     MP8 correct formatting e.g. indenting, meaningful variable names, or comments


     Example Algorithm / Pseudocode
     1. Initialise variables:
       - sentence = "" # Initialize an empty string to store the sentence
       - WordCount = 0 # Initialize a variable to count words
       - SentenceType = "" # Initialize a variable to store the type of sentence
     2. Display a prompt for the user to enter a sentence.
     INPUT sentence
     3. Loop until an end mark (., ?, or !) is encountered:
       a. Read a character from the user.
       b. Append the character to the 'sentence' string.
     4. Split the 'sentence' string into words using spaces as delimiters:
       a. Initialize a list 'words' to store the words.
      b. Initialize an empty string 'CurrentWord' to build each word.
       c. Loop through each character in 'sentence':
         i. If the character is a space:
            - Add 'CurrentWord' to the 'words' list (if 'CurrentWord' is not empty).
            - Reset 'CurrentWord' to an empty string.
         ii. Otherwise, append the character to 'CurrentWord'.
     5. Add the last 'CurrentWord' to the 'words' list (if not empty).
     6. Count the number of words in the 'words' list and store it in 'wordCount'.
     7. Check the last character in the 'sentence' string to determine the sentence type:
       a. If the last character is '.', set 'SentenceType' to "statement."
       b. If the last character is '?', set 'SentenceType' to "question."
       c. If the last character is '!', set 'SentenceType' to "exclamation."
     8. Display the following information:
       - The number of words in the sentence (WordCount).
       - The type of sentence entered (SentenceType).
     9. End the program.


     Example Python program:
     # Initialize variables
     sentence = ""
     WordCount = 0
     SentenceType = ""

                                    NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                 93
     # Prompt the user to enter a sentence
     print("Enter a sentence (end with '.', '?', or '!'): ")


     # Loop until an end mark is encountered
     while True:
        char = input("Enter a character: ")
        sentence += char
        if char in ('.', '?', '!'):
            break


     # Split the sentence into words
     words = sentence.split()


     # Count the number of words
     WordCount = len(words)


     # Determine the sentence type
     if sentence.endswith('.'):
         SentenceType = "statement"
     elif sentence.endswith('?'):
         SentenceType = "question"
     elif sentence.endswith('!'):
         SentenceType = "exclamation"


     # Display the information
     print(f"Number of words in the sentence: {WordCount}")
     print(f"Sentence type: {SentenceType}")


     Example VB.NET program:

Example Java program:


import java.util.Scanner;


public class SentenceAnalyzer {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
     // Initialize variables
     String sentence = "";
     int WordCount = 0;
     String SentenceType = "";
    // Create a scanner to read user input
     Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);


     // Prompt the user to enter a sentence
     System.out.println("Enter a sentence (end with '.', '?', or '!'): ");



     // Loop until an end mark is encountered
     while (true) {
         char character = scanner.next().charAt(0);
         sentence += character;


         if (character == '.' || character == '?' || character == '!') {
             break;
         }
     }


    // Split the sentence into words
     String[] words = Sentence.split("\\s+");
    // Count the number of words
     WordCount = words.length;


                                 NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                             95
             // Determine the sentence type
             if (sentence.endsWith(".")) {
                 SentenceType = "statement";
             } else if (sentence.endsWith("?")) {
                 SentenceType = "question";
             } else if (sentence.endsWith("!")) {
                 SentenceType = "exclamation";
             }


             // Display the information
             System.out.println("Number of words in the sentence: " + WordCount);
             System.out.println("Sentence type: " + SentenceType);


             // Close the scanner
             scanner.close();
         }
     }


     Example C++ program:


     #include <iostream>
     #include <string>


     int main() {
        // Initialize variables
        std::string sentence = "";
        int WordCount = 0;
        std::string SentenceType = "";


         // Prompt the user to enter a sentence
         std::cout << "Enter a sentence (end with '.', '?', or '!'): " << std::endl;


         // Loop until an end mark is encountered
         while (true) {
             char character;
             std::cin.get(character);
             sentence += character;
             if (character == '.' || character == '?' || character == '!') {
                 break;
             }
         }


         // Split the sentence into words
         std::string CurrentWord;
         std::vector<std::string> words;
         for (char character : sentence) {
            if (character == ' ' || character == '.' || character == '?' || character == '!') {
                if (!CurrentWord.empty()) {
                    words.push_back(CurrentWord);
                    CurrentWord.clear();




                                       NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
96
                       }
                    } else {
                       CurrentWord += character;
                    }
                }


                // Count the number of words
                WordCount = words.size();


                // Determine the sentence type
                if (sentence.back() == '.') {
                    SentenceType = "statement";
                } else if (sentence.back() == '?') {
                    sentenceType = "question";
                } else if (sentence.back() == '!') {
                    SentenceType = "exclamation";
                }


                // Display the information
                 std::cout << "Number of words in the sentence: " << WordCount << std::endl;
                 std::cout << "Sentence type: " << SentenceType << std::endl;


                return 0;
            }

      Sample Java code
      import java.util.Scanner;
      public class LargestVolume {
          public static void main(String[] args) {
              Scanner scanner = new Scanner(system.in);
              System.out.println(“Enter the first volume:”);
              double volume1 = scanner.nextDouble();
              System.out.println(“Enter the second volume:”);
              double volume2 = scanner.nextDouble();
              System.out.println(“Enter the third volume:”);
              double volume3 = scanner.nextDouble();
              double largestVolume = findLargestVolume(volume1, volume2, volume3);
              System.out.println(“The largest volume is: “ + largestVolume);
          }
          public static double findLargestVolume(double v1, double v2, double v3) {
              return Math.max(Math.max(v1, v2), v3);
          }
      }

      Sample C++ code
      #include <iostream>

GENERAL COMMENTS

Teachers from many centres are familiar with the content of the syllabus, as it is observed that they guided and taught
the candidates well, and that they knew what to expect in the exams. These teachers should be applauded for the effort
put into preparing the learners for the examinations. According to the responses by the candidates, some parts of the
syllabus were not covered in detail by a few centres. Some centres appear not to have thoroughly covered the whole
syllabus.

Thanks, should also go to the entire Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sports, Arts and Culture, Regional Offices,
Schools, and of course, the Candidates who wrote this examination.

Good responses were received from the centres regarding the quality and standard of the question paper. It is
interpreted, and the style, language, and graphics were executed.

From the comments by teachers on the questions, there were no problems in answering the questions, although in
some cases, candidates did not respond correctly. However, for a few questions, candidates could score good marks.

Evidence also shows that some candidates were not equipped with the knowledge to answer certain questions
successfully, and some did not attempt to answer questions. In the spread of marks for this question paper, it appears
that candidates were generally prepared.

Section A consisted of compulsory questions across the syllabus. In most cases, candidates scored satisfactory marks;
in some cases, the candidates were unprepared.

This year we had 54 candidates, of whom none answered the Technology Part, only two candidates answered the
Communication Part, and the rest answered the Resistant Part in Section B in the question paper.

In 2024, 71 candidates entered to write the exam, but in 2025, there were 54 candidates, of whom no candidates were
absent. We expect that in future the number of candidates increase.

            Q      Expected answer                                                      Marks          Guidance

                   resource is required.                                                        mentioned
                 • It is less costly (cheaper) to recycle paper, wood, glass, metals            AOVR:
                   and plastic than to produce new stock material.
                 • When, e.g. metals are extracted from raw ore, the ore
                   has to be mined, transported, crushed, smelted, cast into
                   ingots, which then are transformed into stock material.
                   These processes use a vast amount of energy, whereas
                   the re-smelting of used metals to form stock material is less
                   expensive.
                 • To extract glass from raw silicon also requires a large amount
                   of energy; re-smelting of used glass uses less energy. It would
                   be ideal to reuse glass bottles, as the smelting of glass requires
                   a significant amount of energy.
                 Resources will last longer for future generations.

    (d) Explain the differences between a PNP transistor and a NPN transistor. Give examples of where each
        transistor is used in your answer

9(d)         The transistors PNP and NPN are BJTs and it is a basic electrical component, used 4                          AOVR
             in various electrical and electronic circuits to build the projects. The operation of                        1x4
             the PNP and NPN transistors mainly utilizes holes and electrons. These transistors
             can be used as amplifiers, switches, and oscillators. In the PNP transistor, the
             majority of charge carriers are holes, wherein NPN the majority charge carriers
             are electrons. The major difference between NPN and PNP transistor is, an NPN
             transistor gets the power when the flow of current runs through the base terminal
             of the transistor. In an NPN transistor, the flow of current runs from the collector
             terminal to the emitter terminal. A PNP transistor switches ON when there is no flow
             of current at the base terminal of the transistor. In the PNP transistor, the flow of
             current runs from the emitter terminal to the collector terminal. As a result, a PNP
             transistor switches ON by a low signal, where an NPN transistor switches ON by
             a high signal.

    (f)     The following questions are about a Schmitt trigger.

           (i)    Draw the symbol for an inverting Schmitt trigger

           (ii)   Explain the function of a Schmitt trigger.

9(f)(i)                                                                                               2      Symbol
                                                                                                             correctly drawn
                  Input                                   Output                                             (2)




9(f)(ii)      In electronics, a Schmitt trigger is a comparator circuit with hysteresis               3      AOVR:
              implemented by applying positive feedback to the noninverting input of a                       1x3
              comparator or differential amplifier. It is an active circuit which converts an
              analogue input signal to a digital output signal. The circuit is named a trigger
              because the output retains its value until the input changes sufficiently to
              trigger a change. In the non-inverting configuration, when the input is higher
              than a chosen threshold, the output is high. When the input is below a different
              (lower) chosen threshold the output is low, and when the input is between
              the two levels the output retains its value. This dual threshold action is called
              hysteresis and implies that the Schmitt trigger possesses memory and can
              act as a bi-stable multi-vibrator (latch or flip-flop). There is a close relation
              between the two kinds of circuits: a Schmitt trigger can be converted into a
              latch and a latch can be converted into a Schmitt trigger.
              Schmitt trigger devices are typically used in signal conditioning applications
              to remove noise from signals used in digital circuits, particularly mechanical
              contact bounce in switches. They are also used in closed loop negative
              feedback configurations to implement relaxation oscillators, used in function
              generators and switching power supplies.

GENERAL COMMENTS
Thanks, should be given to the entire Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sports, arts and culture, Regional
Offices, Schools, Communities Candidates who wrote this examination and other stake holders.
The entries have decreased form 74 in 2024 to 54 candidates in the year 2025. .
Teachers are familiar with the content of the syllabus now guided and taught the candidates well to ensure that they
knew what to expect in the exam. Teachers should be applauded for the effort done to prepare the learners for the
examination. According to the responses of the candidates, it is clear that the whole syllabus was covered by most
centres.
According to the work assessed, one could see that the candidates tried their best to be successful in this examination
with the support of their teachers and their parents.
Good responses were received from the centres regarding the quality and standard of the answer scripts. The question
paper could be well interpreted regarding the style, language and graphics.
From the responses of the candidates on the questions, there were no problems answering the questions. However,
good responses were given for certain questions and candidates could score good marks.
Evidence also shows that quite a few candidates did not have the knowledge and skills to answer certain questions
successfully. This situation can only be mastered when more training is given to teachers on how to teach the syllabus
successfully. It can illuminate this situation. By the spread of marks for this question paper, it looks acceptable, but there
are a few of areas which need to improve.

COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

     (a) Analysis
          Candidate should not write a fictional story about the reason why the product should be made. The situation
          and information given in the paper may not simply be copied or repeated from the paper as an answer.
          Candidates should analyse the given problem. That means to study (something) closely and carefully,
          to find the nature of the given problem by a close and careful examination. How can the problem be solved.
          Appropriate factors should be considered. Candidates should think of, and record all the additional information,
          like: tools, construction, materials.

     (b) Specifications
         Candidates may not copy the specifications given in the paper.
          Candidates can generate other specifications taking into consideration of the following guideline:
          Functionality, ergonomics, aesthetics, materials and construction.
          Generic responses must be avoided. These specifications must be relatively specific. Some candidates
          stated generic specifications like “it must be safe, must look nice, etc.” Specifications must also be justified
          with reasoning.
          A specification could look as follows: E.g. “The product must be made out of aluminium, because it is light
          weight and does not corrode.”

     (c) Design solutions
         Many ideas were not in line with the criteria given. Candidates should draw the ideas according to the
         specifications given. Candidates should come up with a minimum of four possible solutions for them to be
         marked under high band. Most candidates came up with three possible solutions which made candidates to
         lose marks.
          Ideas should also be drawn three dimensionally.
          Detail should be shown in the sketches, many notes should be written.
          Measurements should be added. More than three ideas should be drawn.
          Ideas should be adequately rendered / coloured and enhanced.
          The ideas should also be evaluated.
          Communication has its own marks awarded from 0 – 4marks. Candidates should work hard on their
          sketches to get all the marks.


                                               NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                    117
    (d) Development of proposed solution
          This is the part where candidates of some centres lost valuable marks. In this section of the question paper
          the candidates should take the chosen idea and make further detailed decisions on form, materials and
          construction methods to be used in the final product. In some cases, candidates did not do a sufficient
          development of the final idea.
          This is not simply a repetition of one of the ideas recorded in the previous section.
          The candidates should show processes that are to be followed in the manufacturing and also show details
          of construction.
          Rendering / colouring should be done and measurements should be added.
          The development should also be evaluated.
          Communication showing the expected solution has its own marks awarded from 0 – 4marks. Candidates
          should work hard on their development sketches to get all the marks.

    (e) Presentation
          Candidates of some centres just gave a single view with little or no detail or notes.
          The following is expected in this question. An Isometric sketch or drawing with notes, and an Orthographic
          drawing including dimensions.

          Additional sketches can also be added to show construction detail.
          The isometric drawing or sketches should be rendered showing what the final product should look like.

          Communication has its own marks awarded from 0 – 4marks. Candidates should work hard on their
          presentation drawings of their final solution to get all the marks.

CONCLUSION
Teachers are to read and implement these comments and pointers given. This will ensure a better mark for the
candidates in future.
