       Paper 3



GENERAL COMMENTS

Centres must be commended for the completion and submission of coursework samples from all regions. The quality of
coursework for NSSCAS 2025 was generally of a better standard. There were some centres that produced coursework
that is below average. This indicates that the candidates were not correctly guided by the teacher, or that the candidates
were reluctant to follow the guidance of the teacher. Regional Offices should make sure that Centre Reports are studied
and recommendations drafted for implementation purposes are forwarded from the regions to the schools.

Regional Office should target schools that did not perform well and investigate what the reason is for the substandard
results. In the cases where teachers are not sure what is expected in the folders, they should be trained to ensure that
the candidates can be taught how to compile a folder correctly. On the other hand, if the teacher is not performing, the
principal and head of department at the school should be informed to continuously monitor the work done by the teacher
and the progress of the candidates on the project folders. If possible networking with DNEA, NIED and other regions
with Senior Education Officers as well as relevant stakeholders should be initiated to have teachers capacitated and
assisted on a regular basis. It appears at some centres, the common mistakes made during 2024, were repeated in
the 2025 design folders. This indicates that the learners were not taught correctly by the teacher. A conclusion could be
drawn that Centre Reports are not studied and recommendations not implemented by these centres. Due to the defiant
negligence by some centres, the assistance of the Regional Directors is needed to make sure that Senior Education
Officers and Circuit Inspectors study and analyse these reports and monitor that the recommendations are implemented
at schools that present Design and Technology as a subject.

It is commendable that some centres have read and adhered to the advice given is the respective centre reports. Once
again, Regional Offices, principals and HOD’s are pleaded to take the responsibility of ensuring that folders and projects
are monitored throughout the year in future, especially at the centres where the candidates performed poorly. Towards
the end of the second term the folders should be internally moderated before the marks are dispatched to DNEA for
external moderation. Regional Offices must make sure that NSSCAS schools are provided with the necessary materials,
tools and safety equipment for candidates to build quality products. DNEA observed that some centres’ projects were
compromised by the lack of adequate resources. It is shocking to observe in the photographic evidence included in
the folders, that candidates saw wooden boards on a circular saw not using a fence. Photographs show candidates
sawing wood with their fingers dangerously close to saw blad pushing wood when the blade is running. If a candidate
is to be injured, or loses a finger, under these circumstances, the teacher responsible, as well as the ministry could be
held accountable. A teacher may never let candidates work in the workshop without proper supervision. Candidates
who are not submitting sufficient photographic evidence is a problem when the projects are be moderated. The sample
of work presented for moderation was suitable in most cases and centres generally applied the assessment criteria
appropriately, although, in some cases, this was not at the correct level.

All folders must include clear photographic evidence of the artefacts, in addition to an overall view of the final product,
showing detail to support the awarding of marks.

If sufficient photographic evidence is not submitted, the candidates’ marks will be affected negatively.

COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC ASSESSMENT HEADINGS

Defining
Some of the candidates clearly stated the problem to be addressed but not all gave a concise Design Brief. Candidates
should be encouraged to complete adequate and relevant research in order to form a suitable knowledge base after
formulating the Brief. Only then can the specifications be listed. These specifications must be relatively specific and
must be justified. Some candidates stated generic specifications like “it must be safe” or “must not be big or too small”,
etc. Some candidates included points of specification, but of a generic nature which could be applied to any product.

Research

Some centres research consisted of irrelevant information that was simply written in a paragraph form. This did not lead
the candidate to an idea of what the outcome of the product should be.

Candidates should do research into similar existing products as mentioned in the Design Brief and evaluate these
products regarding cost, material, suitability etc.

                                               NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                  119
Then additional information regarding the processes, material and fittings should be researched to see what is available
locally.

Conceptualising

This is where candidates can show evidence of genuine design creativity. Imaginative and innovative handling of a good
range of concepts and ideas is of essence. Most candidates included a wide range of different ideas enhanced by clearly
annotated sketches. In some cases candidates presented a few drawings that showed too little design capabilities and
tended to follow a single concept. These ideas can be presented most successfully through neatly rendered sketches
and candidates should be encouraged to include notes and dimensions. Annotations should include comments on the
construction, joining methods and materials. Then it is important that the each idea is evaluated as to how an idea might
link to the specification. Placing photocopies of drawings in a folder is not acceptable, because they could be copied
from someone else’s work.

Development

In most cases candidates’ developments met the expected criteria, but in a few cases this part was neglected or
inadequate.

In this section of the folder the candidates should take only the chosen idea and make further detailed decisions on
form, materials and construction methods to be used in the final product. Ideas should be fully developed with good
attention to detail. Candidates are expected to show deep insight and good command of related knowledge. In some
cases candidates found it difficult to apply, and in these cases the final ideas were simply a repetition of one of the
ideas recorded in the previous section. Candidates are expected to also illustrate every step of production with notes
describing the action.

In most cases the final drawings of the Design Solution were generally well-presented and gave sufficient information
with regards to the manufacturing of the product.

Presentation

Candidates were expected to show refined graphical skills including fluent freehand and precise measured drawings.
Most centres could produce drawings with good command of rendering and other enhancement which is commendable.
Centres in the top band produced excellent communication skills and had their work well managed and attractively laid
out.

The following is expected: An isometric drawing / sketch with dimensions and notes. (rendered), an exploded view
(rendered) an orthographic drawing showing detailed dimensions. Then also a cutting list, other material list, a table
showing time planning and a flowchart showing the sequential steps of production.

Product realization (Control; Technical; Product)

Photographic evidence showed that some candidates were able to work on their own and able to work at an acceptable
standard of construction and finish to the extent that the end product could be used. Sadly, some centres could not
provide sufficient photographic evidence to substantiate the credibility of the folders. Some photographic evidence
is just a mere posing activity and no real action is seen which made it difficult for the moderator to clearly distinguish
various safe approaches and processes from the photos.

Notably, photographic evidence showed some candidates operating power tools (such as angle grinders) without the
required protective clothing (leather gloves, eye protection), an unsafe practise that should be prohibited. The teacher
may not allow the candidates to work in

Clear photos of the candidate doing all the processes, as well as clear photos showing the final product. The candidate
must be seen working in the pictures.

Testing and Evaluation

Some candidates included photographic evidence to show the testing of the product, which is commendable. They are,
however, encouraged to link the outcome of the original specifications and make objective judgements on the success
of their products. The section should also include suggestions for further modifications or possible future improvements.
Therefore, centres are implored to ensure that specifications are fully evaluated and tested in this section, which will
guarantee maximum marks for the candidates.




                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     120
Conclusion

Even though the coursework received from the centres for NSSCAS was at a high standard in most cases, it is clear that
centres offering NSSCAS Design and Technology for 2025 as a subject, and failed to achieve good marks, need to get
a d training to standardize the general understanding on the different sub-topics for the design folders.

   Answer
   An (5 marks)
   Lower economic growth in South Africa and Europe                        (2/3)
   •   Exports to South Africa and Europe will decrease because the demand
       for Namibian goods are likely to be less.
   •   Imports from South Africa and Europe to Namibia might have also
       decreased because fewer products were produced in those countries.
   •   Fewer exports will lower the net exports (X-M) of Namibia, decreasing
       aggregate demand (AD)/real GDP of Namibia.
   •   Fewer firms from South Africa and Europe are likely to invest in
       Namibia.
   Higher fuel prices                                                                                  (3/2)
   •   Higher fuel prices lead to cost-push inflation/increasing the production
       costs of firms.
   •   Increased production costs because of higher fuel prices, will lead to a
       decrease in the aggregate supply (AS)/real GDP of Namibia.
   •   Higher fuel prices will increase the price of goods, decrease the
       purchasing power on consumers, decreasing AD.  (Very likely as goods
       are transported over long distances in Namibia.)
   •   Decreasing competitiveness of Namibian products globally.
   •   AD might also decrease further, as consumers spend more on fuel,
       leaving less disposable income to spend on other goods and services.
   •   Lower AD causes firms to invest less, decreasing AS further.

4 (a)  Learners who did not explain how a floating and fixed exchange rate is determined, did not score application
       marks.
    Answer                                                                           8
    Kn (Up to 3 marks)
    •   Exchange rate is the price/value of one currency, in terms of another
        currency. (1)
    •   Floating exchange rate is determined by the market forces of demand
        and supply. (1)
    •   Fixed exchange rate is set by the government/maintained by the
        central bank. (1)
    Ap (Up to 2 marks)
    •   The price of a currency in a floating exchange rate is determined
        where the demand for a currency equals the supply of a currency/
        demand and supply intersect. (1)
    •   the central bank will set the fixed exchange rate by intervening in
        foreign exchange market/changing the rate of the interest. (1)
    An (Up to 3 marks)
    Changes of a floating exchange rate
    •   Depreciation is a decrease in the international price of a currency
        caused by market forces/decrease in demand and/or increase in supply
        of a currency. (1)
    •   Appreciation is an increase in the international price of a currency
        caused by market forces/increase in demand and/or decrease in supply
        of a currency. (1)
    Changes of a fixed exchange rate
    •   Devaluation is a decision by the government to lower the international
        price of a currency. (1)
    •   Revaluation is a decision by the government to raise the international
        price of a currency. (1)                                         Any three

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
Although more learners attempted to evaluate their answers, they still need to develop their evaluation skills fully.

Learners should be encouraged to answer the questions in the context it is asked. They should refrain from merely

General Comments
•       The 2025 AS examination was similar to previous examinations in all respects.
•       The candidates’ overall performance was, by and large, average to below average.
•       In general, many candidates failed to answer in complete, coherent and grammatically correct sentences.  Candidates
        committed numerous language errors, including grammatical and spelling errors.  This was compounded by illegible
        handwritings.
•       Some candidates used pencil in their answer scripts, contrary to the instructions on the cover page of the question
        paper.
•       Some candidates wrote lengthy responses that were not commensurate with the space provided; as a result, their
        answers overlapped into the space for the next question.
•       The candidates generally structured Section B (email) in proper paragraphs, which was pleasing to note.

This task elicited a mixed response from the candidates.   However, there were very few exceptionally impressive
responses.  The majority of candidates struggled to explain the different types of memories.  Some responses were
not derived from the text.  Section B is a directed part of the examination, guided by the prompts or ideas provided in
the question.  This section offers candidates an opportunity to score fair to high marks if they base their responses on
information in the text.  There were also numerous grammatical errors, ranging from poor subject-verb agreement and
spelling to issues with sentence structure.

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS

Teachers are encouraged and advised to conscientise learners that there is only one correct answer in Section A: Part
1 (Multiple-Choice).  There are always distractors which may cause the learners to reconsider their choices.  Learners
need to take time to carefully consider the options and eliminate the incorrect ones.

Learners should be guided to present their responses in their own words when instructed to do so, or they should
paraphrase.  Teachers should expose learners to as many reading comprehension passages as possible.  They should
also expose learners to directed writing activities, helping them identify relevant content ideas.  Teachers should assist
learners in practicing adherence to word limits where specified, as they often write irrelevant content that can detract
from otherwise good responses if they exceed the word limit.  Learners should be made aware that their examination
scripts represent their ideas and responses and should, therefore, ensure that ideas and answers are clearly organised.

Learners should be helped, guided and taught how to respond to Section B questions in order to be empowered with the
correct techniques of answering questions.  Teachers may also spend more time helping learners practice using proper
sentence structures such as subject>verb>object.  Some AS LEVEL candidates, shockingly struggled to express ideas
clearly in meaningful sentences.

On a brighter note, there is clear evidence that some learners from certain centres are well taught and prepared for the
AS examination. The hope is that all centres or schools could do the same.

       Paper 2




GENERAL COMMENTS

There was an improvement in the quality of candidates’ work this year, although there are still some concerns:
•    The lack of punctuation is becoming an issue.
•    In some places, punctuation is used incorrectly, leading to poor sentence structure.
•    Contractions, slang and over-generalisation should be addressed.
•    The use of a lowercase “i” when referring to oneself is widespread.
•    Errors of subject-verb agreement are also becoming increasingly prominent.
•    The repetition of the infinitive “to go work”, “to go look” had occurred in many scripts.  
•    The use of idioms and proverbs should be applied carefully.
•    Too many essays are still exceeding the word count.
•     Sloppy handwriting hampers understanding and reading, which could result in a poor mark.
•    Candidates are frequently starting sentences with dangling or unrelated participle, such as “Running down the
     road, I saw..”, which makes grammar weaker.
The use of the prefix “in” joined with the use of “in” as a preposition is common among candidates, for example:
“inlove” “infront” “inconclusion”, etc. Some teachers seem to ignore this clumsy error. Similarly, words such as “aswell”,
“eachother”,” eventhough”, are not being picked up.
Candidates seem not to know the difference between “were” and “where”, “its” and “it’s”, “their” and “there” “advise”
and”advice”, “practise” and “practice”. These issues should be addressed. Slang such as “gonna” and “wanna” is
unacceptable in standard English. Common words are spelled incorrectly. Negligence seems to play a role here.
Sentences should not begin with “so”. Words such as “like” and “nice” should be avoided.
Essays are sometimes based on themes rather than on the specific topics.   Learners need to be taught to answer
the question and not write broadly on the theme or field.  Failure to adhere to this will result in a poor mark, if any.
Sometimes, large parts of the plot are crossed out which makes reading and understanding difficult.
Many candidates deliberately wrote in very small handwriting in order to fit in a plot that far exceeded the word count.
This practice should be addressed by teachers, as it if unfair to candidates who adhere to the word limit. In many cases,
this approach is futile, as candidates penalise themselves through repetitive ideas, resulting in a weak plot in anyway.


COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Question 1: Citizenship

It should be mandatory for all citizens aged eighteen and above to vote in local and national elections. Outline and
explain your views.

This was the compulsory question and was attempted with mixed results. The meaning of “mandatory” appeared to
be problematic, as many candidates misinterpreted the question. The question required a discussion or argument
about whether voting should be mandatory.   Many candidates wrote broadly about the field of “Citizenship” rather
than addressing the specific topic or the concept of voting as a right or responsibility.  The more successful candidates
understood that the focus was on voters being “forced” to vote, which was the issue they needed to discuss. It was not
enough for candidates simply to repeat the topic. In some cases, the development of ideas did not clearly show the
candidates’ viewpoints, resulting in confusion regarding the application of the concept of mandatory or forced voting.

Question 2: Social trends

The influence of the media on teenagers can deprive them of having heathy relationships and developing social skills.
How far do you agree?

This was a very popular choice, with mixed results.  Candidates should have argued the influence of the media on
relationships and social skills, rather than generalising about social media itself. Many candidates discussed social
trends instead of the effect of media on teenagers. The disadvantages and disadvantages of social media were covered
in many essays. Most essays focused on social media rather than media in general. Many candidates had litttle
understanding of what social skills are. Some candidates, however, were able to produce strong essays that discussed
the effects of media on the development of social skills and on building healthy relationships.



                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     142
Question 3: The Arts

“My shocking revelation about a world-famous piece of art shattered relationships between nations, and I became a
wanted person.” Tell your story.

A few candidates attempted this topic, which was also the most misinterpreted. Candidates were expected to discuss
how the revelation of a famous art piece caused worldwide turmoil and led to the artist becoming a wanted person.
Instead, many plots told a success story. General knowledge of the arts was severely lacking; as a result, the Mona
Lisa was the only painting most candidates could think of.  Some plots focused on the theft or destruction of an art piece.  
This approach led to weak results.

Question 4: Travel and Transport

The economic progress of a country is determined by the quality of its infrastructure. What are your views?

This topic was attempted by a few candidates, with mixed results. Candidates should have elaborated on how good
infrastructure leads to income and, as a result, economical progress. They needed to link quality infrastructure to
economic development. Many candidates confused the concept of “economic progress” and “quality infrastructure”.
Many had little understanding of what “quality infrastucture” entails. Some plots focused on tourism, travel and transport
in general, which resulted in poor marks.

Question 5: Language and communication

His powerful words convinced me that I had not failed but that I had gained valuable experience. Relate the event that
led to this realisation.

This was the most successful topic. Candidates were expected to relate a story in which they attempted something,
failed and were encouraged by someone’s powerful words to achieve success. Many did not link the two main ideas.
Some even produced lengthy motivational speeches or simply discussed language as a tool. A few plots were also
mundane.

Positive suggestions to teachers

Language lessons are crucial.  Concord, tenses and style must be taught and practised.  Greater general knowledge
is also needed.

Emphasis on reading, comprehension and interpretation skills is vitally important. Extensive reading expose learners
to sophisticated and correct use of language, which they can absorb and incorporate into their own writing. Reading is
key.  Learners should be encouraged to summarise the articles they have read.

Spelling is a major concern.   Extensive reading will help address this.   Learners should avoid or practise not using
colloquialisms such as kids, guys. They should also avoid tailor-made responses; it is evident that some learners write
essays beforehand and then try to force them into a particular field or theme.  Word limits must be strictly adhered to.

Learners must number their topics.  Many fail to do so, leaving the examiner to figure out which topic was developed.

Expressions such as “very crucial”, “very essential” should be avoided.

Use the correct pronoun. DO NOT WRITE, for example, “They still vote for whoever you want”.

Learners lack general knowledge, and mundane discussions or plots result in poor marks.  Accurate sentence structures
must be practised, and paragraphing should also be emphasised. The appropriate use of tenses needs to be taught.

      AOD - Evaluation, Judgement and Decision-making

      Award 1 mark for decision made on the viability of green enterprises in Namibia
      Award 4 marks for the evaluation on the viability of green enterprises in Namibia


      How green enterprises are viable in Namibia
      Demand/market share: Green enterprises in Namibia are becoming increasingly viable due to a growing
      market demand for sustainable and environmentally-friendly products and services. Consumers are
      becoming more conscious of their environmental footprint and are actively seeking out products as well as
      services that are eco-friendly.
      The market size for green enterprises in Namibia is relatively small compared to other countries, but
      it is steadily growing as awareness about environmental issues increases. There is a niche market of
      environmentally-conscious consumers who are willing to pay a premium for green products and services.

      Competition: Competition in the green enterprise sector in Namibia is relatively low compared to other
      industries, providing opportunities for new enterprises to enter the market and establish themselves.
      However, as awareness about environmental issues grows, competition is likely to increase, so it is
      important for green enterprises to differentiate themselves and offer unique products or services.

      Seasonality: Seasonality can also impact on the viability of green enterprises in Namibia, as certain
      products or services may be more in demand during specific times of the year. For example, renewable
      energy solutions may be more popular during the dry season when there is more sunlight for solar power
      generation.

      How green enterprises are not viable in Namibia
      Demand: market demand for green products and services in Namibia may be limited. While there is a
      growing global trend towards sustainability and environmental consciousness, the market in Namibia may
      not be as developed or receptive to green products and services. This could be due to a lack of awareness
      or education about the benefits of green products, as well as willingness to pay premium prices for
      environmentally-friendly options. As a result, green enterprises may struggle to attract enough customers to
      sustain their enterprise.

      The size of the market in Namibia may be relatively small compared to other countries. This could limit the
      potential customer base for green enterprises, making it difficult for them to achieve economies of scale and
      compete effectively with larger, more established enterprises.

      Competition: Competition in the green sector in Namibia may also be fierce, as more companies begin

                                          NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
148
           to offer environmentally-friendly products and services. This could lead to price wars and reduced profit
           margins for green enterprises, making it challenging for them to stay afloat.
           Seasonality: Seasonality could also pose a challenge for green enterprises in Namibia. Certain products
           or services may be more in demand during specific times of the year, leading to fluctuations in revenue and
           cash flow. This unpredictability could make it difficult for green enterprises to plan and budget effectively,
           potentially leading to financial instability.
           Accept other relevant answers

      Model answer

      Green enterprise is an enterprise with minimal negative impact on the global and local environment, community
      and economy. According to the case study, 45% of the Namibian population is willing to pay for eco-friendly
      products, which represents over 1 million people, which implies that there is high demand for green products
      which leads to high sales and profits. However, with the increase in demand, the enterprise may not meet the
      customers demand leaving the customers dissatisfied which leads to a decrease in the customers’ base.

      Moreover, in Namibia there is relatively low competition in the green enterprise sector, providing opportunities
      for new enterprises to enter the market and establish themselves. However, as the green enterprise sector
      continues to grow, the competition is likely to increase, thus the green enterprise should differentiate itself by
      adding value and offer unique products or services to customers.

      Green enterprises benefit from aligning with global sustainability trends, which enhances their credibility and
      access to international markets. Locally, they contribute to reducing environmental degradation while creating
      jobs in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture and eco-tourism. The educated and environmentally conscious
      population further supports innovation, ensuring that enterprises can introduce new products as well as services
      with confidence in market acceptance.

      Green enterprise in Namibia is viable because there is a high demand for eco-friendly products because
      people are becoming more conscious of their environmental footprint so are actively seeking out products and
      services that are eco-friendly with almost half of the population willing to buy eco-friendly products as per data
      of 45%. While challenges such as financing and infrastructure remain, the combination of market demand and
      environmental awareness positions Namibia as viable for sustainable enterprises. Green enterprises are not only
      economically promising but also essential for ensuring long-term ecological balance in the country.


8.   Evaluate whether the Acts that govern the utilization of natural resources in Namibia are beneficial
     to an entrepreneur.
     Comments on specific question:
     Most candidates could not explain the Acts nor outline the Acts that govern the utilisation of natural resources.
     Some candidates defined sustainable use of natural resources instead. Most candidates could not link the specific
     Acts to the enterprises e.g Rossing mine is governed by the Mineral Act 33 of 1992. Some candidates gave three
     enterprises and three Acts that apply to all of them instead of giving one enterprise and all the Acts that governs it.

     Answers should include:
     -  An explanation of the Acts that govern the utilization of natural resources in Namibia.
     -  Examples from an enterprise to support a candidate’s answer.
     -  An analysis of the benefits and costs to an entrepreneur of these Acts.
     -  An evaluation and decision on whether the Acts are beneficial to an entrepreneur or not.

      AO     Description                                                                                      Marks

      A      An explanation of the Acts that govern the utilization of natural resources in Namibia           1–2
      0      No creditable content                                                                              0

     Correct answers:
     Knowledge (AOA)
     Acts that govern the utilisation of natural resources in Namibia regulate the exploration, extraction and management
     of minerals, forest, water resources and wildlife in Namibia. They aim to ensure sustainable development,
     conservation and responsible utilization of the country’s natural resources while also protecting the environment and
     biodiversity. Compliance with these Acts is necessary for any individual or organization involved in the exploitation
     of natural resources in Namibia.
     Acts that govern the utilisation of natural resources in Namibia: Forest Act 12 of 2001, Mineral Act 33 0f 1992, Water

                                                NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                    149
resources management Act 2013.

Application (AOB): examples from an enterprise
Namdeb Diamond Corporation:
-  The enterprise adheres to the Mineral Act 33 of 1992 by securing a mining licence, conducting responsible
   exploration of minerals and extraction, complying with environmental and safety regulation within the mine.
-  The enterprise also adheres to the Environmental Management Act and the Forest Act 12 of 2001, which
   regulate the extraction of raw materials and the conservation of natural resources, including forests by
   implementation and maintain a robust Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP), conduct regular
   impact assessments and ensuring compliance with all permit conditions as well as mitigation measure.
-  Namdeb adheres to the Water Resource Management Act of 2013

AOC: Analyses of the main benefits and costs to an entrepreneur of these Acts. Benefits to an entrepreneur
of these Acts:
-    The Acts provide clear guidelines and regulations for entrepreneurs regarding the sustainable utilization of
     natural resources. As a result, this clarity can help entrepreneurs navigate legal requirements and reduce
     uncertainty in their operations.
-    The Acts prioritize environmental protection, ensuring that natural resources are utilized in a sustainable
     manner. As a result, this can enhance the long-term viability of entrepreneurial ventures by safeguarding
     ecosystems and preventing resource depletion.
-    Entrepreneurs can gain access to natural resources through legal channels defined in the Acts, such as
     obtaining mining licences or water rights. As a result, this access can enable them to establish and grow
     enterprises reliant on these resources.
-    Adhering to regulations outlined in the Acts can enhance the credibility of entrepreneurial ventures in the market.
     As a result, compliance with environmental and resource management laws may attract environmentally
     conscious consumers and investors
-    Entrepreneurs who comply with relevant Acts may access government support, incentives or subsidies aimed
     at promoting sustainable resource utilization, as a result, this support can facilitate enterprise growth and
     mitigate financial risks.

Costs to an entrepreneur of these Acts:
-  Ensuring compliance with the Acts may involve significant administrative and operational costs for entrepreneurs,
   as a result, this includes expenses related to obtaining permits, conducting environmental assessments and
   implementing mitigation measures.
-  Strict regulatory requirements can impose a burden on entrepreneurs, especially small enterprises with limited
   resources, as a result, compliance may require additional time, effort and expertise, diverting resources away
   from core enterprise activities.
-  The Acts may impose limitations or quotas on the utilization of natural resources, potentially restricting
   entrepreneurial activities, as a result, entrepreneurs may face challenges in scaling operations or accessing
   sufficient resources to meet market demand.
-  Non-compliance with the Acts can result in legal consequences, including fines, penalties or even suspension
   of enterprise operations. As a result, entrepreneurs bear the risk of legal liabilities if they fail to adhere to
   regulatory requirements.
-  Strict regulatory standards may create a competitive disadvantage for entrepreneurs operating in industries
   reliant on natural resources. As a result, compliance costs can increase production expenses, making it
   challenging to compete with enterprises in less regulated jurisdictions.

AOD: An evaluation and decision on whether the Acts are beneficial to an entrepreneur or not.

Agrees that the acts are beneficial to entrepreneurs
-   Entrepreneurs operate in a responsible and environmentally-friendly manner
-   Entrepreneurs are given a clear understanding of the legal framework within which they can operate
-   Acts create investment opportunities for entrepreneurs in sectors such as mining, agriculture and tourism
-   They promote accountability and responsible enterprise practices that are beneficial to entrepreneurs now
   and in the future

Disagrees that the acts are not beneficial to entrepreneurs
-   Restrict the amount or type of natural resources that an entrepreneur can access, potentially limiting the ability
    to fully utilize resources
-   Require entrepreneurs to go through lengthy and expensive permitting processes in order to use natural
    resources

-   Acts make it difficult for them to start or expand their enterprises, making it not beneficial to entrepreneurs.
-   Acts may be subject to frequent changes or interpretation, creating uncertainty for entrepreneurs and making
   it difficult for them to plan or make investments in utilizing natural resources
-   Acts may not provide sufficient incentives for entrepreneurs to adopt sustainable practices in their utilization of
    natural resources.
Agree and disagree that the Acts are not beneficial to entrepreneurs
-   Entrepreneurs operate in a responsible and environmentally-friendly manner, BUT the Acts restrict the amount
    or type of natural resources that an entrepreneur can access, potentially limiting his/her ability to fully utilise
    these resourcefully
-   Entrepreneurs are given a clear understanding of the legal framework within which they can operate, BUT the
    Acts make it difficult for them to start or expand their enterprises, making them not beneficial to entrepreneurs.

Accept other relevant answers
    Model answer: Rossing Uranium Mine

    The utilisation of natural resources in Namibia is governed by several Acts, notably the Minerals (Prospecting
    and Mining) Act 33 of 1992, the Water Resources Management Act 11 of 2013, and the Forest Act 12 of 2001.
    Rössing Uranium Mine, a mine in Namibia is adhering to these Acts which regulate its mining rights, water use
    and environmental protection. Rössing adheres to these laws through licensing, water management schemes
    and biodiversity conservation initiatives.
    The Minerals (Prospecting and Mining) Act 33 of 1992: The Minerals Act governs the exploration and exploitation
    of Namibia’s mineral resources. It requires enterprises to obtain mining licenses, conduct Environmental Impact
    Assessments (EIAs), and submit Environmental Management Plans (EMPs).
    Rössing Uranium Mine operates under mining licenses issued by the Ministry of Mines and Energy. The mine
    prepares EMPs and EIAs before expansions or new projects. It reports production, safety and compliance
    measures to authorities, ensuring transparency and accountability. Through these measures, Rössing
    demonstrates adherence to the Minerals Act by balancing economic extraction with environmental safeguards.
    Water is a scarce resource in Namibia, making its management critical. The Water Resources Management
    Act 11 of 2013 regulates its use, and conservation of water resources, requiring permits thereby promoting
    sustainable practices. Rössing Uranium Mine relies on NamWater’s supply scheme, which is regulated under the
    Act. The mine implements water recycling and treatment systems to minimise wastage. Continuous monitoring
    ensures that water discharged meets legal quality standards. By adopting efficient water management practices,
    Rössing aligns with the Act’s objectives of sustainability and pollution control.
    Although Namibia is largely arid, forest and vegetation resources remain vital for biodiversity and environmental
    health. The Forest Act 12 of 2001provides for conservation, fire prevention, and sustainable use of forest produce.
    Rössing Uranium Mine undertakes biodiversity monitoring and vegetation management programs. Rehabilitation
    projects include replanting indigenous species in disturbed areas. Fire prevention measures are enforced to
    comply with forest fire control provisions. These initiatives reflect Rössing’s commitment to environmental
    stewardship under the Forest Act.
    Obtaining mining licenses, water permits and environmental approvals under the Acts is costly since it includes
    legal fees, environmental studies and ongoing audits. The Acts impose limits on water usage, land use and
    vegetation clearance. These restrictions can slow down expansion projects and reduce operational flexibility.
    The Forest Act and Minerals Act require rehabilitation of mined land and biodiversity monitoring. This adds long-
    term costs for replanting, soil stabilisation and environmental reporting.
    However, these Acts ensure resources are not depleted which secures the mine’s long-term viability and
    operational continuity. Compliance with legislation builds trust with government, communities, and international
    stakeholders. It enhances the mine’s reputation and reduces conflict. Adhering to the Acts minimises pollution,
    land degradation and ecological damage. This reduces liability risks and potential penalties, while aligning with
    global sustainability standards.
    While the Acts impose financial and operational costs, they also come with benefits by ensuring sustainability,
    protecting the environment and strengthening stakeholder relations. For Rössing Uranium Mine, the balance
    leans toward long-term gains, as compliance secures both continued access to resources and international
    credibility in the uranium market.
    It is, therefore, evident that the Acts that govern the utilisation of natural resources are beneficial to the
    entrepreneurs. When Rossing Uranium complies with the Acts, it leads to building a good reputation for the
    enterprise, which can attract investors who may provide extra funds to expand the mine and, therefore, the
    enterprise will be sustained in the long run. Since Rossing Uranium is a profit-driven enterprise, it may not
    fully comply with the Acts, as the government controls the volume of minerals to be extracted which leads to
    lower productivity and, therefore, Rossing mine might experience low sales which will result in lower profit.
    Consequently, non-compliance may lead to penalties, suspension or a permit revoked.

Positive suggestions to teachers:
-   Teachers should teach all the specific objectives in the syllabus.
-   Teachers should see to it that learners have fully mastered the assessment objectives.
-   Teachers should discourage learners from listing when answering questions, especially evaluation questions.
-   Candidates should refrain from repeating positive or negative analysis when justifying their decisions(AOD).
Specific positive suggestions:
AOA
-  Teachers are encouraged to provide enough notes to learners on all specific objectives for an AOA question.
-  Teachers must reinforce core entrepreneurial concepts through structured lessons and revision activities.
AOB
-  Encourage learners to connect classroom learning with local entrepreneurial activities, making application
   more authentic and relevant.
-  Provide learners with opportunities to apply theoretical knowledge to practical scenarios, such as simulated
   enterprise projects or role-play exercises.
AOC
-  Use group discussions, debates and comparative case studies to sharpen analytical skills.
-  Encourage learners to support their analysis with evidence, moving beyond description to deeper reasoning.
AOD
-  Teach learners to justify their answers with evidence, moving beyond description to deeper analysis.
-  Guide learners to weigh alternative strategies, considering risks, costs and benefits before making decisions.
-  Provide structured opportunities for learners to justify their recommendations with logical arguments and
   supporting data.

Overall recommendation
-  Teachers should adopt a balanced approach, ensuring that learners are trained across all four assessment
   objectives rather than focusing on some.
-  Regular formative assessments can help identify strengths and areas for improvement early.
-  Positive reinforcement and celebrating small successes will motivate learners to engage more deeply with
   each assessment objective.

    more customers as they would want to buy quality products and receive good customer care (1).
    However, training comes with costs. One of the main costs is the financial constraint that comes with training
    in terms of expertise and training materials (1). Jumbo Charcoal will need to allocate budgets for the trainers,
    technology platforms or books to be used which can reduce the sales and revenue of the enterprise as money will
    be spent on the training needs (1).
    Problem experienced and wrong answers:
    Some learners gave a one-sided analysis focusing only on either the benefit or the cost, while it should be on both
    sides. Analysis should be on the element of the marketing mix or the two examples given, two analysis points.
    (2 x 2 = 4 marks)

5   Analyses of sustainable practices
    Assessment Objective A: Knowledge and understanding (2 marks).
    Specific comment on the question
    Well answered, as most candidates scored full marks for stating two sustainable practices.
    How the question is marked:
    Practice 1 to sustain enterprise opportunity in the future stated: 1 mark.
    Practice 2 to sustain enterprise opportunity in the future stated: 1 mark.
    Expected answers:
    Sustainable practices are: triple bottom line, sustainable use of resources, operational efficiency, good customer
    service, building a reputable and trustworthy brand.
    Assessment Objective B: Application and Investigation: 6 marks
    Specific comment on question
    Fairly well answered although the majority of the candidates only scored 2 marks, here as they gave a basic
    application of how their stated techniques will sustain their enterprise in the future. Candidates could not indicate
    in their application how the chosen techniques could lead to enterprise sustainability.
    How question is marked:
    The first technique to sustain enterprise opportunity in the future stated.
    Application on how the technique under the first practice will be implemented in the solution chosen to sustain the
    enterprise in the future: maximum of 3 marks
    The second technique to sustain enterprise opportunity in the future stated.
    Application on how the technique under the second practice will be implemented in the solution chosen to sustain
    the enterprise in the future: maximum of 3 marks
    2 x 1 mark: basic application: only describes how it will be applied.
    2 x 2 marks: detailed application: describes and explains how practice or technique will be applied.

                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                157
2 x 3 marks: more detailed application: describes and explains how practice or technique will be applied and how
this application will allow the enterprise to be a success in the future.
Expected correct example of an application of a technique.
Application:
Practice 1: Sustainable use of resources: In the production of briquettes, Jumbo Charcoal can adopt sustainable
use of resources by prioritising recycling and renewable inputs. Instead of relying solely on fresh wood, the company
can collect agricultural wastes such as maize stalks, peanut shells or sawdust from local carpentry workshops,
turning what would otherwise be discarded into valuable products. This approach reduces deforestation, minimizes
waste, and lowers carbon emissions while ensuring a steady supply of raw materials. Ultimately, sustainable
resource use not only protects the environment but also strengthens the company’s long-term resilience, positioning
Jumbo Charcoal as a responsible brand that meets customer demand while safeguarding future generations.
There are no marks awarded for knowledge: donation. Marks are only awarded for the application, therefore,
learners should ensure they explain in detail.
Problem experienced and wrong answers:
Candidates applied one technique only. Some only gave a basic description of how they will apply their technique
to their enterprises, while others analysed instead of applying.
Some candidates only gave one practice and gave two techniques for that practice.
Assessment Objective C: Analysis: 8 marks
Specific comment on question
Fairly well answered although majority of the candidates analysed, but could not analyse in more detail, allowing
them to score a maximum of 4 marks only.
How the question is marked:
Practice 1 to sustain enterprise opportunity in the future stated.
Analysis of one cost: 2 marks and one benefit : 2 marks of the application on how the practice will be implemented
in the solution chosen to sustain the enterprise in the future.
Practice 2 to sustain enterprise opportunity in the future stated.
Analysis of one cost: 2 marks and one benefit: 2 marks of the application on how the practice will be implemented
in the solution chosen to sustain the enterprise in the future.
1 x 1 x 1 x 1 mark: basic analysis
2 x 2 x 2 x 2 marks: detailed analysis
Expected correct example of answer:
For Jumbo Charcoal, adopting sustainable use of resources in briquette production involves both a cost and
a benefit. The key benefit, however, is the long-term resilience and market advantage gained by reducing
deforestation, lowering carbon emissions, and appealing to environmentally conscious customers. This not only
safeguards natural resources but also strengthens Jumbo Charcoal’s reputation as a responsible brand, ensuring
steady demand and competitiveness in the future.
Indicate how the enterprise will be sustained in the long run. The technique should lead to growth of the
enterprise
The main cost lies in the initial investment required to shift toward eco-friendly practices, such as sourcing
agricultural waste instead of fresh wood and training staff in sustainable methods. These changes require money
and time before results are visible.
Indicate that when an enterprise does not consider the certain technique there is no sustainability
The key benefit, however, is the long-term resilience and market advantage gained by reducing deforestation,
lowering carbon emissions and appealing to environmentally conscious customers. This not only safeguards
natural resources but also strengthens Jumbo Charcoal’s reputation as a responsible brand, ensuring steady

NB: Sustainability should focus on the enterprise, how the enterprise will survive over the years or what is

Problem experienced and wrong answers:
Candidates could not explain how the technique will sustain the enterprises in the long run, but explained how

Example:
Good customer care: good customer care can play a crucial role in ensuring Jumbo Charcoal’s sustainability in
the future by building trust, loyalty and long-term relationships with its customers. When customers feel valued
through responsive service, clear communication and consistent product quality, they are more likely to remain
loyal and recommend the brand to others, which reduces marketing costs and stabilises demand. At the same time,
strong customer care allows Jumbo Charcoal to gather feedback on its sustainable briquette production practices,

     helping the company refine processes and align with consumer expectations for eco-friendly products. The main
     benefit is the creation of a resilient customer base that supports the company’s sustainable mission, ensuring both
     profitability and environmental responsibility in the long run. This becomes a more detailed analysis of a benefit
     which warrants another mark.

     Assessment Objective B: Application and Investigation (2 marks)
     Specific comment on question.
     Well answered as the majority of the candidates scored two marks as they applied the resources to their enterprise
     operations.
     How question is marked:
     First description of how the resource available will be used in a learner's chosen idea: 1 mark
     Second description of how the resource available will be used in a learner's chosen idea: 1 mark

     Expected correct example of application of resources to enterprise.
     Availability of funds: there are funds available for green enterprises in Namibia and Jumbo Charcoal will have to
     apply for funding from the Environmental Investment Fund (EIF). The funding will assist the enterprise to pay for
     operational costs. (1)

     Availability of labour: the unemployment rate in Namibia is very high among the youth, therefore, employing
     people to work for Jumbo Charcoal to produce briquettes will not be difficult. (1)

     Problem experienced and wrong answers:
     Some candidates could not apply the two resources and explain how they could easily acquire them. Some could
     only apply one resource instead of two.

     Assessment Objective D: Evaluation, Judgment and Decision-making: 4 marks
     Specific comment on question
     Fairly well answered as the majority of candidates scored 3 marks for making a choice (1) and giving a basic
     justification using two resources (2) why they made their choice. They could not give a detailed justification for them
     to score all 4 marks. Some candidates did not make a choice at all and, hence, lost all 4 marks. Some candidates
     justified using the factors of viability.
     How question is marked:
     Whether a chosen idea is feasible or not feasible/ or implied that it is feasible or not feasible by evaluation of the
     resources applied in a chosen idea is granted. (1 mark)
     Justification of why the learner's chosen idea is feasible or not feasible using the cost benefit analysis of the
     resources applied in a chosen solution. (1, 2 or 3 marks)
     Expected correct example of a choice made and an evaluation using two resources (paragraph)
     Choice made: Briquette production is feasible. (1)
     Evaluation
     Briquette production by Jumbo Charcoal is feasible because they can easily obtain funds from the Environmental
     Investment Fund (EIF) since they offer grants and support initiatives in waste management as well as Green
     projects in Namibia. For Jumbo Charcoal, which already operates as Namibia’s largest exporter of barbecue
     charcoal, the green initiative angle strengthens its eligibility for funding. Briquette production fits neatly into this
     framework because it adds value to existing charcoal operations, reduces waste and promotes efficient energy
     use. However, the availability of green imitative funding is conditional to sustainability compliance and it is such a
     lengthy and complex process to meet the funding requirements.
     Labour availability for Jumbo Charcoal in Namibia is relatively strong, supported by rural employment opportunities
     and a high rate of youth unemployment, so it will be easier for Jumbo Charcoal to secure labour for briquette
     production because the charcoal industry already employs thousands of rural workers, since it does not require
     skilled workers. However, due to the physically demanding work, often involving long hours outdoors, exposure
     to dust and smoke, as well as repetitive manual task some workers may prefer alternative employment in sectors
     where conditions are less harsh.
     1 mark: Basic evaluation using 1 resource
     2 marks: Basic evaluation using 2 resources
     3 marks: Detailed evaluation using 2 resources.

     Problem experienced and wrong answers:
     The majority of the candidates could not evaluate, but only repeated what they had written in the application. Some
     candidates gave a one-sided justification with benefits only and no cost.

                                                                                                                   159
7.   Assessment Objective B: Application and Investigation: 2 marks
     Specific comment on question
     Fairly well answered as most candidates could not reference correctly using APA as a prescribed format.
     How question is marked:
     Referencing using APA style: 1 mark
     Consistent APA referencing: 1 mark
     Using any 3 sources even if not APA referenced: 1 mark
     Appropriate presentation of work if layout has most of the proper headings: 1 mark

     Expected correct example of an answer:
     Surname, Initial. Year of publication. The title of the book. Town: Publisher.
     Siyanga, R. 2022. Excellent Entrepreneurship grade 12 AS level learners’ book. Windhoek: Zebra Publishing
     Problems experienced and wrong answers:
     Most of the candidates do not know how to use APA referencing and did not consistently reference their work using
     the APA style of referencing. Some candidates did not have any in-text citation to support the sources that they
     referenced at the end.

     POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS:
     • Encourage learners to adopt the new report format or layout, ensuring they write in paragraphs rather than
       listing ideas. Subheadings such as AOA, AOB, AOC, and AOD should no longer appear in reports. Instead,
       learners should structure their work using: Introduction, Findings, Analysis of the Marketing Mix, Analysis of
       Sustainable Practices, Conclusion and Referencing.
     •   Ensure the correct Marking Grid is applied. Some teachers have mistakenly used the old grid with 3 marks and
         (3 marks) allocated for the conclusion. Please use the updated grid, which allocates 2 marks and 4 marks for
         the conclusion.
     •   Provide clear guidance to learners on conducting research into three different enterprises. Learners should
         then select the enterprise they consider most suitable and prepare a detailed report on it.
     •   Support learners in identifying opportunities that directly connect to the problems they have highlighted.
     •   Guide learners in applying their chosen opportunity to reduce or address the identified problem effectively.
     •   Emphasise the importance of detailed analysis, including:
         -   Costs and benefits of the identified problem
         -   Strategies to sustain the enterprise in the future
         -   The marketing mix chosen by the learner
     •   Remind learners to cite sources and provide evidence to strengthen their arguments or justifications.
     •   Provide learners with clear APA referencing guidelines to ensure proper academic practice.

General:
Time management is deemed to be a huge challenge for candidates to balance out their responses. Candidates seem
to mismanage their time. As a result, the extended writing
Most candidates did not fully answer questions 2, 3, and 4.
A clear improvement in the weak responses was detected. However, most candidates still fall short as far as expression
is concerned. They mostly used common structures as well as common vocabulary.
Once again, question analysis still needs attention.

1   (a) Weak responses failed to have a title, name of school or event. Some gave events which were not
        concert-focused, thus losing out on the brief. They also lacked the atmosphere of the event and the
        impact, it had on the planners, organisers, service providers, attendees and the performers. Vis-
        à-vis, successful responses did well with clear stipulations and parameters, going further to give a
        post-mortem of the event in a bid to display long-lasting impact. Responses were expected to be
        formal. Some had colloquial vocabulary like ‘vibe’; ‘chill’ ‘, crazy’ amongst others. Spelling errors were
        visible in these, exited for excited, principle for principal, excreta for etcetera, high schoolers for high
        schooler or pupils or learners, to mention a few. Stronger responses successfully responded to the
        question. Most candidates were familiar with the conventions of a news story. More so, the concerts
        had names and venues. Paragraphs were expected to be shorter with simple to complex sentences in
        use. Of note, some of the best responses displayed new or uncommon vocabulary in the responses,
        which proved that the candidates are well read, placing them in the sophisticated band for expression.
        This is a sure sign that a great deal of effort is being poured into the candidates by the teachers;
        hence, such positivity is appreciated.

1   (b) Even though there was a general improvement in responding to the reflective commentary, many
        candidates still struggled to write reflectively. Hence, the reflective style needs more attention: most
        learners tend to merely analyse their writing without reflecting on it. Generally, most candidates
        managed to discuss form, structure and language with varying success. While others managed,
        some fell short by discussing one out of three or both language and structure and leaving out the
        others. This led to poor responses as some candidates narrated without the correct structure, which is
        Point, Evidence, Example (PEE). All points on Form, Language and Structure must be fully discussed
        in a balanced manner, using clear examples. Merely stating that discourse markers were used is not
        a reflection whatsoever and cannot be awarded marks. The same goes for just mentioning the uses
        of linguistic devices and short sentences without displaying the effect thereof regarding the creation
        of the atmosphere and the impact of the concert. In addition, often the discussions became generic
        instead of text-specific. Simply stating that discourse markers were used to create a flow in writing can
        still only warrant a ‘limited’ mark band.

2   This task was a descriptive response. Several candidates responded well, whilst others struggled to
    articulate “The Little Piece of Heaven” clearly. Some candidates did well on this task with a coherent
    display of imagery and atmosphere. Furthermore, the candidates were expected to create a sense of voice
    that should have referred to sound, light and movement. Unfortunately, weak responses opted to narrate
    instead of writing a descriptive piece. Moreover, it was a pity that some potentially strong candidates also
    narrated instead of responding descriptively. This is a clear case of question analysis not being done
    effectively.

3   This task was an argumentative response, which needed the candidates to respond to the editor of a local
    newspaper to two contrasting emails or letters. Strong candidates who selected this question did well in
    bringing a juxtaposition of arguments. They did well with a strong sense of voice, proposing and opposing
    the couch potato view. On the contrary, some gave weak responses without a balance of opinions. This
    also led to narrations instead of arguments, lacking firm definitions of a “couch potato”. The weaker
    responses also lacked the advantages or disadvantages of the situation when they related to it. Once
    again, question analysis was lacking as only a handful of candidates referred to the article mentioned in
    the prompt. They were expected to respond to the article mentioned in the question.

        8167
       Paper 2



General
The general standard of this session was satisfactory.
Some candidates appeared to struggle with time management, leading to the second question was either rushed or
incomplete. All but a few candidates managed to demonstrate at least a basic understanding of their selected texts, and
many showed signs of genuine engagement with them.
Poetry and All the Bright Places remained the most popular genres this year. Answers reflecting a wide range of
performances were seen on each of the texts attempted by the candidates.
Candidates should use their introductions (thesis statements) to set out generally their interpretation of both the text and
the question as a framework on which their analysis can be structured.
Furthermore, rhetorical questions should be avoided as a literary essay focuses on analysis of the given text.
Candidates should focus on the ways the writers use language, form and style to create meaning. If a learner continuously
uses “then” it reflects a narrative summary or paraphrase of the given text.
Moreover, the focus should not be confused with writing an analytical essay based on style, structure and language.
The focus in a literary essay is always on the way writers present the text, not on who the target audience is or the main
purpose of the text.
While language is not assessed in this paper, many candidates demonstrated weakness in spelling, expression and
sentence structure which may impede meaning.
Candidates should avoid writing in the first or second person as well as starting their sentences with “the poem talks
about...” Many candidates also use ‘author,’ ‘poet’ and ‘playwright’ interchangeably.
General Mark Scheme:
Use the generic mark scheme levels to find the mark. Place the answer in a level first. Look for the “best fit” of the
answer into a level. An answer needs to show evidence of most, but not necessarily ALL, of the qualities described in a
level in order to be placed in that level. Then award a mark for the relative position of the answer within the level.
Candidates may address the question in many different ways. There is no one required answer or approach. Also avoid
penalising answers for leaving out a particular focus. Reward what is there, showing what you are rewarding in your
comments.
Consider all strands and weigh up the performance as a whole in placing the answer in a level, then show that you have
done so in the summative comment.  
Each answer is marked out of 25, in accordance with the general marking criteria.
Assessment objectives
All assessment objectives are equally weighted, and all are considered in assessing each essay.  
Each level in the marking criteria is divided into strands corresponding to the assessment objectives:
L1: Knowledge and understanding (K/U)
L2: Analysis (AN)
L3: Personal response (P)
L4: Communication (C)

 L1 Knowledge and understanding
 Respond with understanding to literary texts in a variety of forms, from different cultures with an appreciation
 of relevant contexts that illuminate readings of the texts.  
 L2 Analysis
 Analyse ways in which writers’ choices of language, form and structure shape meanings and effects.
 L3 Personal response
 Produce informed independent opinions and interpretations of literary texts.  
 L4 Communication
 Communicate a relevant, structured and supported response appropriate to literary study.

All the centres opted for poetry as one of the selected genres. Please note that poetry is optional on this level.

Question 1

    (a) Select two poems from your list of set texts. Discuss the ways in which the poets of these poems
           present loss.
Question Answer                                                                                                        Marks
     A        Select two poems from your list of set texts. Discuss the ways in which the poets of these poems           25
              present loss.
              Indicative content:
              Mark according to the levels of response marking criteria.
              The points below are illustrative and are not intended to be exhaustive. Any other appropriate
              point should be credited.  

              Responses might include the following points:

              ●    identify and analyse the linguistic or literary devices   
              ●    identify the loss they are presenting
              ●    comparison of ways the poets present the theme
              ●    a holistic approach
              ●    secure justification of arguments
              ●    wider references in relation to the task set

Futility and Soldier, Rest! were the most popular poems selected for this question. Other selections included Pity Me
Not, Foreign, The Migrant, These are the times we live in and Telephone Conversation.
While most selections were appropriate for the theme of loss, several candidates failed to link their arguments and
analysis to the theme of loss, as required by the question.
Weaker responses merely summarised the texts without thoroughly analysing how the poets present the theme of loss.
Stronger responses developed clear links to their thesis statement and holistically analysed both poems, highlighting
differences and similarities. These candidates elaborated on the type of loss presented in the poems (i.e. loss of love or
loss of life), which ensured that their responses remained focused on the requirements of the task.

         the pebble represented “upper and lower class love”. Candidates simply identified the rhyme scheme and
         overall structure of the poem without linking it back to love.

        to identify and explain the subtle effects of literary techniques in the poem (i.e. alliteration, volta, change in

Positive suggestions to teachers:
•  Teachers should discourage candidates from using superfluous expressions such as “brilliant author”, “insightful
   use of imagery” or “the author’s exceptional use of lexis”. These expressions are arbitrary and do not constitute a
   personal response.
•  Whenever a reference is made to literary techniques such as the structure of the poem, rhyme and rhythm, imagery
   or pathos or ethos, it is imperative that candidates give a reason why it is important and link it to the requirements
   of the question. They have to focus on very specific effects created.
•  Teachers should instruct candidates not to start their answers with a quote. It is better to teach candidates to start
   their writing with a solid thesis statement, which they then continue to prove by using strong points, evidence and
   analysis.
•  Also note that when analysing an extract or poem, it is imperative to focus on the entire text. If a poem has seven
   stanzas, the importance of all the stanzas in relation to the task needs to be discussed. Moreover, when answering
                                             NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                181
    the (b) part of the question paper, candidates should not rely heavily on parts outside the given extract.
•   Line references do not suffice. Candidates must quote and explain the effectiveness of the quote in relation to their
    thesis statement or topic sentence.
•   It is not necessary at this level to explain literary devices. Rather than discuss the effect created by the specific
    image, we would rather waste time providing a definition.
•   Responses which rely on a summary of the set texts are not successful.
•   Successful responses focus closely on the writing of the texts and how the writer presents the meaning and content
    to the reader.
•   Successful responses use analysis of specific references and quotations to support the points made. This is
    particularly important for the (a) questions, where candidates select their own references to answer the question
•   There is no word count requirement for this paper. Please discourage candidates from spending time on counting
    words.
•   Candidates should avoid vague phrases such as “and so much more” or “of sorts”. They should also not use
    general adjectives such as “good” and “bad” as these are vague descriptors and do not constitute a thorough
    analysis.
•   Encourage candidates not to use “author” “poet” and “playwright” interchangeably. Candidates should also use
    “novel” instead of “the book”.
•   Encourage candidates to use PEEL paragraphs. Each paragraph should have a clear topic sentence, explanation
    and evidence which link to the requirements of the question and their thesis statement in their introduction.
•   Language is not assessed in this component, but common spelling errors or using advanced vocabulary incorrectly
    can impede meaning. Encourage candidates to use simple (but complete) sentences and emphasise that correct
    (British) spelling is still important. Candidates should not use advanced vocabulary if they do not know the meaning.
•   Candidates should refrain from using figurative language (such as “it leaves a sour taste in the reader’s mouth)
    as this does not constitute an appropriate analysis.

GENERAL COMMENTS

This one was the fifth examination to be taken as NSSCAS First Language Khoekhoegowab. The number of candidates
who took the examination in 2025 dropped slightly compared to previous years. There is a bit of improvement at
most of the centres as others performances are satisfactory. It was evident among the centres that the candidates
were prepared and trained how to approach the questions. Those centres and teachers who put more effort into their
teaching are applauded.

Exceptional responses: This year again saw some responses that were so exceptional – presented in such an
excellent manner. Those centres and teachers are applauded for their hard work. Some excerpts from these responses
are included as examples of the “strong responses”.

Passages: The three passages on which the questions were set: Queston 1, 2 and 3 were understood by the majority
of the candidates. Of the two optional questions: Question 2 appeared to be the most popular for many candidates
although the answers to Question 3 were also satisfactory. This means that the candidates could understand all three
passages and questions respectively. There was a significant difference in performance between those who opt for
Question 2 and those who opt for Question 3 with those who opted for Question 2 performing slightly poorer because
of the way they understood the (b) question.

Question 1,2,3 – (b) questions

Some of the candidates did not keep to the required length of the short pieces of a maximum number of words per short
piece (120-150 word limit) and exceeded it in their writings which can caused them to lose marks.

COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Question 1

(a) This question asked candidates to comment on how the author uses language and style to convey his
    strong feelings and opinions about the concept of Ubuntu.
    This question proved to be understood by the candidates whereby they could link the feelings and opinions
    of the author to the language and style used by the author. It was good to see that most of the candidates
    could identify different phrases in the passage, explain them and describe their uses in the passage.
    At some centres candidates identified punctuation marks as symbols, describing insignificant phrases and
    could not be credited for that.
    •    No identification of punctuation marks and its use is needed.
    •    Answers on language and style differ from texts (passages) to texts (passages). It means different features
         of language and style will be identified which could not be found in other texts used and not the same parts
         of speech.

(b) Candidates were asked to write a speech as a primary school teacher who had heard Thabo Mbeki
    delivering the speech. The children in the school asked what the president said. Using mostly your own
    words, write what you plan to say to them. Base your answer on the material in the original speech.
    This question was well-attempted by a number of candidates.
    •   Some candidates did not understand but followed the instructions well. They could not plan and identify
        the main parts (information) of the speech which was supposed to be simplified into Khoekhoegowab
        according to the language level (ability) of primary school learners and how these learners can make
        use of the Ubuntu concept in their daily lives.
    •   Some of the candidates still do not know the structures of speech, and or how to write them as some
        started with the introductory paragraph: greetings and identifying of different audiences present, which
        others did not do that.




                                            NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     184
Centres are advised to attend to the following:
•    Work more on language and style on different texts, meaning, identification in a passage and how to apply it into
     (a) questions.
•    Stick to the word limit (120 – 150 words). Only the main part was needed!
•    Attend to the context, audience and purpose. It is the appropriate language used that determines whether the text
     is well-written and not the so-called “format” of the text.
•    Candidates should be given exercises on how to re-use any language from the original passage.
•    Pay more attention to written work, such as letters, speeches or summary writing.
•    Candidates should be prepared to give a holistic commentary instead of bits and pieces (isolated fragments of
     meanings of phrases and individual words with no effect on the question).

Question 2

(a) Candidates were asked to comment on the way the author uses language and style to convey an
    atmosphere of mystery, suspense and anxiety in the narrative.
     •   This one was the most chosen one of the optional questions. It was attempted by some of them who
         did not produce good answers. However, there were a few who attempted the question successfully by
         creating an atmosphere of mystery, suspense and anxiety as required.
     •   The key concept in the question: mystery, suspense and anxiety was not well understood and how to
         use it in their writings by some of those who attempted the question.
     •   Language and style are supposed to be linked to the identification of the atmosphere of mystery,
         suspense and anxiety.

              Candidates should be trained how to identify certain key elements, phrases and or language
               features in a text, which might be linked to what is required in the text.
              Again it is reiterated that candidates should focus their answers on those details that support the
               key concept in the question instead of dwelling on general responses on every small detail on
               “language and style”.

(b) Candidates were asked to use mostly their own words, continue the story as if they were the same narrator,
    based on their answer on the material in the original text. They do not need to conclude the story.
     •   This question proved to be difficult, and or misunderstood by a few candidates who tried to attempt
         it. They used the main passage content to write it as a summary and or rewrite what had already
         happened in their own way/style.
     •   They were supposed to follow-up with what happened from the start to where it ends and then
         continue the story by using their imagination.

              What many candidates appeared to be lacking is exercises on different type of activities such
               as classroom exercises by using reading texts (prescribed textbooks of Grade 10-11). Teachers
               should provide enough exercises and give feedback. Practice makes perfect!

Question 3

    during her visit to the Maasai people.
     •   This one was also one the least popular of the optional questions attempted by some of the

              More exercises should be given on language and style and how to link them with the other part

(b) This question asked candidates to imagine they were one of the Maasai people and had observed the

     •   A friendly letter was required to be written which was done by all of them.
     •   The candidates do not pay attention to the word limit of 120-150 in (b) questions and exceeded the
         word limit.

GENERAL COMMENTS
Overview performance: This one was the fifth examination to be taken as NSSCAS First Language Oshikwanyama.
