the first time. There was slight improvement in the performance of candidates this year compared to the previous year.
It is evident that some centres made little or no effort to prepare their candidates for this examination. Disparities among
centres in the way candidates approached the questions were observed again this year. Centres that have become
perennial good performers are applauded!

Ovahongwa vamwe onghee ngaho tava ngongo ashike ouleshwa, vamwe otava mbwalangadjeke omayelifo, vamwe
tava yelifa ashike noitumbula ya dja mouleshwa. Aishe ei otai ulike kutya, ovahongwa vahapu otava nyengwa
okunyamukula omapulo ombapila ei, oshinima osho tashi va kanifile oitwa.
Time constraints:
A number of candidates were unable to complete the examination. In several instances, candidates wrote excessive
length in their responses to the unrestricted question (a), producing lengthy responses that left little time for part (b).
It was also observed that most of the candidates spent much of their time on question 1 and less attention on either
question 2 or 3, and they ended up not finishing either question 2 or 3. This imbalance in time management made an
impact on the overall quality and completeness of their work.

Exceptional Responses
This year, we observed an impressive standard of work from a select group of candidates. Their responses reflected a
deep command of the language, combined with a notable ability to express their ideas with clarity and conviction. The
commitment and skill of the teachers at these centres deserve high praise. To illustrate the quality of these outstanding
efforts, we have included extracts from their work as examples of strong responses.

Passages: The three passages on which the questions were set were accessible to most candidates. It was however
noted that a few candidates did not show an in-depth understanding of the passages. Of the elective questions,
Question 3 appeared to be the most popular one for many candidates. A good number of candidates also attempted
Question 2. There was no significant difference in performance between the two questions, but the quality of responses
for Question 3 was slightly better than Question 2.
Generic approach to the questions: It was observed that most of the candidates could not manage their time
effectively. As a result, the candidates spent much of their time on question 1 and less attention on either question 2
or 3, and they ended up not finishing either question 2 or 3 e.g. candidates copied the question first (wasting time);
they comment on the style used in the text in the first paragraph; they then comment on the passage paragraph by
paragraph. This often leads to fragmented responses (commentaries). Commentaries should at best be holistic.

COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Question 1
This question has two parts: (a) commenting on the way the author uses language and style to convey his strong
feelings and opinions about the concept of Ubuntu, and (b) writing:

    (a) This question assessed candidates’ ability to comment on the way the author uses language and style
        to convey his strong feelings and opinions about the concept of Ubuntu. Specifically, it examined their
        understanding of how the author conveys his opinions about the concept of Ubuntu.
         Successful responses required candidates to demonstrate their comprehension of the passage and the
         author’s intentions by effectively employing similar language and stylistic techniques in their own writing.
         The passage itself was characterised by a formal and persuasive tone. The author effectively utilized a
         rich vocabulary, incorporating strong and persuasive language to convey their message. High performing
         candidates recognized that the author intends to encourage people to return to the true spirit of Ubuntu.

         To effectively answer this question, candidates needed to identify and analyse specific words and phrases
         that possess persuasive power and reassure the reader. These observations should then be linked to the
         quotations from the passage that directly support the author’s viewpoint.

        This question assessed candidates’ ability to comment on the way the author uses language and style
        to convey an atmosphere of mystery, suspense, and anxiety in the narrative. In particular, it examined
        their understanding of how the author sustains tension and engages the reader through descriptive
        techniques.

        Successful responses required candidates to demonstrate their comprehension of the passage and the
        author’s intentions by effectively employing similar stylistic features in their own writing. The passage
        itself was characterised by vivid imagery, sensory detail, and a gradual build-up of suspense. The
        author employed descriptive vocabulary, figurative language, and carefully varied sentence structures
        to create a sense of unease and anticipation.
        High-performing candidates recognised that the author intends to immerse the reader in the narrator’s
        fearful experience of exploring the abandoned house. To answer this question effectively, candidates
        needed to identify and analyse specific words and phrases that heighten the atmosphere of dread and
        mystery, such as references to silence, shadows, and the feeling of being watched. These observations
        should then be linked to quotations from the passage that directly support the author’s technique of
        sustaining suspense and anxiety

    (a) Candidates were asked to comment on the way the author uses language and style to convey how the author

          This question assessed candidates’ ability to comment on the way the author uses language and style to
          convey her feelings during her visit to the Maasai people. In particular, it examined their understanding of
          how the author expresses culture shock, fascination, and admiration through her narrative voice.

          Successful responses required candidates to demonstrate their comprehension of the passage and the
          author’s intentions by effectively employing similar descriptive and expressive techniques in their own writing.
          The passage itself was characterised by a lively, personal, and reflective tone. The author used exclamations,
          rhetorical questions, and figurative comparisons to highlight her amazement and emotional reactions to the
          Maasai way of life.

          High-performing candidates recognised that the author intends to share her sense of wonder and discovery,
          while also acknowledging the differences between her own culture and that of the Maasai. To answer this
          question effectively, candidates needed to identify and analyse specific words and phrases that reveal her
          excitement and surprise, such as her use of idiomatic expressions and vivid contrasts between modern and

          support the author’s viewpoint and emotional response.

                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
    192
Recommendations to Teachers
Teachers play a pivotal role in shaping the quality of candidates’ responses, and their continued dedication is
commendable. To further strengthen performance, the following recommendations are offered:
Positive practices to continue:
•   encourage candidates to contribute positively and consistently, building confidence through structured practice and
    reinforcement;
•   provide opportunities for timed practice under examination conditions to help learners manage their time effectively;
•   share exemplars of strong responses, highlighting clarity, logical flow, and effective use of language;
•   promote collaborative learning through peer review, enabling learners to refine their ideas and sharpen critical
    thinking;
•   reinforce the importance of formal, professional language in written work, discouraging casual expressions;
•   celebrate progress, however small, to motivate learners and sustain improvement.
Areas for improvement:
•   place greater emphasis on balanced coverage of all questions, ensuring candidates do not devote
    disproportionate effort to one section;
•   train learners to produce concise, purposeful responses that avoid unnecessary elaboration or repetition;
•   guide candidates towards holistic commentary, integrating analysis rather than commenting paragraph by
    paragraph;
•   encourage structured planning before writing, ensuring logical flow and completeness in responses;
•   support learners in critically engaging with challenges by not only identifying difficulties but also suggesting
    practical solutions;
•   teachers should read the syllabus carefully, with particular attention to the learning and assessment objectives, so
    that they can guide learners towards achieving them;
•   the syllabus should be taught from the very beginning of the year, before introducing other material, to ensure
    learners fully understand the objectives they are expected to meet during the course;
•   learners should be exposed to different types of passages (polemic, narrative, and descriptive) and trained to
    focus on both the questions and the content of the text;
•   teachers should train learners to answer questions directly, avoiding unnecessary digression.

        Paper 2



1   GENERAL COMMENTS

    Strengths
    •     Creativity and engagement: Many learners attempted original ideas, unusual images and personal touches
          to their writing which portrayed a level of creativity and originality.
    •     Understanding of topic and prompts: Most of the candidates could understand and answer the question
          paper to the best of their abilities, although some of them had limited vocabulary and could not express
          themselves well.
    •     Use of anecdote: For narrative tasks, several learners used a personal story effectively to ground their
          piece and create means for their writing to flow as required by the topics.
    •     Recognition of audience: In some discursive pieces, learners adjusted tone and register, especially with
          the voice overs; their tone became more conversational and joyful as required by the topic.
    •     Attempted structure: Many answer scripts showed an awareness of structural features (introduction/body/
          conclusion).
    •     Neat and eligible writing: Many learners wrote neatly and eligibly.

    Weaknesses
    •     Lack of clear introductions and conclusions: Many learners failed to establish context or wrap up their
          ideas effectively.
    •     Elongated approaches to the answering the questions: Some of the candidates answered the questions
          with unrelated narration and only attempted to answer the question in the last paragraphs.
    •     Poor paragraphing and number of words: Ideas were often jumbled together without logical progression or
          thematic grouping while not sticking to the number of words.
    •     Inconsistent tenses: Learners frequently shifted between past and present tense, disrupting narrative flow.
    •     Limited vocabulary: Overuse and change of basic idioms and figures of speech (e.g Ehafo lambishi meumbo
          mwa tomwa) weakened the figurative impact.
    •     Incorrect or lack of punctuation usage: Most of the learners did not use different types of sentences,
          paragraphs and punctuation marks correctly.

2   COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

SECTION A:

1   This question was considerably a popular choice for many learners:
    “Konima youlefimbo eshi nda kala ndihe po pomukunda, onda alukila, nonda mona nghee natango
    ovahongwa tava, hongelwa koshi yomuti wakula onghalo oyo ya faafana naanaa naayo twa li muyo.”
    Shanga ehokololo kombinga yefimbo omuhokololi a li mofikola monghalo ya faafana naayo ya tumbulwa
    metetekelo. Moshinyolwa shoye kwatela mo omaliudo ehafo nomadimbuluko efimbo olo.

    This question required effective use of memory and reflection; many failed to balance present observation with the
    past. Emotional recollection is subtlety demanded. Learners would often incoherently join their present observation
    with their past memories or vice versa. Learners could not express their emotions or memories fully or in detail.
    Common weaknesses:
    Vague nostalgia of the memory of the school under a tree: Learners used general statements about “Onda
    li nda hafa” without concrete scenes or specific objects that evoke the past. Emotional depth was lacking, the
    reminiscence was told, not shown.

    Confused time frame of the past memories and the current observations: Candidates often move between
    past and present awkwardly when trying to put together a memory (back in the day) compared to current observation
    (seeing the school now). Learners often focused on the present scene without adequately developing the past
    memories. While others did not even return to their previous school for their emotions to be evoked in order for
    them to experience nostalgia as requested by the prompt.
    Underdeveloped emotion of what the memories: The essay states “Onda li handi kwena kehafo” rather than
    demonstrating why and how this feeling surfaced.

    Corrective advice:

    •   Ovahongwa vahapu ova nyamukula eli, ashike ovanini vomuvo va nyamukula mondjila.
    •   Vahapu vomuvo inave lifefifa ve litule monghalo oyo va pewa kepulo, meemhito dihapu ova shanga ashike
        omashongo okuhongelwa koshi yomuti, ngaashi oilipwedi, omutenya, omhepo, naikwao, nonande epulo ola
        hala menyamukulo laye mu kale edimba lehafo nokutyapula okuhongelwa koshi yomuti osho yo omadimbukulo
        oo nao a pumbwa okukala e na edimba lehafo.
    •   Mepulo omu ovahongwa ova teelelwa va nyole momupersona wotete pamukalo wokulifefifa navamwe ova
        nyola momupersona omutivali osho shihe li mondjila.

2   This question too was chosen by most candidates:
    Nyola oshinyolwa oshikwakundjodjomona koshi yoshipalanyole “Oudano wovashikingalo” moshinyolwa
    shoye kwatela mo onghalo yovanhu, onhele, omawi nomalinyengo opo omuleshi a faafanife naasho sha
    li tashi ningwa.

    This question appeared to be less challenging but learners failed to follow the prompts that required them to look
    at people, the setting (scene or place) and the sounds at this particular music event. Many learners’ attention was
    fixed on speaking about the performers and what they are well known for rather than describing the event and
    following the prompts to speak about the people at the event and all the other aspects that make up the entire
    question.
    Common weaknesses:

    Over-reliance on labeling of the music show: Writing “it was loud” or “the crowd was big” without supplying
    evidence.
    Ignoring spatial description at the music show: Failure to place the reader in the venue (where the stage is,
    the light, the smell).

    Corrective advice:
    Ovalongwa vahapu ova kufa po epulo eli vo ove li nyamukula nawa. Ovahonga okwa li va teelelwa va kwatele mo
    oupendulifimadiladilo ngaashi:

    Onghalo yovanhu, onhele, omawi nomalinyengo, opo omuleshi a faafanife naasho sha li tashi ningwa, oihopanenwa:
    •   Onhele: Oukoshoki, omatuwa, okuya mo, nomafutilo pomuvelo, omalamba, omambako, oikulya, oikunwa
        nosho tuu.
    •   Ovanhu: Omaliudo avo, omidjalo, omalihumbato ava nosho tuu.
    •   Omawi: Omaweelelo mokule, eemwilwa, eenghuwo dehafo, omakuwililo nosho tuu.
    •   Omalinyengo: Engungumano, emboboloko lovanhu, elandulafano, eendanisa, omalwoodi, ovanhu tava denge
        eemhadi pedu, okupandula/eemhandu.

    Use description of sound at the music show as an anchor: Start with a specific sound and expand outward to
    physical details.
    Map the music scene visually: For instance, encourage learners to describe the venue imaginatively in their
    writing — entrance, stage, audience, exit points — and then use spatial language.

    Layer sensory details at the music show: Combine sights (lights), smells (dust and specific food available),
    tactile sensations (vibration through feet) and social cues (how the crowd moved).

3   Candidates who chose this question did not do justice to the question:
    Owa talela po omaumbo avali ovakwanedimo voye omafimbo a yooloka, ovakwanedimo vomeumbo limwe
    ova li va wanenwa kwaasho ve na, omanga ovakwenedimo vomeumbo likwao va li ovanalwisho nove hole
    omaliko. Nyola oinyolwa ivali oikwakundjodjomona ya yoolokafana, pokati (koitya 250 - 300) kukeshe
    oshinyolwa kombinga yokukala kwoye momaumbo aa avali moulefimbo wetalelepo loye. Moshinyolwa
    shoye kwatela mo omalihumbato nomaukwatya avo.

    The challenge is that the question required nuanced characterization (creating a specific set of character for the
    different families while focusing on their behaviours, separately), parallel structure (creating a credible opposite of
    the other), avoidance of moralizing (learners may lapse into sermonizing rather than showing behaviour through
    scenes by linking it back to what they personally find right or wrong but may not be generally viewed as such),
    and subtlety in comparison (comparing the one writing or piece to the other without noticeably appearing so). The
    requirement to create believable contrasts without resorting to clichés (common and widely known norms that are
    reflected daily) is unavoidable in such a question.
    Many learners who chose this question did not possess the ability to show that the one family was content with
    that they had and that the other family was greedy. The learners’ focus was on the good or bad behaviour of either
    family without following the prompts correctly to expose their content or greed through their behaviour and speech.

    Common weaknesses:
    Moralising tone when referring to the two families: Learners lapse into sermonising rather than showing
    behaviour through scenes. They would preach about a certain thing that was done or not done by a specific family
    member rather than focusing on showing their behavior.

    Stereotyping of the two families: One family becomes an exaggeration (saints’ vs villains) without realistic
    motivations. They claim that these families are bad with very little to no evidence shown in their writing.
    Poor contrast technique in comparing the two families: Many learners listed good or bad qualities and
    immoralities instead of weaving contrast through parallel incidents.

Learners did not build tension slowly, show the pre-match expectation, the unfolding play, the unexpected turning point,
followed by immediate reactions.

7   This question was chosen by many learners:
    Nyola oinyolwa ivali tai kondjifafana (pokati koitya 250-300 ku keshe oshinyolwa) ya nuninwa
    ovakwashiwana, tai ka holoka mushimwe shomoifokundaneki moshilongo. Oshinyolwa shimwe otashi
    popile kutya ovadali vanakanena otava lele ondebula, noshinyolwa shikwao otashi popile kutya ounyuni
    wonale ovadali ova li vena omhango hai etifa oidjemo iwa movana. Moinyolwa yoye kwatela mo onghalo
    yelunduluko lomafimbo neenghedi.

    This question required evidence and distinction from the learners. It is a question that can be answered by
    comparing two discrete, entirely different norms. The question required cultural insight and balanced analysis
    of these two different eras of child rearing. Many learners approached this question with biasness towards the
    parents that they felt were rearing and bringing their children up in a manner that they personally agreed with.
    Learners used generalizations that made it seem as though child rearing is the same or supposed to be the same
    everywhere. They made their experiences and their truths be the poster of how nowadays and olden parents
    supposedly raised their children. Learners could have identified explemplary (desired) ways in both rearings; they
    may be different but it doesn’t necessarily depict that one form of child rearing is better than the other.
    Common weakness

    Lack of binary thinking when it comes to child rearing: Presenting the eras as wholly good or bad without
    argument in difference and not necessarily portraying as better than the other. Learners failed to present both sides
    fairly, or to offer synthesis and recommendations.
    Unsubstantiated cultural claims: Making assertions about norms without evidence with sentences that are
    backing up their claims to show that they have drawn their conclusions from a certain narrative or a factual
    analysis.

    Superficial coverage: Many learners were covering many points briefly without exploring any in depth which

    Confusing fact and opinion: Presenting opinions as facts.

    Thesis with a clear stance: Learners need to be impartial, they should present a nuanced thesis - One that
    considers multiple sides of an issue and avoids oversimplification (e.g. “The internet is a powerful tool whose
    benefits are contingent (provisional) on access and literacy”) meaning that although it is a great tool, it is not
    accesible and user friendly to all.

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
•   Embed planning in everyday practice: Make quick planning when writing non-negotiable. Learners write better
    once their work is planned and mapped out properly.
•   Genre-based mini-layout: Teach each genre explicitly - layout, tone, three or four hallmark features (a sign of
    authenticity) and practice them in short timed exercises.
•   Frequent micro-feedback: Use focused correction - one or two high-impact errors per script (tenses, paragraphing,
    argument structure). Too many corrections overwhelm learners.
•   Peer review with checklists: Train learners to use targeted checklists (e.g., “Does this paragraph have one idea?”)
    when giving feedback.
•   Oral rehearsal: For speeches and voice-overs, require the learner to read aloud; performance improves editing and
    rhythm which will prepare them for targeted writing.
•   Model texts and shadowing: Provide annotated exemplar responses for each prompt showing strong opening lines,
    effective transitions and concluding moves. Use “shadow writing” where learners re-write a paragraph in their own
    voice.
•   The teachers should teach learners to interpret different questions as candidates only understand one part of the
    question and begin to answer the question without looking into the guiding prompts. The questions have the main
    question and then the prompts.
•   The marking scheme/grid should be availed to each learner and used to train them on expected standard on how
    each section (Section A Imaginative writing and Section B writing for audience) should be answered.
•   Learners should be advised to expose themselves to different types of reading materials for them to be able to
    answer longer pieces, and to make their writing pieces more interesting and stronger in vocabulary as well.
•   Practical exposure to questions should be done at Centre’s, so that candidates can be familiar with writing of two
    (2) contrasting pieces for one question.
•   In conjunction with the syllabus and other available materials plus Oshikwanyama Orthography Latest Edition 3
    should be used to avoid unnecessary grammatical errors.
•   Teacher should train their learners on all different types of tasks that are likely to be asked in Section B, please refer
    to syllabi for this.
•   The teachers should teach learners how to write different paragraphs, short sentences and use punctuation marks
    correctly and also how to stick to the word limit to avoid passing the word limit which may result in redundancy.

By fostering these skills, we can empower learners to express themselves with clarity, creativity.

GENERAL COMMENTS
Performance: This one was the sixth examination to be taken as NSSCAS First Language Oshindonga. The number
of candidates who took the examination has slightly increased although a few centres wrote the examination for the
first time. There was slight improvement in the performance of candidates this year compared to the previous year.
Some centres made little or no effort to prepare their candidates for this examination. Disparities among centres in the
way candidates approached the questions were observed again this year. Centres that have become perennial good
performers are applauded!

General comments
•   Aalongwa yamwe oya ngonga ashike okaleshwa
•   Aalongwa yamwe oya mbwalangandjeka ashike omayelitho.
•   Aalongwa yamwe oya yelitha ashike niitumbula ya za mokaleshwa pehala lyokufatulula niitya yawo yene.

Time constraints:
A number of candidates were unable to complete the examination. Some candidates could not complete question (b) of
either Question 2 or 3, potentially due to excessive length in their responses to the unrestricted question (a). It was also
observed that most of the candidates spent much of their time on Question 1 and paid less attention to either Question
2 or 3, so they ended up not finishing either question 2 or 3.

Passages: The three passages on which the questions were set were accessible to most candidates. It was, however,
noted that a few candidates did not show an in-depth understanding of the passages. Of the elective questions,
Question 3 appeared to be the most popular one for many candidates. A good number of candidates also attempted
Question 2. There was no significant difference in performance between the two questions but the quality of responses
for Question 2 was slightly better than Question 3.
Generic approach to the questions: It was observed that most of the candidates could not manage their time
effectively. It is important that candidates should not copy the question first (wasting time); that they should comment on
the style used in the text in the first paragraph; that they should then comment on the passage paragraph by paragraph.
This often leads to fragmented responses (commentaries). Commentaries should at best be holistic.

COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Question 1
This question has two parts: (a) commenting on the way the author uses language and style to convey his strong
feelings and opinions about the concept of Ubuntu and (b) writing a speech, supposedly given to students at one's
school as a primary school teacher:

    (b) This question assessed candidates’ ability to comment on the way the author uses language and style
        to convey his strong feelings and opinions about the concept of Ubuntu. Specifically, it examined their
        understanding of how the author conveys his opinions about the concept of Ubuntu.
         Successful responses required candidates to demonstrate their comprehension of the passage and the
         author’s intentions by effectively employing similar language and stylistic techniques in their own writing.
         The passage itself was characterised by a formal and persuasive tone. The author effectively utilized a
         rich vocabulary, incorporating strong and persuasive language to convey the message. High performing
         candidates recognised that the author intends to encourage people to return to the true spirit of Ubuntu.

         To answer this question effectively, candidates needed to identify and analyse specific words as well as
         phrases that possess persuasive power to reassure the reader. These observations should then be linked to
         the quotations from the passage that directly support the author’s viewpoint.
         Aalongwa opo ya mone iitsa yomupondo mepulo ndika, oya pumbwa okuyamukula epulo kondandalunde,
         mpono nee taya kutha mo elaka nomuhingo, gwa longithwa komunyoli ngoka tagu kwatakanitha oshikalimo
         shokaleshwa nepulo, e ta yelitha niitya nenge omaiyuvo ge mwene i ikolelela kelalakano lyomunyoli, opo u
         ulike euvoko lyokaleshwa osho wo epulo.

204
POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
Teachers play a pivotal role in shaping the quality of candidates’ responses and their continued dedication is
commendable. To further strengthen performance, the following recommendations are offered:

Positive practices to continue:
•   Encourage candidates to contribute positively and consistently, building confidence through structured practice as
    well as reinforcement;
•   Provide opportunities for timed practice under examination conditions to help learners manage their time
    effectively;
•   Share exemples of strong responses, highlighting clarity, logical flow and effective use of language;
•   Promote collaborative learning through peer review, enabling learners to refine their ideas and sharpen critical
    thinking;
•   Reinforce the importance of formal, professional language in written work, discouraging casual expressions;
•   Celebrate progress, however small, to motivate learners and sustain improvement.

Areas for improvement:
•   Teachers should place greater emphasis on balanced coverage of all questions, ensuring candidates do not
    devote disproportionate effort to one section;
•   Train learners to produce concise, purposeful responses that avoid unnecessary elaboration or repetition;
•   Guide candidates towards holistic commentary, integrating analysis rather than commenting paragraph by
    paragraph;
•   Encourage structured planning before writing, to ensure logical flow and completeness in responses;
•   Support learners in critically engaging with challenges by not only identifying difficulties but also suggesting
    practical solutions.
•   Teachers should read the syllabus carefully, with particular attention to the learning and assessment objectives,
    so that they can guide learners towards achieving them.
•   The syllabus should be taught from the very beginning of the year, before introducing other material, to ensure
    learners fully understand the objectives they are expected to meet during the course.
•   Learners should be exposed to different types of passages such as polemic, narrative, and descriptive to be
    trained to focus on both the questions and the content of the text
•   Teachers should train learners to answer questions directly, avoiding unnecessary digression.

        Paper 2


1   GENERAL COMMENTS
    Strengths
    •   Creativity and engagement: Many learners attempted original ideas, unusual images and personal touches
        to their writing which portrayed a level of creativity and originality.
    •   Understanding of topic and prompts: Most of the candidates could understand and answer the question
        paper to the best of their abilities, although some of them had limited vocabulary and could not express
        themselves well.
    •   Use of anecdote: For narrative tasks, several learners used a personal story effectively to ground their piece
        and create means for their writing to flow as required by the topics.
    •   Recognition of audience: In some discursive pieces, learners adjusted tone and register, especially with the
        voice overs; their tone became more conversational and joyful as required by the topic.
    •   Attempted structure: Many answer scripts showed an awareness of structural features (introduction/body/
        conclusion).
    •   Neat and eligible writing: Many learners wrote neatly and eligibly.

    Weaknesses
    •     Lack of clear introductions and conclusions: Many learners failed to establish context or wrap up their
          ideas effectively.
    •     Elongated approaches to the answering the questions: Some of the candidates answered the questions
          with unrelated narration and only attempted to answer the question in the last paragraphs.
    •     Poor paragraphing and number of words: Ideas were often jumbled together without logical progression or
          thematic grouping while not sticking to the number of words.
    •     Inconsistent tenses: Learners frequently shifted between past and present tense, disrupting narrative flow.
    •     Limited vocabulary: Overuse and change of basic idioms and figures of speech (e.g Enyanyu megumbo
          mwa tselwa mbishi) weakened the figurative impact.
    •     Incorrect or lack of punctuation usage: Most of the learners did not use different types of sentences,
          paragraphs and punctuation marks correctly.

2   COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS
    SECTION A:

1   This question was considerably a popular choice for many learners:
    “Konima yuulethimbo sho nda kala ndaahe po pomukunda, onda galukile po nonda mono nkene natango
    taya longelwa kohi yomuti omunene, onkalo ndjoka ya faathana naanaa naandjoka twa li muyo.” Nyola
    ehokololo kombinga yethimbo omuhokololi a li mosikola monkalo ya faathana naandjo ya tumbulwa
    metetekelo. Moshinyolwa shoye kwatela mo omaiuvo genyanyu nomadhimbuluko gethimbo ndyo.

    This question required effective use of memory and reflection; many failed to balance present observation with the
    past. Emotional recollection is subtlety demanded. Learners would often incoherently join their present observation
    with their memories past or vice versa. Learners could not express their emotions or memories fully or in detail.
    Common weaknesses:

    Vague nostalgia of the memory of the school under a tree: Learners used general statements about “Onda li
    nda nyanyukwa” without concrete scenes or specific objects that evoke the past. Emotional depth was lacking, the
    reminiscence was told, not shown.
    Confused time frame of the past memories and the current observations: Candidates often move between
    past and present awkwardly when trying to put together a memory (back in the day) compared to current observation
    (seeing the school now). Learners often focused on the present scene without adequately developing the past
    memories. While others did not even return to their previous school for their emotions to be evoked in order for
    them to experience nostalgia as requested by the prompt.

    Underdeveloped emotion of what the memories: The essay states “Onda li tandi lili omahodhi genyanyu’’ rather
    than demonstrating why and how this feeling surfaced.

    206
Corrective advice:
•  Aalongwa oyendji oya hogolola epulo ndika ihe oyendji inaye li yamukula mondjila.  Oyendji oya nyengwa okweeta
   uumbangi wiiningwanima tayi popile  omaiuvo genyanyu nomadhimbuluko gokulongelwa kohi yomuti. Iiningwanima
   yimwe mbyoka ya hololwa miinyolwa yawo kayi na uuningilo.  Oshiholelwa:  Omulongi naalongwa  ayehe oya li
   haya li iikulya ya londa pombanda yomuti pethimbo lyokafudho. Oyendji oya hokolola etamukululo lyosikola peha
   lyokunyola omadhimbuluko nenyanyu pethimbo ya li mosikola kohi yomuti.
•  Mepulo ndika aalongwa oya li ya tegelelwa ya nyole momupersona gwotango nomutitatu momukalo gokwiifethitha
   ihe yamwe oya nyola momupersona omutiyali.

2   This question too was chosen by most candidates:
    Nyola oshinyolwa oshikwakundjondjomona kohi yoshipalanyolo “uudhano waahikingalo.” Moshinyolwa
    shoye kwatela mo onkalo yaantu, ehala, omawi nomainyengo opo omuleshi a faathanithe naashoka sha li
    tashi ningwa.

    This question appeared to be less challenging but learners failed to follow the prompts that required them to look
    at people, the setting (scene or place) and the sounds at this particular music event. Many learners’ attention was
    fixed on speaking about the performers and what they are well known for rather than describing the event and
    following the prompts to speak about the people at the event and all the other aspects that make up the entire
    question.
    Common weaknesses:

    Over-reliance on labeling of the music show: Writing “it was loud” or “the crowd was big” without supplying
    evidence.
    Ignoring spatial description at the music show: Failure to place the reader in the venue (where the stage is,
    the light, the smell).

    Corrective advice:
    Epulo ndika olya yamukulwa kaalongwa oyendji noye li yamukula lela nawa.  Osha li sha simana ya kwatele mo
    uupenduthi madhilaadhilo mbuka meudhilililo:

    Onkalo yaantu, ehala, omawi nomainyengo opo omuleshi a faathanithe naashoka sha li tashi ningwa, iiholelwa:
    •   Ehala: uuyogoki, oohauto, ostage, omafutilo pomweelo, omalamba, omambako, iikulya niikunwa nosho tuu.
    •   Aantu: omaiuvo, omizalo.
    •   Omawi: omakudhilo muule, omaigidho, oomwiilwa, okuhakela omake, oonkugo, oondigolo nosho tuu.
    •   Omainyengo: engungumano, embomboloko lyaantu, elandulathano, oondanisa, edhengo lyoompadhi pevi
        nomakuyunguto.

Use description of sound at the music show as an anchor: Start with a specific sound and expand outward to
physical details.
Map the music scene visually: For instance, encourage learners to describe the venue imaginatively in their writing
— stage, audience, exit points — and then use spatial language.

Layer sensory details at the music show: Combine sights (lights), smells (dust and specific food available), tactile
sensations (vibration through feet) and social cues (how the crowd moved).

3   Candidates who chose this question did not do justice to the question:
    Owa talele po omagumbo gaali gaakwanezimo yoye omathimbo ga yooloka; aakwanezimo yegumbo
    limwe ya li ya gwanenwa kwaashono ye na, omanga aakwanezimo yegumbo ekwawo ya li aanalwiho
    noye hole omaliko. Nyola iinyolwa iyali iikwakundjondjomona ya yoolokathana (pokati kiitya 250-300
    kukehe oshinyolwa) kombinga yokukala kwoye momagumbo ngaka gaali muulethimbo wetalelopo lyoye.
    Moshinyolwa shoye, kwatela mo omaihumbato nomaukwatya gawo.

    The challenge is that the question required nuanced characterization (creating a specific set of character for the
    different families while focusing on their behaviours, separately), parallel structure (creating a credible opposite of
    the other), avoidance of moralizing (learners may lapse into sermonizing rather than showing behaviour through
    scenes by linking it back to what they personally find right or wrong but may not be generally viewed as such),
    and subtlety in comparison (comparing the one writing or piece to the other without noticeably appearing so). The
    requirement to create believable contrasts without resorting to clichés (common and widely known norms that are
    reflected daily) is unavoidable in such a question.




                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                  207
    Many learners who chose this question did not possess the ability to show that the one family was content with
    that they had and that the other family was greedy. The learners’ focus was on the good or bad behaviour of either
    family without following the prompts correctly to expose their content or greed through their behaviour and speech.
    Common weaknesses:

    Moralizing tone when referring to the two families: Learners lapse into sermonizing rather than showing
    behaviour through scenes. They would preach about a certain thing that was done or not done by a specific family
    member rather than focusing on showing their behavior.
    Stereotyping of the two families: One family becomes an exaggeration (saints’ vs villains) without realistic
    motivations. They claim that these families are bad with very little to no evidence shown in their writing.

    Poor contrast technique in comparing the two families: Many learners listed good or bad qualities and
    immoralities instead of weaving contrast through parallel incidents.
    Epulo ndika olya yamukulwa kaalongwa aashona yowala, ihe inaye li yamukula nawa.  Omayamukulo gomepulo
    muka ngoka taga holoka mo oge na okukala ga pambathana nokutsa kumwe miitopolwa ayihe.
    •   Moshitopolwa shotango iitsa itayi endele pamwe niitsa yomoshitopolwa oshitiyali, shika osha yela kutya kapu
        na ethikithopamwe lyiitsa koombinga adhihe tayi ulike epingathano.
    •   Aalongwa oya ndjondjomona owala momumbwalangandjo, ihe inaya eta mo iitsa mbyono tayi ulike
        omaihumbato nuukwatya waakwanezimo mbono tawu gandja uumbangi wokugwanenwa nolwiho.
    •   Omagumbo naga kale ga yoolokathana osho wo omikunda moka mu na aakwanezimo mboka.

4   Many candidates chose this question:
    Nyola okahokololo kombinga yuudhano wokatanga kokoompadhi moka ospana onene nohayi shi enditha
    nawa shito momaudhano ya dhengwa shi etitha ohenda. Moshinyolwa shoye, kwatela mo shoka wa li wa
    tegamena, shoka inoo itaala nonkumwe.

    This question was the least challenging due to the fact that it requires descriptive context (senses and spatial
    cues) makes this accessible (known and available) to every learner; many learners can draw on direct sensory
    experience to generate a convincing description. Partially because they can relate to this sort of question and
    may have experienced it to some degree, from others or themselves. But learners still failed to tackle the specific
    prompts that required them to express disbelief and shock! Many learners were too excited to write descriptive
    paragraphs about their favourite players without paying attention to what is fully required from them.

    Common weaknesses:
    Over-exaggeration or clichés: Phrases like “the stadium exploded” are used without fresh images to support
    these claims.

    Failing to convey the moment of shock during the loss of the team: Learners recount the score but do not
    render the communal disbelief and would often use the word disbelief itself to express the disbelief they speak of.
    Poor pacing when building anticipation of the soccer match: Too much preamble and hurried, underwritten
    climax. Learners did not build tension slowly, show the pre-match expectation, the unfolding play, the unexpected
    turning point, followed by immediate reactions.

    Aalongwa oyendji oya kutha po epulo ndika ashike oyendji oya mana po ethimbo mokuhokolola omadhengathano

    ya eta nkene sha ende opo dhi ye mo.

6   Nyola oshipopiwa sha nuninwa aagundjuka kohi yoshipalanyolo: “Uunamapya nUuniimuna owo
    shikwetepo mokuhulitha po onkalo yoluhepo moshilongo.” Moshinyolwa shoye, kwatela mo
    omathaneko neinekelo.
    Common weaknesses:
    Weak argumentation of how agriculture eradicates poverty: Learners assert agricultural benefits but provide
    no evidence, examples or realistic processes.

    Overuse of platitudes (common arguments): Relying on empty appeals rather than concrete agricultural
    statistics or case examples.

    Corrective advice:
    Epulo ndino olya yamukulwa kaalongwa oyendji, ashike oyendji inaye li uva ko.  Aalongwa oyendji oya fatulula
    owala uunamapya nuuniimuna nkene wa simana, kaye shi kutya otaya popi naapulakeni yeni po, ano aapulakeni
    yawo. Inaya ya muule womadhiladhilo gawo okuyoolola pokati kiiyamakuti, omiti dhomokuti nosho wo uunamapya
    nuunimuna kondandalunde.   Inaya eta omikalo kondandalunde ndhono aagundjuka taya vulu okulongitha taya
    pitile muunamapya nuuniimuna opo ya tidhe po oluhepo.  Ano inaya kwatela mo iisimanitsa.

    Ethaneko: Aagundjuka aaholike totii po iikunino yeni, mu imonene iiyemo yeni.
    Einekelo: Konima otashi vulika oshikunino shoye shi koke e to gandja iilonga  kaagundjuka, wu kale omugandji
    gwiilikolomwa meni nopondje yoshilongo shono tashi yambula po iiyemo yepangelo, opo iipangelo, oosikola
    noopate dhi tungwe.

    Use credible examples: Encourage the use of illustrative case studies or hypothetical articles (small-scale farmer
    adopting micro-irrigation) — these do not need to be real statistics but must be plausible (realistic) and specific.
    Rhetorical devices: Train learners to use rhetorical questions, repetition, contrasts and direct address to the
    audience to make the speech persuasive.

7   This question was chosen by many learners:
    Nyola iinyolwa iyali tayi kondjithathana (pokati kiitya 250-300 kukehe oshinyolwa) ya nuninwa aakwashigwana
    tayi ka holoka mushimwe shomiifokundaneki moshilongo. Oshinyolwa shimwe otashi popile kutya aavali
    yanakanena otaya lele ondembula, noshinyolwa oshikwawo otashi popile kutya muuyuni wonale, aavali
    oya li ye na ompango hayi etitha iizemo iiwanawa moyana. Miinyolwa yoye kwatela mo onkalo yelunduluko
    lyomathimbo noohedhi.

    This question required evidence and distinction from the learners. It is a question that can be answered by
    comparing two discrete, entirely different norms. The question required cultural insight and balanced analysis
    of these two different eras of child rearing. Many learners approached this question with biasness towards the
    parents that they felt were rearing and bringing their children up in a manner that they personally agreed with.
    Learners used generalizations that made it seem as though child rearing is the same or supposed to be the same
    everywhere. They made their experiences and their truths be the poster of how nowadays and olden parents
    supposedly raised their children. Learners could have identifiied explemplary (desired) ways in both reairings; they
    may be different but it doesn’t neccesaliry depict that one form of child rearing is better than the other.
    Common mistakes

    Lack of binary thinking when it comes to child rearing: Presenting the eras as wholly good or bad without
    argument in difference and not necessarily portraying as better than the other. Learners failed to present both sides
    fairly, or to offer synthesis and recommendations.
    Unsubstantiated cultural claims: Making assertions about norms without evidence with sentences that are
    backing up their claims to show that they have drawn their conclusions from a certain narrative or a factual analysis.




                                             NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                 209
    Corrective advice:
    Aalongwa mboka ya kutha po epulo ndika oya yamukula hwepo ihe inaya eta mo iizemo yomauteku ngoka ga
    pulwa mepulo. Onkene oya li ye na okuyamukula ngeyi:

    Aanona yaamati oya tekulilwa okweedhilila iimuna nuuna ya ka kokola omagumbo gawo otaya ka vula okusila
    iimuna oshimpwiyu nokuputudhila ooyana iimpwiyu mbika monakuyiwa.
    Aalongwa inaya longitha iisimanitsa yelunduluko noohedhi. Aalongwa oya tegelelwa ya nyole iinyolwa tayi
    pingathana.

8   This question was chosen by a handful of learners
    Omagazina oye ku pula wu nyole oartikela kombinga yuuwanawa nuuwinayi womakwatathano
    wopamalungula. Nyola oartikela ndjoka. Moshinyolwa shoye kwatela mo omadhilaadhilo taga popile
    oombinga adhihe shi thike pamwe.

    This question, the same as the previous one required impartial evaluation and synthesis of complex, multi-faceted
    impacts and many learners were challenged by this. Learners have evident biased positions although the question
    specifically asked them to avoid leaning on a side more than another. Although many learners had a plathora of
    good that the internet has to offer, they then leaned into it not being a good thing based on few disadvantages that
    they showed. This showed contrary to what they had expressed in their writing.
    Common weaknesses:

    Bias and imbalance towards the internet not being good: Learners often favor one side heavily or write a list
    rather than evaluate trade-offs (what can be done to better what is mentioned to not be good).
    Superficial coverage: Many learners were covering many points briefly without exploring any in depth which
    appeared more like listing and not detailed explanations.

    Confusing fact and opinion: Presenting opinions as facts.
    Corrective advice:

    Aalongwa oyendji oya kutha po epulo ndika, ashike yamwe oya nyengwa okuthikitha pamwe omayamukulo ga
    kwatela mo oombinga mbali (omauwanawa nomauwinayi) moshinyolwa shimwe sha faalelathana.   Poompito
    odhindji otaya nyengwa okufatulula kutya omalungula  oshike osho wo okuthamununa muule iisimanitsa mbyono
    tayi koleke uuwanawa nuuwinayi womakwatathano gopamalungula.

    Corrective advice:

    Uuwanawa
    Okuninga omakwatathano gomeendelelo popepi nokukule pamikalo dha yooloka pae-mail, whatsapp, pakupopya
    niikwawuo oyindji
    •    okukonga uuyelele pa-interneta
    •    iifokundaneki tayi gandja uuyelele komalungula
    •    okupupaleka onkalo yekongo lyiilonga nosho tuu

    Omauwinayi
    •      ondilo yelongitho lyomalungula
    •      uunkundi womeho
    •      okupikwa ko-tik-tok ndele to dhimbwa iinakugwanithwa yoye nosho tuu.
    Thesis with a clear stance: Learners need to be impartial, they should present a nuanced thesis - One that
    considers multiple sides of an issue and avoids oversimplification (e.g. “The internet is a powerful tool whose
    benefits are contingent (provisional) on access and literacy”) meaning that although it is a great tool, it is not
    accesible and user friendly to all.

    Evaluate trade-offs of the internet: Teach the cost–benefit paragraph - state advantage, qualify it, present
    disadvantage, and conclude with measured evaluation.
    Use real-world implications: Encourage learners to consider different stakeholders (students, parents, employers)
    and how the internet affects each differently.

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
•   Embed planning in everyday practice: Make quick planning when writing non-negotiable. Learners write better
    once their work is planned and mapped out properly.
•   Genre-based mini-layout: Teach each genre explicitly - layout, tone, three or four hallmark features (a sign of
    authenticity) and practice them in short timed exercises.

                                             NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     210
•   Frequent micro-feedback: Use focused correction - one or two high-impact errors per script (tenses, paragraphing,
    argument structure). Too many corrections overwhelm learners.
•   Peer review with checklists: Train learners to use targeted checklists (e.g., “Does this paragraph have one idea?”)
    when giving feedback.
•   Oral rehearsal: For speeches and voice-overs, require the learner to read aloud; performance improves editing and
    rhythm which will prepare them for targeted writing.
•   Model texts and shadowing: Provide annotated exemplar responses for each prompt showing strong opening lines,
    effective transitions and concluding moves. Use “shadow writing” where learners re-write a paragraph in their own
    voice.
•   The teachers should teach learners to interpret different questions as candidates only understand one part of the
    question and begin to answer the question without looking into the guiding prompts. The questions have the main
    question and then the prompts.
•   The marking scheme/grid should be availed to each learner and used to train them on expected standard on how
    each section (Section A Imaginative writing and Section B writing for audience) should be answered.
•   Learners should be advised to expose themselves to different types of reading materials for them to be able to
    answer longer pieces, and to make their writing pieces more interesting and stronger in vocabulary as well.
•   Practical exposure to questions should be done at Centre’s, so that candidates can be familiar with writing of two
    (2) contrasting pieces for one question.
•   In conjunction with the syllabus and other available materials plus Otjiherero Orthography Latest Edition should be
    used to avoid unnecessary grammatical errors.
•   Teacher should train their learners on all different types of tasks that are likely to be asked in Section B, please refer
    to syllabi, particularly different types of voice over formats.
•   The teachers should teach learners how to write different paragraphs, short sentences and use punctuation marks
    correctly and also how to stick to the word limit to avoid passing the word limit which may result in redundancy.

By fostering these skills, we can empower learners to express themselves with clarity, creativity.

GENERAL COMMENTS
Performance: This one was the fifth examination to be taken as NSSCAS First Language Otjiherero. The number
of candidates who took the examination have slightly decreased, although a few centres wrote the examination for
the first time. There was no improvement in the performance of candidates this year compared to the previous year.
Some centres made little or no effort to prepare their candidates for this examination. Disparities among centres in the
way candidates approached the questions were observed again this year. Centres that have become perennial good
performers are applauded!

Examples of responses: As with the previous years, excerpts from weak and strong responses are given again to
guide centres in preparing their candidates for the examinations at this level.

Passages: The three passages on which the questions were set were accessible to most candidates. It was, however,
noted that many candidates did not show an in-depth understanding of the passages. Of the elective questions,
Question 3 appeared to be the most popular one for many candidates. A good number of candidates also attempted
Question 2. There was no significant difference in performance between the two questions but the quality of responses
for Question 2 was slightly better than Question 3.

Generic approach to the questions: It was observed that centres have a generic approach to answering questions,
in that candidates should copy the question first (wasting time); that they should comment on the style used in the text
in the first paragraph; that they should then comment on the passage paragraph by paragraph. This often leads to
fragmented responses (commentaries). Commentaries should at best be holistic. Pondondo ndji ku undjirwa kutja
ovarorwa ve parange mourizemburuka ave ha rire ovandu mba hongwa oviṋa moviuru kutja “eziriro roye uta nai …
mokarukondwa okatenga raisa …kuzambo mokarukondwa oketjavari tjanga kutja okuwira mondjira … okuzambo u
kaende okarukondwa kokarukondwa.” Ombura aihe omahungi maye rire warwe nu rumwe ayehe katji maye hepa
okuzirwa munda umwe aruhe. Ku undjirwa komurorwa okuzira momuano omumbomba a ha tara otjiṋa kotjimwetjimwe
na mbi hi nonḓengu okunyamukurirako – mbi hi nozonḓura poo ongeṋena ndji za eta komazuvakero waindi ehungi.

Time constraints: A number of candidates could not finish the examinations and could be seen rushing through
Question 2 or 3. Worse, some only wrote a few lines for the (a) question leaving the (b) question open.

    A number of candidates only grasped a superficial understanding of the concept and could not give a
    perceptive commentary on the “strong feelings” of the author. Many concentrated on the author’s opinions
    only which were often lifted from the passage.

    tjandje kave po. Ami ee ripura kutja me katja vi ku Tjikuu. Posiya tji me tara mozondiyamanda nḓa ri mu
    indji ondjupa ee munu kutja Tjikuu kamaa pindike. [TARA: Ehungi nda ryamisiwa komurungu ndi kari
    nombameno ndja ri mu indi orini nu otji ra rire ereze tjinene.]

    Otjihorera 2
    Mba ri ambatemwa, nokuhimwa ambi hi na muano warwe okutjita. Ee nyongoha okuyaruka nondjira ndji
    mbe ya na yo. Ondjupa yongoldo me twara kehi roruyano. Avehe mbu twa ri pamwe omeho wavo aaye
    twiiwa i yozohanya zomutenya tji maze ve vete. [TARA: Ehungi tji mari ryama komurungu ri sokukara
    moruveze otjingerwo nu momuano womaungurisiro weraka tjimuna nga womutjange ngwi omuini ape nao.]

Question 3

(a) Candidates were asked to comment on the way the author uses language and style to convey how the
    author felt during her visit to the Maasai people. This one was the most popular of the optional (elective)
    questions and it was well-attempted by a number of candidates. Some candidates could actually not read
    in between the lines to deduce the author’s feelings, arrived at wrong conclusions and did not score good
    marks. From the author’s language and stylistics one could see that she wanted to share her sense of
    surprise, amusement and admiration emanating from her encounters with the Maasai culture.
    The following are excerpts from strong and weak answers taken from candidates’ responses:

    Strong responses

    Otjihorera 1
    Nao mokutjanga kwe omundu womiṱuka nokaheho nu otjaa raisa okutemwa kwe na imbwi ounyakuvi
    mbwa ri awe mu kambura momuano woviravaerise nomapuriro: “Ovikwaye? Kape novihape oviveruke?
    Opondjenda tjiri!” Nai tjandje orondu tja temisiwa i yeriro rOvamaasai. [TARA: Eraka nomiano vyokutjanga
    (omiṱuka nokaheho) nomuano eye mbwee rimunu momuinyo (okutemwa nounyakuvi) mavi horoka nawa.]

    Otjihorera 2
    Omutjange ngwi mokutjanga kwe u yeta okaperendero kutja omurese ma mune omerimwino we tjimuna tji
    ma tja, “ongwe tji mai pusaura otjimenyona tji ya zu nokukambura”. Ihi matji raisa ondjoroka nokuhimwa
    avihe pamwe. [TARA: Ma panguṋuna ame ripurire kepuriro nu tjinene hi otjizo tjaro: “… okuraisa omuano
    mbwee rimunu momuinyo”.]

    Weak responses

    Otjihorera 1
    Eraka eye nda ungurisa ra ri ekande paari yarisa kutja ouyenda mbwi we mu kurisa mounongo otjomundu
    tjimuna paa tja “owo ombwa tjita kutja mbi paturure omeho tjimuna okutarera ongwe tji mai pusaura
    otjimenyona tji ya zu nokukambura”. [TARA: Otjikwaye tji matji raisa eraka ekande mba nai?]

    Otjihorera 2
    Komaandero wa kara noviṋa okutarera mbya ri “onyama yamuaha ku ye” orondu kaa yenene okupunda.
    “Ovo aave imbura nokurora ondoro nokutaka omaoko” wa tene nao orondu ya ri ondjova yanyoko ndji u ha
    rire. [TARA: Kapakahu kutja omurorwa ngwi aa vanga okutja vi. Tjaa ha yenene okupunda okutja oviṋa
    vyamuaha indi ae keriumba mo?]


(b) This question asked candidates to write the main part of a letter to a friend as one of the Maasai people
    telling him or her about his or her impression of the visitors. A significant number of candidates attempted
    this question successfully. Some candidates wrote as if they were the author (one of the visitors) and lost
    marks. It was noted that candidates at some centres could not score good marks as a result of notable
    time constraints. Some of those produced lengthy answers at Question 1 (a) and (b), with some producing
    a combined three to four pages for the two!

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS

Otja tji pe raisiwa aruhe pe munika aayo omaningira nga kaku ungurirwa kaparukaze. Vandu voyetu okuungura oviṋa
omuano umwe okuza kombura nga kombura nokuundjirako omarundurukiro kamaunguriro omawa wovandu mba tya
okuyenda komurungu. Omaningira nga aruhe maye kara amaye kotoka omuano ape mbwa sana nga tji pa soroka.

1.   Me yarukire po rukwao kutja, rutengatenga orapota ndji ngai haamenwe otjepu ariyerike rombongarero
     yotjirihongwa kutja oposikore oini, opondondo yozosikore nḓa kutwa kumwe poo kutja opondondo yorukondwa.

2.   Ombongarero yotjirihongwa ndji ngai tare mouṱenḓune mbu ri po nu i zikamise o Plan of Action ku maku
     ungurirwa ndji nomayuva Due Dates.

3.   Otjiṋa tjimwe tji tja munika momahongero nomerihongero woverihonge pondondo yo-AS okwo ngwi okutja
     ozomiṱiri ze pereitekera overihonge uriri, tj. “tji maku zu nyamukurira komaungurisiro weraka nomiano
     vyokutjanga okuraisa … nana omikoka kehi yomuano eraka mbu ra ungurisiwa tjazumba arire mbi wa
     nyaturura tji mo tjanga”. Mu sokutara pamwe kutja (i) ovi oviṋa mbyo tji mavi raisa … nokutja (ii) mave
     twa po vi momatjangwa. Ngave ungurire metuwo romahongero mu tare pamwe. Overihonge nambano
     va yaruka okunyamukurira koviṋa kangamwa avihe na mbi hi na indji ohambwarakaṋa (ongeṋena)
     komazuvakero waindi ehungi. Ohoṋi onene koverihonge vetu okutja “omutjange wa ungurisa ondja kutja
     omurese ma hekane … wa ungurisa onḓe okuraisa kutja omuhewo wa yanda”. Ozosenda tjiva ze honga
     ovarorwa kutja mokarukondwa okatenga ngave tamune oviraise vyokuresa avihe mbya ungurisiwa. Omu
     vya ri tjiri!

4.   Overihonge ngave pewe orapota ndji wina kutja ve hungirire ko ku na Miṱiri. Omarorero woposikore, nge
     pwikirwa ozombapira zomarorero tjimuna ndji, kaye nombatero ndoovazu mba overihonge kave hongerwe
     poo kave hongerwe nawa. NB. Omiṱiri ndji ha yenene okupura ombapira yomarorero yondondo oyo ndji i
     honga okutja ngunda mai hepa okuripangiṋa (nokupangiṋiwa).

                                                                                                               217
5.   Otja kosirambesa ehungi ndi etenga aruhe mari rire ezuvise (epoporore), inga oyevari maye yenene
     okurira kutja ehandjaure poo eserekarere. Okutja overihonge ve sokukara amave ripura nao rukuru ave
     ha karira ovokutambatamba. Okutja nambano ovo tji va tjiwa nao mave sokukara amave ripura kutja nu tjii
     motona yaro, ovatjangerwa, otjiṱo mu ra tjangerwa nu amwe rimanga omaungurisiro weraka mari yenenisa
     vi ovikaṋena vyetjangwa kaaṋi ndo. Imbi ovo mave sokutjita ngunda amave rese.

6.   Kape vatere overihonge okutja “omutjange ma ungurisa eraka ekande, oukahu …” ndoovazu eye ke na
     imbwi ouhatoi ouzuvakwa na wina kutja oro ri nongeṋena yatjike okuraisa mbi mbya tamunwa mepuriro.

7.   Pa ri otjivarero otjingi tjoverihonge mba kakatera komaungurisiro woviraise vyokuresa opuwo –
     nangarire mbi hi na indji onḓengu ovyo ndji vya weza ku indi ehungi.

8.   Arikanee vandu voyetu ovasuverwa eziriro ngari hungame OTJIZO tji tja yandjwa mepuriro, a rire
     okunyamukurira koviṋa kotjimwetjimwe: ngari rire OTJIMUMBUMBWA. Otjizo atji tamunwa “otjizera”
     uriri mokarukondwa nga okatenga keziriro.

9.   Oviungura vyo-AS vi sokumanuka momakweze yevari nga omatenga – oruveze orusupi! Okutja ngatu
     ute rukuru, atu ka temba kozosikore zomayuva womasuviro. Wina katu nokutjiwa oviṋa mbi rityakaṋa
     momakaendisiro wotjiungura tjomahongero.

10. Epuriro ndi ku ku ha undjirwa eziriro ndi (rhetorical question – epuriro eume momambo warwe) mari
    yende amari piti momuhunga. Ngamwa epuriro ndi ri mehungi nambano ra rira ndo opuwo nokuhina
    maraisiro omasemba wohambwarakaṋa yaro komazuvakero wehungi.

11. Eraka kari rihongwa motjiuru! Omahungi ya panguka, arihe ri noviṋa vyaro. Ndoovazu omutjange wa
    tjanga “otjomundu omutenga, outjavari poo outjatatu” tja ṱunu vi komazuvakero waindi ehungi? Kaku
    yandja ovihorera vya “ami, ove eye” otjomapingenambo nge ri mehungi nokuyandera mbo opuwo.

12. Me mu zerire po omaunguriro omawa kutja tu kapite pomaunguriro wo-2026 nu tu ṱizire ondondo
    yomahongero wOtjiherero kombanda otja pu tu vanga.
