1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

Strengths
•    Creativity and engagement: Many candidates attempted original ideas, unusual images and personal touches to
     their writing which portrayed a level of creativity and originality.
•    Understanding of topic and prompts: Most of the candidates could understand and answer the question paper
     to the best of their abilities, although some of them had limited vocabulary and could not express themselves well.
•    Use of anecdote: For narrative tasks, several candidates used a personal story effectively to ground their piece
     and create means for their writing to flow as required by the topics.
•    Recognition of audience: In some discursive pieces, candidates adjusted tone and register, especially with the
     voice overs; their tone became more conversational and joyful as required by the topic.
•    Attempted structure: Many answer scripts showed an awareness of structural features (introduction/body/
     conclusion).
•    Neat and eligible writing: Many candidates wrote neatly and eligibly.

Weaknesses
•    Lack of clear introductions and conclusions: many candidates failed to establish context or wrap up their ideas
     effectively.
•    Elongated approaches to answering the questions: Some of the candidates answered the questions with
     unrelated narration and only attempted to answer the question in the last paragraphs.
•    Poor paragraphing and number of words: Ideas were often jumbled together without logical progression or
     thematic grouping while not sticking to the number of words.
•    Inconsistent tenses: Candidates frequently shifted between past and present tense, disrupting narrative flow.
•    Limited vocabulary: Overuse of basic idioms and figures of speech such as “eyuva ra i kooHengua na Ngore”
     weakened the figurative impact.
•    Incorrect or lack of punctuation usage: Most of the candidates did not use different types of sentences,
     paragraphs and punctuation marks correctly.

2.   COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

SECTION A:

1.   This question was considerably a popular choice for many candidates:
     “Kombund’ oruveze orure ndu mba zengire ami mba kotoka kokarongo ketu nu e vaza ovahongwa amave hongerwa
     kehi yomuti omunene, tjimuna tji pa ri ku ami.” Tjanga ehungi ohunga nomayuva omutjange ngwi tjaa hiti osikore.
     Momatjangero woye ngamu munike ondjoroka nomerizemburuka woruveze orukuru.

     This question required effective use of memory and reflection, but many failed to balance present observation with
     the past. Emotional recollection is subtlety demanded. Candidates would often incoherently join their present
     observation with their past memories or vice versa. Candidates could not express their emotions or memories fully
     or in detail.

Common weaknesses:
Vague nostalgia of the memory of the school under a tree: Candidates used general statements about “mba
ri nondjoroka” without concrete scenes or specific objects that evoke the past. Emotional depth was lacking; the
reminiscence was told, not shown.
Confused time frame of the past memories and the current observations: Candidates often move between past
and present awkwardly when trying to put together a memory (back in the day) compared to current observation (seeing
the school now). Candidates often focused on the present scene without adequately developing the past memories.
While others did not even return to their previous school for their emotions to be evoked in order for them to experience
nostalgia as requested by the prompt.
Underdeveloped emotion of what the memories: The essay states “Mba kamuna ehoze rondjoroka tji ra toto” rather
than demonstrating why and how this feeling surfaced.

Corrective advice:
Replace “Mba ri nondjoroka” with a 2–3 line scene: “Ozondjora zondjoroka zounatjona aaze zuvakere hembandina
nozondundu, za rungwa mu nokurimuna okutjeverwa nounyaṋu nu itji tja tjita kutja mbi zemburuke omayuva ngee yoro
                                             NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                219
nao wina. Omayuva ngu mba ri kehi yomuti tjingewo.”

2.   This question too was chosen by most candidates:
     Tjanga etjangwa ehandjaure kehi yepu ndji: “Otjitjitwa tjomizumbi.” Momatjangero woye tara kovandu, oruveze
     ongondoroka nozombosiro kokutja omurese ma sore okurisenginina nawa na ihi otjitjitwa.

     This question appeared to be less challenging but candidates failed to follow the prompts that required them to look
     at people, the setting (scene or place) and the sounds at this particular music event. Many candidates’ attention
     was fixed on speaking about the performers and what they are well known for rather than describing the event and
     following the prompts to speak about the people at the event as such as all the other aspects that make up the
     entire question.

     Common weaknesses:
     Over-reliance on labeling of the music show: Writing “it was loud” or “the crowd was big” without supplying
     evidence.
     Ignoring spatial description at the music show: Failure to place the reader in the venue (where the stage is,
     the light, the smell).

     Corrective advice:
     Use description of sound at the music show as an anchor: Start with a specific sound and expand outward to
     physical details.
     Map the music scene visually: For instance, encourage candidates to describe the venue imaginatively in their
     writing, such as stage, audience and exit points and then use spatial language (“komamuho kwa ri...”“komanene
     kwa ri…”).
     Layer sensory details at the music show: Combine sights (lights), smells (dust and specific food available),
     tactile sensations (vibration through feet) and social cues (how the crowd moved).

3.   Candidates who chose this question did not do justice to the question:
     Ove wa karyangera omaṱundu yevari movikando pekepeke; eṱunḓu indi orimwe ra yakurire nu ra ri nohange
     nongaro yaro yehupo ngunda indi orarwe ara ri neraru momuinyo nokusuvera oviṋa. Tjanga omatjangwa yevari
     omahandjaure ngu maye haṋika (arihe romambo pokati ko-250 nga ko-300) ohunga nomakarero woye pu
     nomaṱunḓu nga. Momatjangero woye ngamu munike ozongaro zomeritjindiro nozoundu.

     The challenge is that the question required nuanced characterisation (creating a specific set of character for the
     different families while focusing on their behaviours, separately), parallel structure (creating a credible opposite of
     the other), avoidance of moralising (Candidates may lapse into sermonising rather than showing behaviour through
     scenes by linking them back to what they personally find right or wrong but may not be generally viewed as such),
     and subtlety in comparison (comparing the one writing or piece to the other without noticeably appearing to do so).
     The requirement to create believable contrasts without resorting to clichés (common and widely known norms that
     are reflected daily) is unavoidable in such a question.

     Many candidates who chose this question did not possess the ability to show that the one family was content with
     what they had and that the other family was greedy. The candidates’ focus was on the good or bad behaviour of
     either family without following the prompts correctly to expose their content or greed through their behaviour and
     speech.

     Common weaknesses:
     Moralising tone when referring to the two families: Candidates lapse into sermonising rather than showing
     behaviour through scenes. They would preach about a certain thing that was done or not done by a specific family
     member rather than focusing on showing their behaviour.
     Stereotyping of the two families: One family becomes an exaggeration (saints’ vs villains) without realistic
     motivations. They claim that these families are bad with very little to no evidence shown in their writing.
     Poor contrast technique in comparing the two families: Many candidates listed good or bad qualities and
     immoralities instead of weaving contrast through parallel incidents.

     Corrective advice:
     Indirect characterisation of the behaviour of the families: Use dialogue, objects and reactions rather than
     labeling (“greedy”) directly. Instead of “Eṱunḓu rareru momuinyo kaari vanga okuvatera”, ovahonga ngave raise
     oruveze eṱunḓu rimwe pu ra panḓa okuhanasana otjiṋa otjiṱiṱi posiya otjinahepero tjimuna omeva ngunda indi
     orarwa a ra yandja eta raro esenina - show and do not tell.




                                               NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     220
4.   Many candidates chose this question:
     Tjanga ehungi ohunga nehore rotjimbere indu otjira otjinene notjinautoṋi ouingi tji tja taarerwe okuhina kurivatera.
     Momatjangero woye ngamu munike ombepo yomaundjiro, okuhina ngamburiro nokukumwa.

     This question was the least challenging due to the fact that it requires descriptive context (senses and spatial
     cues) makes this accessible (known and available) to every learner; many candidates can draw on direct sensory
     experience to generate a convincing description, partially because they can relate to this sort of question and may
     have experienced it to some degree, from others or themselves. But candidates still failed to tackle the specific
     prompts that required them to express disbelief and shock! Many candidates were too excited to write descriptive
     paragraphs about their favourite players without paying attention to what is fully required of them.

     Common weaknesses
     Over-exaggeration or clichés: Phrases like “the stadium exploded” are used without fresh images to support
     these claims.
     Failing to convey the moment of shock during the loss of the team: Candidates recount the score but do not
     render the communal disbelief and would often use the word disbelief itself to express the disbelief they speak of.
     Poor pacing when building anticipation of the soccer match: Too much preamble and hurried, underwritten
     climax show that candidates did not build tension slowly, show the pre-match expectation, the unfolding play of the
     unexpected turning point, followed by immediate reactions.

SECTION B:

5.   This question was seldom chosen by candidates
     Orupa rwozondendera nomahwa rwa tanda okukara noporoharama yomatjiukisiro wondjeverero yokuti na mbi ri
     mu ko kotjiwaṋa. Tjanga etjangwa reraka romuwonge wozombuze romehi rokongotwe ovapuratene ndi mave zuu
     oporoharama tji mai kaenda onamuinyo. Momatjangero woye ngamu munike enyando nondjoroka.

     The few candidates who chose this question tackled it rather well while taking tone and audience into consideration.
     They were radio presenters who were presenting or showcasing the event as requested by the topic. Candidates who
     chose this topic are higher achievers and are well vested in the general knowledge of nature and its conservation.

     Common weaknesses
     Only a few candidates did not address the proper audience or use the right register when it came to this question.
     Others seemed to approach it more as an interview platform rather than them articulating what they have observed
     at the event.

     Corrective advice
     Candidates did not express joy as the prompt indicated when doing a voice for the nature conservation program.
     For instance, they could have written, “Tjiwaṋa tjovapuratene, ove tji u he ri mba hi nokutjiwa kutja uri pi! Eṱe matu
     rimunu nawa mominyo ngunda amatu tjevere okuti nozondendera kwetu. Indjee… Indjee motjivaro tu yoroke
     pamwe ndino!”

6.   This question was chosen by many candidates:
     Tjanga ehungi ndi mari hungama ovandu omitanda nda zikamene komambo nga: “Otutumbo novikunwa eeziriro
     komayerururiro wousyona”. Momatjangero woye ngamu munike ongurameno onamasa nomaundjiro wamunda
     omuwa.

     Although many candidates chose this question with the thought in mind that it is an easy and relatable topic,
     they failed, in many cases to mention how agriculture can curb poverty. Their repetitive statement was, “mitanda
     pendukee mu yandje ombango kotutumbo novikunwa, ovyo eeziriro komayerururiro wousyona”, without stating
     how exactly agriculture can curb poverty with valid supportive statements such as “mitanda pendukee mu yandje
     ombango kotutumbo novikunwa, ovyo eeziriro komayerururiro wousyona mena rokutja tji wa kunu poo okutumba
     ovinamuinyo mo yenene okuvirandisa o munu ko otjimariva tji mo yenene okurihupisa na tjo.” The following
     sentence was more explanatory and descriptive in a sense that it provided evidence of how agriculture provides a
     solution to eradicate poverty.

     Common weaknesses
     Weak argumentation of how agriculture eradicates poverty: Candidates assert agricultural benefits but provide
     no evidence, examples or realistic processes.
     Overuse of platitudes (common arguments): Candidates rely on empty appeals rather than concrete agricultural
     statistics or case examples.




                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                  221
     Corrective advice
     Use credible examples: encourage the use of illustrative case studies or hypothetical articles (small-scale farmer
     adopting micro-irrigation) — these do not need to be real statistics but must be plausible or realistic and specific.
     Rhetorical devices: Train candidates to use rhetorical questions, repetition, contrasts and direct address of the
     audience to make the speech persuasive.

7.   This question was chosen by many candidates:
     Tjangera otjiwaṋa omatjangwa yevari ngu maye pitasana (arihe romambo pokati ko-250 nga ko-300) nu ngu
     maye kapita mu imwe yozongoramambo nḓe pita pevapayuva. Etjangwa ndi etenga ri noumune wokutja ovanene
     moruveze rwanambano va haraharisa ozotjikira tjinene kovanatje, ngunda ndi oritjavari amari raisa kutja, oruveze
     orukuru ovanene ovawa va ri noveta. Momatjangero woye ngamu munike ombepo yomarundurukiro wotuveze
     nondanaukiro mozongaro zomeritjindiro.

     This question required evidence and distinction from the candidates. It is a question that can be answered by
     comparing two discrete, entirely different norms. The question required cultural insight and balanced analysis of
     these two different eras of child rearing. Many candidates approached this question with bias towards the parents
     who felt were rearing and bringing their children up in a manner with which they personally agreed. Candidates used
     generalisations that made it seem as though child rearing is the same or supposed to be the same everywhere.
     They made their experiences and their truths be the poster of how nowadays and older parents supposedly raised
     their children. Candidates could have identifiied exemplary (desired) ways in both rearings; they may be different
     but it does not necessarily depict that one form of child rearing is better than the other.

     Common mistakes
     Lack of binary thinking when it comes to child rearing: Presenting the eras as wholly good or bad without
     argument in difference and not necessarily portraying as better than the other. Candidates failed to present both
     sides fairly, or to offer synthesis and recommendations.
     Unsubstantiated cultural claims: Candidates made assertions about norms without evidence with sentences
     that are backing up their claims to show that they have drawn their conclusions from a certain narrative or a factual
     analysis.

     Corrective advice
     Candidates should use a balanced structure when wiriting: Teach the two-plus-one approach: two sections
     describing each era and then a combination that weighs strengths and suggests contemporary best practice.
     Define terms and scope of era and years that are being referred to: encourage candidates to specify which
     society or time they refer to, or to use “moviwaṋa ovingi” to avoid overgeneralisation.
     Include modern inferences: ask candidates to suggest actionable recommendations for parenting today based
     on lessons from the past.

8.   This question was chosen by a handful of candidates:
     Ove wa ningirwa i yomangasina okuvetjangera okaartikeri ohunga nouwa nouvi mbu ri momimari vyomotungovi
     mu mu hakaenena otjiwaṋa. Tjanga okaartikeri nga. Momatjangero woye ngamu munike ombepo yokuhina
     ngarera koumune auyevari.

     This question, the same as the previous one required impartial evaluation as well as synthesis of complex, multi-
     faceted impacts and many candidates were challenged by this. Candidates have evident biased positions although
     the question specifically asked them to avoid leaning to one side more than the other. Although many candidates
     had a plethora of good that the internet has to offer, they then leaned into it not being good based on a few
     disadvantages that they showed. This was contrary to what they had expressed in their writing.

     Common weaknesses
     Bias and imbalance towards the internet not being good: Candidates often favour one side heavily or write a
     list rather than evaluate trade-offs, what can be done to better what is mentioned to not be good.
     Superficial coverage:  Many candidates were covering many points briefly without exploring any in depth which
     appeared more like listing and not detailed explanations.
     Confusing fact and opinion: Candidates presented opinions as facts.

     Corrective advice
     Thesis with a clear stance: Candidates need to be impartial and should present a nuanced thesis that considers
     multiple sides of an issue and avoids oversimplification “The internet is a powerful tool whose benefits are contingent
     (provisional) on access and literacy” means that although it is a good tool, it is not accesible and user friendly to all.
     Evaluate trade-offs of the internet: Teach the cost–benefit paragraph - by stating an advantage, qualify it,
     present disadvantage and conclude with measured evaluation.
     Use real-world implications: Encourage candidates to consider different stakeholders such as students,
     parents or employer and how the internet affects each differently.

                                                NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     222
3   POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
•   Embed planning in everyday practice: make quick planning when writing non-negotiable. Candidates write better
    once their work is planned and mapped out properly.
•   Genre-based mini-layout: teach each genre explicitly, layout, tone, three or four hallmark features, a sign of
    authenticity and practise them in short timed exercises.
•   Frequent micro-feedback: use focused correction or one or two high-impact errors per script such as tenses,
    paragraphing or argument structures. Too many corrections overwhelm candidates.
•   Peer review with checklists: train candidates to use targeted checklists such as “Does this paragraph have one
    idea?” when giving feedback.
•   Oral rehearsal: for speeches and voice-overs, require learners to read aloud; performance improves editing and
    rhythm which will prepare them for targeted writing.
•   Model texts and shadowing: provide annotated exemplar responses for each prompt showing strong opening
    lines, effective transitions and concluding moves. Use “shadow writing” where candidates re-write a paragraph in
    their own voice.
•   The teachers should teach candidates to interpret different questions as candidates only understand one part of
    the question and begin to answer the question without looking into the guiding prompts. The questions have the
    main question and then the prompts.
•   The marking scheme/grid should be available to each learner and used to train them on the expected standard on
    how each section, Section A: imaginative writing and Section B: writing for audience should be answered.
•   Candidates should be advised to expose themselves to different types of reading materials for them to be able to
    answer longer pieces and to make their writing pieces more interesting as well as stronger in vocabulary as well.
•   Practical exposure to questions should be done at centres, so that candidates can be familiar with writing of two (2)
    contrasting pieces for one question.
•   In conjunction with the syllabus and other available materials plus Otjiherero Orthography Latest Edition should be
    used to avoid unnecessary grammatical errors.
•   Teacher should train their candidates on all different types of tasks that are likely to be asked in Section B. Please
    refer to the syllabus for this.
•   The teachers should teach candidates how to write different paragraphs, short sentences and use punctuation
    marks correctly as well as how to stick to the word limit to avoid passing the word limit which may result in
    redundancy.

By fostering these skills, we can empower candidates to express themselves with clarity, creativity and confidence.

       Paper 2



1.   GENERAL COMMENTS
Based on previous year’s (2024) question paper 2, this year’s question paper seems to be fair as per candidates’
responses. Different responses from candidates were fair and indeed good, though there were some candidates who
could not achieve competence in some questions they chose.

Generally, candidates need to be exposed to a variety of sources such as narrative writing, descriptive writing and
argumentative writing, because the examination paper is assessed in those areas. This will help candidates to know
the structure, tone and logic each essay is demanding.

This year (2025) candidates repeated the same answering method of not capturing the main keywords (verbs) in each
question before attempting them. Through the help of teachers, candidates are advised to read and comprehend any
question they opt for and prepare better, so that the emphasis of their writing should be based on their understanding
of the question.

In addition, most of the candidates have a problem with punctuation marks, spelling or using vocabulary in the correct
way, therefore it affected the grammar and structure of their writing. All that must be taught thoroughly to answer the
question properly. A good example of wrong vocabulary usage: in Part A Question 4 (see Question Paper 2, 2025),
candidates were expected to write about how a successful team was been defeated. Vanona kuna kuuyunga asi: “Tupu
pwapita siruwogona sipanagona nare sina konkomwene mo mbara zimwe”. Nkango kukonkomwena/kukonkomoka
azo ku zi ruganesa koyikwamema kapi zina ku liza neyi ana kusimwitira, mpamwe ngano kuna zi ruganesa morupe
rwefanekeso ngangesi asi: “mbara kwa hwililire noureru ngwendi mema gana kukonkomoka.”

The length of their writing needs more improvement; some candidates could not write 500 to 600 /250 to 300 words
required per question. All candidates must adhere to the guidance, word guideline required not to write less than the
required number of words.

Instructions were clear and most of the candidates selected one question from each part of the question paper as
required, but there were a few candidates who only answered one question in Part One only and did not select any from
Part B.

     This question expected candidates to recall all their memories, when they used to be taught under a huge tree,
     and those memories should create a feeling of joy in them.

        being taught under a huge tree, which used to be his classroom during his school days. Upon answering this
        question, candidates were expected to write on this topic in the first person, in which they were supposed to
        narrate all exciting or joyful old memories that tree had given.
      Some candidates who did well, focused on reviewing their old memories on how the tree used to offer them
        a conducive environment, for instance during break when they used to fetch their soft porridge and bring it
        to the very same tree to eat. Awo hena kava simwitilire ekurutji eli omu ngava danaukire mo nsene murongi
        mutupu. Ngamoomu: kuronda keguru valitjide, ku ronda vakanyange enyango, ano vamwe kudiworoka omu
        ngava va havarekere mo yidwara yousigwe. Ano poyiruwo yimwe nsene murongi ana handuka awo ngava
        duka walihane, morwa kapi kwa kere evero konkondwa ezi zomositji.
      Candidates that did not do well, focused on their general story about going to school, disadvantages and
        advantages of being taught under the tree and they did not touch on the exciting memories. Ano varongwa
        vamwe kava simwitilire tupu kuhamena omu ngava dimbi sure mepangero lyorutandu. Yina kara asi kapi yina
        kuuyunga kuhamena sure zomositji neyi ngayi va hafesa.

FIRST LANGUAGE RUMANYO
        8195
       Paper 1



1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

In this examination, candidates’ overall performance was at an average level, showing little difference compared to
the previous examination. The question paper featured passages that were similar in nature to those used previously,
covering a range of topics such as adventure, environmental issues and political matters.

The majority of candidates attempted Question 3 in addition to the compulsory Question 1, while only a few opted for
Question 2. Across all questions, it was observed that many candidates encountered noticeable challenges and, as a
result, did not produce the quality of work expected at this level. Furthermore, it was observed that a significant number
of candidates either did not attempt certain parts of the question they had chosen or provided only partial answers. This
trend was particularly evident across several sections of the paper indicating a lack of comprehensive understanding or
inadequate time management. Such omissions and incompetence has been identified as major factors contributing to
the overall poor performance of candidates in this examination.

However, there were a number of candidates who demonstrated commendable effort and understanding of their tasks.
These candidates were able to perform well or better, showing a clear comprehension of their work. They expressed
their thoughts effectively and provided accurate, well – structured, and high – quality responses as required.

In Question 1, the compulsory question, candidates generally did not perform well. However, many misinterpreted the
information from the passage and presented it differently from the intended meaning, which negatively affected their
marks. Candidates did not demonstrate a clear understanding of the passage and this challenge was also evident in
Question 1(b) where many candidates failed to interpret the question correctly and applied inappropriate approaches
in their responses. Moreover some candidates did not consider the intended audience when writing and also a wrong
format of speech writing was frequently observed.

Question 2 was chosen by few candidates, most of whom failed to demonstrate adequate understanding of the question.
In Question 2 (a) candidates struggled to identify relevant language features and recognize the author’s style, with many
simply selecting random words and explaining their meanings without relating to the author’s purpose. In addition,
some candidates used unrelated proverbs and idioms in their responses, instead of identifying and explaining the
figurative language used in the passage.

Overall responses from some candidates were narrative or phrase-based, lacking clarity, coherence and depth of
analysis.

In Question 2 (b), it was also observed that a considerable number of candidates were unable to demonstrate the
required knowledge and skills to continue the novel. Consequently, many left the question unanswered, while others
provided incomplete or partially relevant responses.

By the look of things candidates who opted for Question 3 performed relatively better, particularly in Part (a) although
performance in 3 (b) was less impressive. The passage appeared more familiar to most candidates enabling them to
demonstrate a good understanding to effectively organize their ideas to convey what the author was trying to express.
Many showed the ability to identify key points, provide relevant explanations and support their answers with appropriate
examples from the text. However, there were some candidates who struggled to analyze and interpret the passage
in depth, often providing incomplete or superficial responses. For Part (b) candidates were unable adequately to
demonstrate their understanding of the question. Instead of writing a personal letter describing their impression of the
visitors or tourists, many candidates misinterpreted the task and presented themselves as the tourists who visited the
Maasai people. Even so, there were some candidates who demonstrated a good understanding of the question. They
remained focused and were able to write the letter effectively by using the main part from the passage as required.

2.   COMMENT ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS
Question 1 ( Lipuro 1)

Shingi shavashongwa kapi tompolire nawa mulipurol lino olyo lyakaliro shi lyapamutininiko. Ovino kwakundamine
mwamudona vitwa vyavashongwa. Vashongwa vyavaditopelire mukuyuvha mbundi yamushitjangwa nakuyikwata

1.   GENERAL COMMENTS
Most learners demonstrated a good understanding of relatable topics like environmental issues, adventure, and sports.
However, several areas need improvement.

*Common Challenges*
•    Many candidates started sentences with conjunctions, affecting writing structure and coherence.
•    Some learners exceeded or fell short of the word count.
•    Proverbs, idioms, and sayings were often misused.
•    Some candidates selected topics they couldn’t fully express, and figurative language, rhetorical questions, and
     proverbs were underutilized.

2.   COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

Question 1: Narrative Essay
•    Learners wrote in the present tense instead of the past tense, as required.
•    Candidates failed to link their stories to the question, writing about general topics instead.
•    Essays often lacked introductions and conclusions. (Vashongwa kwatimwitilire mushirugho sho shinantani,
     mulivango lyashirugho pito osho vava pulire.)
•    Vashongwa kwatimwitilire tupu vi vhurauka vyavo va hana kutamekera pavishorokwa ovyo vya twalidililiro kuvi
     vhurauka vinya.

Question 2: Descriptive Essay (Music Show)

     vyokukushuva shuva yira makwareko, vilika vyalingwanito mwaka navimwe nka ngoli opo va vetanga dimusika.)

FIRST LANGUAGE SETSWANA
        8196
       Paper 1



1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

Greater emphasis should be placed on training candidates to understand what is expected of them when responding to
this paper. In particular, candidates require further guidance on analysis and language effects, including the identification
of the author’s language choices, the communication of clear viewpoints, and sustained engagement with the text.
Learners should also be trained to correctly identify a range of language features, support their responses with relevant
examples, and clearly explain how these features create specific effects.

Many candidates tended to paraphrase or repeat the content of the passages without sufficient reference to language
and style. Consequently, examiners should encourage candidates to focus more on analytical responses rather than
simple retelling. In addition, candidates should consistently be reminded to adhere to the required word length in their
responses.

2.   COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Knowledge and Understanding

     the text.

One candidate misunderstood the requirements of this question. Instead of adapting Thabo Mbeki’s speech for a

candidate did not meet the communicative purpose of the task.

Potso 3 (a)

All learners selected this question, which required an analysis of how the author uses language and style to convey
her experiences during her visit to the Maasai people. However, most candidates did not sufficiently quote or refer to
specific words, phrases, or sentences to support their points.

Learners were expected to identify how the author expresses feelings such as surprise, amusement, curiosity, and
admiration, and to explain how these language techniques convey her emotions. Furthermore, candidates should
have discussed how these stylistic choices enable the reader to understand and share the author’s reactions to the
Maasai.

The expected response would demonstrate perceptive understanding, using relevant textual evidence to support
explanations of how language and style create effect.

(a) Style
    •      Description with some narrative element
    •      Non fiction adventure :informal travel writing.
    •      Slightly humorous with some irony.

Feelings during her visit to the Maasai people

    Before arrival and overview of the visit (Paragraph 1 and 2)
    •      Shocked /surprised (what ? I cried)
    •      Disbelief/ignorant /pity (“No healthy fruit? No vegetables? Poor people”)
    •      Overreacting (Julius just smiled shook his head)
    •      Emphasises culture shocks – (think polygamy! Witchdoctors! And most of all lion hunting!)

    Apparent contradictions of Maasai culture (paragraph 3)
    •      Admission of previous ignorance (of course)
    •      General comments / observation (live with one foot in the past and one in the present)
    •      Surprise (remarkably)

    Willingness to learn (paragraph 4)
    •      Attitude of group (curious travellers)
    •      Appreciation of culture (nothing more than tree branches and cow dung, but welcoming home)
    •      Awareness of difference (vastly different lives)
    •      Curiosity (we begged)

    The women and their dance (paragraph 5 and 6)
    •      Enthusiasm to join the culture (At once)
    •      Enthusiasm to join the culture (jumped up and threw myself)
    •      Enthusiasm to join the culture (trying to repeat)
    •      Reaction to the questions (I blushed)
    •      Awareness of her status (it struck me …)

Learners were expected to write an informal letter demonstrating engagement with the passage and personal reflection.
Candidates were required to use descriptive language and construct clear, coherent sentences to communicate

3.   POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS TO TEACHERS/EXAMINERS
•    The examiner should encourage candidates to use idioms and proverbs in their writing to enrich language
     expression.
•    Learners should be encouraged to read through their work after completion to correct unnecessary mistakes and
     improve clarity.
•    Teachers should encourage learners to write confidently when given the opportunity.
•    While errors are not severe, learners’ vocabulary remains limited and requires development.
•    Examiners should provide learners with more passages and train them on how to analyse and write using the
     language and style employed by the author.
•    Learners should be consistently reminded of the correct formats for writing newspaper articles, diary entries, and
     letters.
•    Continuous attention should be given to punctuation, spelling, and orthography to improve overall language
     accuracy.
•    Examiners should regularly review their own reports to identify areas for improvement and enhance their teaching
     strategies in the classroom.
•    Learners should be encouraged to read questions carefully and with full understanding before attempting to
     answer, to ensure appropriate and accurate responses.

GENERAL COMMENTS

Since only two learners wrote this paper, the majority of the topics were not selected.

Firstly, the examiner should emphasise to the learners the importance of consistently using idiomatic expressions in
their continuous writing (go natetsha puo), as this contributes significantly to language richness and authenticity.

Secondly, the examiner should emphasise to the candidates the importance of remaining calm and reading the topics
carefully and with full understanding. Misinterpretation of questions continues to be a challenge and has a negative
impact on performance, particularly when candidates write on an incorrect topic. For instance, in the topic “Makasine o
go kopa gore o kwale athikele e mo go yone o bontshang botlhokwale poelo morago ya tshidimosetso”, one candidate
misunderstood the task and wrote about the President encouraging the youth to refrain from bad lifestyles, which was
irrelevant to the requirements of the question.

Furthermore, the examiner should teach the candidates to avoid unnecessary repetition of ideas. Instead, they should
be guided to develop their points logically and maintain a clear and coherent flow of ideas in order to sustain the reader’s
interest.

Lastly, candidates continue to use incorrect or inappropriate words in their sentences, which affects both clarity and
meaning. Examples include:

COMMENTS ON THE INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

SECTION A: Imaginative Writing

1   Candidates were expected to use imagination and descriptive language to create a sense of joy and
    meaningful memories. The focus of the topic was not on negative interpretations of the tree, but rather
    on the positive emotions evoked by the image. Learners were required to describe the joy experienced
    when looking at the picture, the impact the tree had on their lives, and how it contributed to shaping their
    character. Furthermore, candidates were expected to reflect on the valuable lessons, such as discipline
    and unity, that were learned under the tree, and how the group associated with it progressed positively in life.
    However, one learner misinterpreted the topic and focused on negative aspects, which detracted from the
    intended purpose of the question. This resulted in a response that lacked the required tone of joy, nostalgia,
    and appreciation.

2   One learner selected this topic but did not explore it in sufficient depth. Instead of focusing on the excitement,
    atmosphere, and enjoyment of a music show, the learner concentrated excessively on negative behaviour,
    such as alcohol abuse, drug use, and fighting among attendees. As a result, the descriptive element of the
    task was weakened.
    This topic was considered one of the easiest, as most learners are exposed to music from an early age, including
    at school level, and some even aspire to become artists. Learners were expected to describe a lively and exciting
    event, such as a festive day like Christmas or a popular music festival attended by large crowds. Effective
    responses would have captured the joyful mood, the anticipation of the audience, the inclusivity of all age groups,
    and the powerful sound of the music filling the village. Some candidates could have described how the quality of
    the sound allowed people to enjoy the show even from outside the venue, thereby enriching the sensory detail of
    the piece.

                                                NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     248
3   This was a contrast question; however, many learners failed to address it correctly. Instead of balancing
    the topic by writing two separate descriptive pieces of between 250–300 words each, learners focused
    more on one part and neglected the other. Candidates were required to create a clear contrast while also
    developing a sense of expectation, disbelief, and surprise.
    The topic required learners to contrast two families: one that demonstrated discipline, where parents maintained
    authority and guided their children appropriately, and another that lacked discipline. In the second scenario,
    learners were expected to describe how parents repeatedly changed the Wi-Fi password to control access,
    while children secretly gained access and subsequently displayed disrespectful behaviour towards their parents.
    Failure to balance the two descriptions resulted in incomplete and uneven responses.

4   This topic was mainly selected by male learners, as soccer is a popular sport among boys. Many responses
    were engaging and demonstrated a clear sense of expectation, disbelief, and surprise. Learners described
    how a well-known team was unexpectedly defeated 4–0, leaving supporters shocked and disappointed.
    Some candidates effectively conveyed the emotional impact of the loss, including the embarrassment
    experienced by fans and the disappointment that led some supporters to consider abandoning the team.
    Learners were expected to emphasise the high expectations with which fans attended the match, contrasted with
    the unexpected outcome that left them surprised and disheartened upon returning home.

SECTION B: Writing for an Audience (discursive / argumentative)

5   This topic was not popular among candidates, as it required familiarity with the voice-over script format,
    which many learners have not sufficiently mastered. In addition, the topic demanded adequate background
    knowledge of environmental conservation and the ability to adopt an appropriate public-awareness tone
    while creating a sense of appreciation and enthusiasm. Consequently, candidates with limited vocabulary
    and insufficient exposure to functional writing found the topic challenging and opted for more familiar options.

6   This topic was generally accessible to learners, as it focused on agriculture as a means of eradicating
    poverty within the general population. Learners were expected to demonstrate an understanding that a
    country which does not produce its own food remains economically vulnerable. Furthermore, candidates
    were required to explain how communities can begin on a small scale by practising subsistence farming
    within their households to ensure food security. Thereafter, learners could have expanded on how farming
    on a larger scale may generate income, enabling parents to support their families, including paying school
    fees to ensure better educational opportunities for their children.
    However, only a few learners selected this topic, despite its relevance and practical nature.

7   As observed in Section A, learners once again focused excessively on one part of the question instead of
    balancing both sections. In particular, candidates concentrated on the first part, which discussed parents
    who are overly lenient, excessively friendly, and lacking in discipline. Learners highlighted how children,
    being highly aware of their rights, often overrule their parents. Some responses attributed this behaviour
    to the influence of drugs and social media.
    In contrast, the second part, which required learners to describe parenting practices in earlier times, was
    insufficiently developed. Learners were expected to explain how parents in the past were strict, authoritative,
    and respected, with their decisions regarded as final. The lack of balance resulted in incomplete responses.

8   Most learners did not select this topic, which required a discussion of the advantages and disadvantages
    of social media. While learners were expected to acknowledge the benefits of social media, such as
    timely access to information and updates on national events, they were also required to discuss its
    negative effects. These include cyberbullying, school dropouts, and the risk of depression and suicidal
    behaviour among the youth. The limited selection of this topic suggests uncertainty in handling balanced
    argumentative or discursive writing.

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
•   The examiner should encourage candidates to incorporate idioms and proverbs appropriately in their writing in
    order to enrich language use and expression.
•   Candidates should be encouraged to read through their work upon completion to correct avoidable errors related
    to spelling, grammar, and sentence structure.
•   Morutabana a rotloetse baithuti go kwala ba seka ba tshaba go kwala fa nako e ba letlelela.
•   Diphoso ga se tse dikgolo; bogolo ke gore tlotlofoko e santse e tlhaela. This indicates that while errors are not
    severe, learners’ vocabulary remains limited and requires further development.

GENERAL COMMENTS
•   There was a slight improvement shown in the candidates’ work compared to last year on the (a) questions.  A good
    number of candidates were able partly to analyze the passages, using correct quotes from the authorsʼ opinions
    expressed in the passages, However, most candidates still struggle to analyze the text using correct language
    features to prove their point of analysis.

•   It was observed that candidates were more comfortable to analyze a polemic text as they found it difficult to analyze
    the descriptive and narrative ideas found in Passages 2 and 3.  The issue of reusing the same ideas without any
    alterations to suit the audience is a concern for every candidate.  Ignoring the key points of the questions which
    should lead to a good answer that can focus on specific purpose is still lacking in many responses.  The choice of
    vocabulary is still a challenge as is connecting the tone of voice to the original text.
•   Generally, candidates seem to understand the content of question (a)s – the authorʼs feeling, opinions on the
    passages, however, it should be clear that the content for each passage and the specific question requires
    candidates to focus on specific purpose and audience, therefore, there should be appropriate vocabulary, tone and
    style used for each response.

•   Some candidates did not finish Paper 1.  After marking all the scripts, it was concluded that the candidates write
    very long responses: two to three pages for (a) question, which hinders them from completing their examination
    paper, as most of their time is used for question 1 only.  Therefore, they should be guided on time management.
•   Some candidates also wasted time on rewriting the question statements on top of their answers, which is not
    necessary, because markers use question papers to ensure what is being answered, so candidates need to be
    discouraged to avoid it, to save time.

1   (b) A good number of candidates scored above average in the speech question, but most of them presented
        the key points just as expressed by the first speaker, while they were expected to paraphrase the
        ideas to reflect a clear comprehension, in a simpler language suitable for children at primary level
        as the focused audience of the question.  Therefore, the aspect of purpose and audience should be
        taken into consideration.

2   (a) This question proved to be a strong and less answered compared to Question 3.   For those who
        chose it, their response was not convincing enough, from the authorʼs intention to the language
        features expected to be commented on.  There was mystery, suspense and anxiety.  The author was
        entertaining the reader by telling a suspenseful story while creating themes of curiosity and courage,
        therefore, that was language enough for analysis including the bravery and curiosity which lead to
        discovery.  Instead they were retelling the story again with no analysis techniques to be observed.

    helps your content to stand out as it pulls the reader closer to you, with an appropriate structure, logic or making
    sense or valid reasoning, pieces of writing should be coherent in a unified whole, the use of language imaginatively
    to create specific effects on the reader “ the application of the figurative language or figures of speech including

FIRST LANGUAGE THIMBUKUSHU

       Paper 1



Key messages

A key reminder will be the general objective of what his paper assesses. It states candidates get assessed on their
ability to: read with understanding and produce a coherent analysis of a range of text types, now they know they will
respond to 2 of 3 texts. Candidates have to prove they can identify and understand all three passages from the polemic
(compulsory on question one), narrative and descriptive one.

Again, it should be noted that question 1 (a and b) is compulsory. The choice is on question 2 a and b or question 3a and
b. Another point worth noting is, (a) questions are for commenting on language and style of the author. This is achieved
by the candidates, when they demonstrate their knowledge and understanding of the passage first and foremost. They
should be able to identify the message in the passage and intention of the message by the author before they analyse
the language or identify the relevant ideas and language features/devices from the passage to comment on them. That
is to comment this is what helped the author convey his/her message. The words from the passage MUST always be
in quotation marks “”.

To answer (a) questions, it is wise not to simply make an observation of the language features and list them but rather
mention what the author says and be guided by the language or the style that reveals it. An example of lifted languages
like, “the author used a metaphor “he is a lion” and “s/he is showing how to use it well”. Such a method of response is
wrong and does not respond to the demand of what the paper assesses as alluded to above. It is also important to say
there is no need for excessive writing that includes all the analysis of language features and forms as it is not relevant
to that particular question. Pay attention to the demand and the language in the particular text.

On (b) question there is no need for exceeding the word limit unduly. Be straight to the point and keep in mind the word
limit. Another emphasis is on (b) questions, which are for basing the language closely to that in the passage by following
the question asked to the audience will change, the format will change, the style will change and many others. Re-use
of some phrases in the passage is possible in some cases but not to copy and paste; it is to rephrase it and make it
fit the context of the question at hand,. The task should sound like the language and the style used in the passage to
show that one understands.

1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

Most candidates appeared to do well with question 1 and 3 passages. Those who understood the passages responded
by writing well and meeting most needs of those passages compared to question 2. There was an evident level of clear
detail and accurate understanding in 1a-b and 3a-b compared to 2a-b.

The worrying sign, however, was there were a number of students who could not finish responding and left blank spaces.
When those occurred, it was most often on the last question, so perhaps time was limited, although it increasingly
appeared that because of excessive writing on (a) questions (2-3 full pages) which is generally needless.

On some scripts there were visible differences in the attempt to comment on the language and style on(a) questions.
This question requires stating your understanding of the passage according to what the author is implying, then close
reference from the passages for language and comment on the language which was not done very successfully by
many candidates.

On (b) questions using own words is important but it should not be your own made up words from an unrelated instructed
question. This way of attending to the tasks makes it lack sufficient clarity or precision to gain adequate credit. Copying
or lifting’ of material to answer an entire question was one of the reasons for marks not being awarded in (b) questions.

There was a tendency to write too many words on all questions. It is acceptable with the (a) questions but not up to
3 pages full; it is also important that less than a page does not give adequate content to grade on. It is definitely not
acceptable with (b) questions to write a whole page or a page and a half for 120 -150 words. This was mostly done
by those who instead of reusing the language copied and over-copied. Some became over-creative and reworded the
same ideas which is unacceptable.

Question 1
Most candidates did pretty well on both of these questions. There was a visible understanding of the passage, however,
a few still lifted language features without commenting on it and without the knowledge and understanding of the overall
                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025

passage. The passage is a speech of Thabo Mbeki on Ubuntu. The candidates needed to know that the passage is
about Ubuntu, a traditional African philosophy that means “a person is a person through other people.”

1   (a) Comment on the way the author uses language and style to convey his strong feelings and opinions
        about the concept of Ubuntu.

          Some of the knowledge and understanding which could be used/What do we expect from the
          candidates in this question:
          • to encourage people to return to the true spirit of Ubuntu in the African value that emphasises humanity,
            compassion and interconnectedness.
          • Thabo Mbeki wants to remind South Africans that even though the country has achieved democracy,
            many people still act selfishly and ignore the needs of others.
             -   He aims to: criticise the rise of greed and individualism that weaken social unity.
             -   inspire citizens to rebuild a caring and united society based on Ubuntu.
             -   promote moral values such as respect, equality, and shared humanity.
             -   challenge everyone to apply the spirit of Ubuntu in his/her everyday actions to fight against poverty,
          			inequality and violence.
          • In essence, he intends to reawaken moral and social responsibility as well as to show that true freedom
            and progress come from living together in harmony and compassion.

    All these above sum up some the knowledge and understanding candidates needed to respond to the task
    successfully.

    An example:
    He has clearly written the passage in a persuasive and reflective style, as he seems to aim at encouraging South
    Africans to work together in the spirit of Ubuntu to rebuild unity, compassion and moral values in the nation. The
    exact reveals that Thabo Mbeki believes in Ubuntu and he seems to uses strong and emotional language to show
    his deep feelings about the loss of Ubuntu in society. His tone appears to be serious and caring because he wants
    people to realise that selfishness and greed are destroying unity as well as kindness. He also suggests with the use
    of the words, “greedy individualism is destroying our social cohesion” and intends to express his disappointment.
    The use of “we” and “our” by the author is intended to make everyone feel included and responsible for bringing
    back the spirit of ‘Ubuntu.’

    The author sees Mbeki’s use of rhetorical questions like “Is this the kind of society Steve Biko visualised?” as a
    way to persuade, inspire and make the audience think deeply about their situation. He also quotes famous leaders
    such as ‘Mandela, Biko, Tutu and Obama’ who are great symbols to support his message and show that ‘Ubuntu’ is
    important for all humanity. The author repeatedly uses the word “Ubuntu” which could mean that he aims to remind
    readers of its importance and wishes to encourages them to live by it every day. Overall, the author’s ideas about
    language and style of Mbeki’s speech seem to show his strong belief that practising Ubuntu can help build a caring
    and peaceful nation.

    (b) You are a Primary School Teacher who heard Thabo Mbeki deliver the speech. The children in your
        school have asked you what the president has said. Using mainly your own words, write what you
        plan to say to them, basing your answer on the material in the original speech.
          Some of the knowledge and understanding which could be used/What do we expect from the candidates on
          this question:

          •   Candidates should show that they understand the main ideas and message of Thabo Mbeki’s speech.
          •   They should identify key points the president made, such as unity, working together, the meaning of
              Ubuntu, and the importance of building a better society.
          •   Candidates are expected to paraphrase the ideas rather than copy phrases directly from the speech.
          •   The response should reflect clear comprehension, showing they can explain complex ideas in simpler
              language suitable for children.
          •   Candidates should write in a friendly, simple and age-appropriate style, imagining they are speaking
              to primary school children

    An example:
    Good afternoon, Learners, yesterday I had the chance to listen to President Mbeki speak. He talked about how
    important it is for all of us “to work together and care for one another.” He explained the idea of “Ubuntu,” which I
    understood as we are all connected and that our actions affect other people. The president reminded us that if we
    want our country to be strong and fair, we must help each other, be kind and respect everyone. He repeated to us
    that even small things we do, like being honest, sharing and being responsible, can make a big difference in our
    communities. He encouraged everyone to think about others and work together so that we can all live in a happier
    and safer country.

2   Most candidates did not choose this question. It appeared to be too demanding to imagine all that has to

    (a) Comment on the way the author uses language and style to convey an atmosphere of mystery,
        suspense and anxiety in the narrative.
         Some of the knowledge and understanding which could be used/What do we expect from the candidates in
         this question:
         •    The author intends to entertain the reader by telling a thrilling and suspenseful story while also exploring
              themes of curiosity, courage and the connection between the present and the past.
         •    Through the narrator’s adventure in the mysterious, abandoned house, the author aims to create tension
              and excitement, keeping the reader engaged and eager to find out what happens next.
         •    Additionally, the story conveys a sense of mystery and wonder about heritage and ancestral legacy,
              especially through the discovery of the golden calabash, which symbolises luck, family history, and
              cultural identity.
         •    The author also encourages the reader to reflect on how bravery and curiosity can lead to discovery,
              even in the face of fear of the unknown.

    In short, the author wants to entertain, thrill and inspire reflection on heritage and courage.

    An example:
    The author seems to create an atmosphere of mystery, suspense, and anxiety through careful use of language
    and style that is explicit. He also appears to describe the ruined house vividly as having an “ancient door which
    was covered in spider webs” and “the walls were bare, painted a faded purple,” which appears to evoke a sense of
    decay and strange feelings. The author still appears to use sensory details like “shadowy depths”, “rasping sound,
    a scratching whisper”, “dust that billowed into small clouds,” with the idea of making the reader feel the narrator’s
    fear and tension, by appealing to the sense of sight, sound and touch.

    The author appears to insert suspense which is intensified through the narrator’s hesitation and inner thoughts, with
    rhetorical questions like “Would it really matter if I opened this door?” which the author seems to use to emphasize
    uncertainty. The author’s use of short, abrupt sentences, such as “Thud! I fell into a deep, dark hole,” give the
    impression of intensifying the action and fear. The introduction of the faceless old woman and the supernatural
    voice by the author seems to add to the mystery, while the gradual revelation of the hidden treasure appears to
    sustain curiosity and excitement. Overall, the language and style of the author intend to make the reader feel
    anxious, intrigued and compelled to continue reading the story.

    (b) Using mostly your own words, continue the story as if you were the same narrator. Base your answer
        on the material in the original text. You do not need to conclude the story.
         •   Students are expected to continue the story, maintain the narrator’s perspective by keeping the voice,
             tone and style consistent with the original story.
         •   Learners are expected to extend the story plausibly, building on the events and established atmosphere
             of mystery, suspense, adventure.
         •   They can introduce new events, discoveries, or thoughts of the narrator, but they must fit logically within
             the story’s progression.
         •   The learner’s continuation should avoid copying whole sentences from the original text, although some
             key phrases or ideas can be referenced.
         •   Emphasis is on paraphrasing and original expression while staying true to the narrative.

    An example:
    I picked up the golden calabash carefully, feeling its heavy weight in my hands. It shone brightly in the flashlight
    and I realized it was very important, not just because it was a treasure, but because it belonged to my ancestors.
    While holding the golden calabash, I looked around the basement, feeling nervous and wondered if someone was
    watching me. I could not help but notice the walls were covered in strange marks, such as brought a chill to my
    spin. Remembering the earlier voice of an old woman, my heart beat faster as I struggled to find the way out of
    the shadow, shining the torch-light into the dark corridor ahead of me. My mind started playing tricks on me, I
    thought I saw something, as fear was creeping in. I wanted to explore more and find out all the secrets hidden in
    this strange, old house but I had to leave and fast!

(a) Comment on the way the author uses language and style to convey how she felt during her visit to the
    Maasai people.
      Some of the knowledge and understanding which could be used/What do we expect from the candidates in
      this question:
      •    Point out how the author expresses her feelings of surprise, amusement, curiosity and admiration.
      •    Refer to techniques such as vivid descriptions, imagery, humour, idioms, contrasts, personal
           reflections and direct speech/dialogue.
      •    Note the use of first-person narrative to make the account personal and engaging.
      •    Explain how these techniques show her emotions and help the reader understand her reactions to
           Maasai culture.
      •    Show understanding of how the author’s tone and style convey culture shock as well as
           fascination.

      An example:

      The author seems to use a lively and humorous style to convey her surprise, curiosity and admiration during
      her visit to the Maasai people. She frequently used exclamations and questions, such as “What? No healthy
      fruit? No vegetables? Poor people!” which suggests her astonishment at their diet. Her first-person narrative
      appears to make the account personal and engaging, allowing the reader to experience her reactions first
      hand.

      The author’s vivid imagery and comparisons also seem to illustrate her feelings; for example, “like catching
      sight of a leopard munching on a freshly caught gazelle” looking to convey both excitement and wonder. The
      author notes “high point of my trip” which may indicate excitement and satisfaction of the trip. The author’s
      humorous commentary on cultural differences, such as laughing at being considered “ancient by Maasai
      standards,” suggest a playful tone while expressing her fascination.

      Through these techniques, the author intends to communicates her emotional journey of culture shock,
      amusement and admiration effectively making the reader share her experience.

(b) Imagine you were one of the Maasai people and observed the visitors closely. Using mostly your own
    words, write the main part of a letter to your friend in which you tell him/her about your impression of
    the visitors. Base your answer on the material in the original text.
      Some of the knowledge and understanding which could be used/What do we expect from the candidates on
      this question:

      •   They should write from the point of view of a Maasai person, imagining themselves observing the
          visitors.
      •   They must reflect the thoughts, feelings and cultural perspective of someone from the Maasai
          community.
      •   The letter may also include observations of the visitors, such as their reactions to Maasai traditions,
          dances and daily life.
      •   Learners may mention the visitors’ curiosity, excitement, surprise or amusement, drawing on specific
          events described in the passage: for example participation in the dances, questions about Maasai life,
          reactions to lion hunting, or the diet.

      An example:
      Dear Mukoya

      Last week, we welcomed visitors from far and it was quite an unforgettable experience! They seemed amazed
      when they discovered that we live without ‘electricity or running water.’ They also asked questions about ‘our
      food, cattle, and traditions’.
      Then came a time when the women visitors joined ours in their dance. It was funny to watch them trying to
      imitate our traditional dancing movements and songs. They laughed a lot at their failed attempt to dance, but
      we enjoyed teaching them. Later, when the men attempted ‘adumu’, our jumping dance, the crowd laughed
      even more because their men could hardly jump high!
      At one point, nine visitors “squeezed into one of our huts”. You know how small they are. They were visibly
      not used but said nothing, which made us smile. They were interested and curious about everything, “our
      food, our families and even witchdoctors.” Watching their interest made me proud of our Maasai culture and
      reminded me how special our traditions truly are.

      Your friend

      Kutenda

     observing them and stating that candidates see them is not commenting on language and style.

     article.

1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

Based on previous year’s (2024) question paper 2, this year’s question paper seems to be fair as per candidates’
responses. Different responses from candidates were fair and indeed good, though there were some candidates who
could not answer some questions they chose correctly.

Generally, candidates need to be exposed to a variety of sources such as narrative writing, descriptive writing and
argumentative writing, because the examination paper is assessed in those areas. This will help candidates to know
the structure, tone and logic demanded in each essay.

This year (2025) candidates repeated the same answering method of not capturing the main keywords (verbs) in
each question before attempting to answer them. Through the help of teachers, candidates are advised to read to
comprehend any question they opt for to prepare better, so that the emphasis of their writing should be based on their
competence in answering the question.

In addition, most of the candidates have a problem with punctuation marks, spelling or using vocabulary in the correct
way, therefore it affected the grammar and structure of their writing. All that must be taught thoroughly to answer the
question properly. A good example of wrong vocabulary usage: in part A question 4 (see the question paper 2, 2025),
candidates were expected to write about how a successful team was defeated. Vanona kuna kuuyunga asi: “Tupu
pwapita siruwogona sipanagona nare sina konkomwene mo mbara zimwe”. Nkango kukonkomwena/kukonkomoka
azo ku zi ruganesa koyikwamema kapi zina ku liza neyi ana kusimwitira, mpamwe ngano kuna ziruganesa morupe
rwefanekeso ngangesi asi: “mbara kwa hwililire noureru ngwendi mema gana kukonkomoka.”

The length of their writing needs more improvement; some candidates could not write 500 to 600 /250 to 300 words
required per question. All candidates must adhere to the guidance, word guideline required not to write less than the
required number of words.

Instructions were clear and most of the candidates selected one question from each part of the question paper as
required, but there were a few candidates, who only answered one question in part one only and did not select any from
part B.

•    Educators are advised to encourage candidates to select topics about which they have prior knowledge, so that
     they are able to answer them correctly unlike choosing topics in a random way.

•    Teachers should encourage candidates to use figurative language which should be used in the right way, because
     it helps show markers they have a broader picture and understanding of the topic.

1   GENERAL COMMENTS

This was the third external examination under the new syllabus. 88 candidates were entered for this examination.
During the first year there were 65, then 56 candidates. There were 11 centres that offered German Foreign Language
on AS level, only two centres had more than 10 candidates, thus 57 candidates’ speaking tests were moderated. The
same mark schemes as the previous year were used.

In general, it was established by the moderators that this year examiners awarded marks for the presentation (Part A)
correctly but were still more generous when awarding marks for Parts B and C of the speaking examination. It must be
mentioned that teachers were generally forthcoming and friendly during the speaking examination.

Overall, the quality of the recordings was clear. Teachers and candidates could be heard equally clearly. Fewer centres
presented the speaking examination with the teacher’s voice closer to the microphone than that of the candidate. This is
appreciated by the moderators, as the candidate’s speaking ability is tested. There were less background noises on the
recordings, which was also appreciated by the moderators. It needs to be mentioned that candidates need to present
some statistics, to show that they have researched the topic and they should compare Namibia with some other country
where German is spoken, such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria or Lichtenstein, or just present the topic about one of
these countries. The mentioning of statistics was generally done this year.

When teachers conduct the speaking examination, they do not have to address their candidates in the “Höflichkeitsform
Sie”, nor the other way around. They address them the same way as they would when teaching them, which could
include the name of the candidate and “du”. The candidates may answer with the name of the teacher and “du” as well.
Teachers are advised to stick to one format of addressing and not hop between the two possibilities of informal and
formal. Fewer examiners hopped between the two forms this year.

Teachers should mention when they switch from one section to the next, such as we have completed Part A, the
questions for Part B are as follows. For the 2025 oral examination this was adhered to by all the centers.

It is good to mention at the end of the recording of each candidate “end of sample”. Teachers also must record only
once all the information about the centre and the examination have taken place. It does not have to be repeated at the
beginning of each candidate’s oral. Regarding the beforementioned aspects, examiners also adhered to the advice
given in last year’s report.

In future, teachers should mention the general topic, such as Medien and then the specific topic on which the candidate
does his or her presentation. The specific topic should be of a conflicting nature, or the candidate should make a
provocative statement and then explore that in his or her presentation, such as “Social media only influence teenagers
negatively.” The comparison part should not be contained in the title. Most centres this year only had prepared
presentations on the general topics.

When a candidate asks a question to be repeated, he or she should not be presented with a completely different
question by the teacher. Teachers may rephrase the original question, but should refrain from long, elaborate questions.

2   COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

The speaking examination for the Foreign Language German AS learners consists of three parts.

Every year there are five general topics available for the Foreign Language German AS learners and they then choose
one of the topics to do their presentation on, going into more detail on the chosen topic. Thus, there is no question
paper available, only a mark scheme for this specific examination. This year all five general topics were spoken
about, the most popular one being “Arbeit und Freizeit / Entspannung”, and the least used was “wissenschaftlicher
und medizinischer Fortschritt”. It must be mentioned here that 14 candidates prepared presentations about seemingly
random topics, not taking into consideration the five prescribed topics of that specific year.




                                             NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                               267
Part A is a presentation by each learner which should not be longer than three minutes, but also not shorter than two
and a half minutes. Overall, this was not a problem although some learners were allowed to present for almost four
minutes. It should be mentioned that three minutes are sufficient and that learners may be stopped. The rest of the
presentation, should there be some parts not presented, could be used for the second part, where questions are asked
about the presentation of the learner. At the end of the presentation the teacher should announce the end of this part
or introduce the second part.

Learners must make some reference to a German-speaking country. Some statistics should be presented to show
that the candidate has done some research on the topic. Most centres accommodated this successfully during this
examination session. Learners may make use of AI but should make the contents of their presentation “their own”.
How AI constructs texts, was used by some candidates as is. Learners should be made aware of the fact that they start
their presentation with a controversial statement. How to present a topic should be practised during the Grade 12 year.

If a learner asks a question in this section already, the teacher should answer the question and not ignore it or prompt
the candidate to continue without answering the candidate’s question. The marks given for questioning then will go
towards Part B.

Teachers should ask “new”questions on the topic presented. Questions should be formulated to explore the presentation
on a wider level, or on parts which the learner has not been able to present due to the time constraint.

Part B is the first conversation. Its contents should cover the topic of Part A. The teacher thus needs to be prepared
to ask the learner questions and give enough time for the learner to answer. It is very important that in Part B as well
as in Part C the learner needs to ask the teacher at least two questions. Should the learner not do this close to the
end of each conversation, the teacher must prompt the learner to do so. Questions asked by the teacher should
be on AS level, specifically asking for reasons and explanations. This part of the speaking examination should be
spontaneous and not learned off by heart before the time. It should not be longer than seven minutes and not shorter
than 6 minutes.

Part C is the second conversation which should also last about seven minutes and not be shorter than 6 minutes.
Altogether the speaking examination should thus be close to 17 minutes long, but NOT longer than 20 minutes. The
learner needs to ask the teacher at least two questions in this section as well. Should the learner not do this close to the
end of this part of the conversation, the teacher must prompt the learner to do so. If only one question is asked during
each conversation, the maximum mark for this category is 3 marks out of a possible five. When no questions were
asked, no marks can be obtained. In both conversations the questions that are put to the teacher should have to
do with the topic being discussed. Teachers should be aware that even though learners must ask them questions,
they as teachers should keep their answers concise. It is a speaking examination for the learners.

In Part C questions on the other four topics for that specific year are supposed to be asked. The teacher does not
have to cover all four topics. Two could be sufficient as well, for that matter. Neither in Part B nor in Part C the answers
to possible questions should be learned off by heart. Both conversations should be spontaneous. Questions asked in
this part should be on AS level (and not on O level). Many examiners teach both grades and thus are familiar with the
topics of O level, but must at the same time be aware of the difference in levels between Grades 11 and 12.

Actions needing attention and suggestions to examiners

Just as for the essay paper, learners need to make use of the correct phrases when expressing an opinion: meiner
Meinung nach, ich denke, ich meine, was halten Sie davon wie denken Sie darüber, was ist Ihre Meinung dazu (NOT
darüber) u. Ä (NOT in meiner Meinung, in deiner Meinung nach – no preposition at the beginning for the latter). Another
phrase that needs attention: Das hängt von … ab (NOT das davon abhängen). The correct form of verbs in the Perfekt
should also be practised as from Grade 10, e.g. essen – gegessen (NOT ge-essen). The difference between Uhr and
Stunde needs to be clear, also when to use which word in which context. The people living in Namibia are Namibier in
German, NOT Namibianer.

When replying in the warm-up, many candidates chose the wrong congruency: Wie geht es Frau? It must be: Wie geht
es Ihnen or Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau followed by the surname of the teacher? Also, ich wohne bei meiner Mutter or
ich wohne mit meinen Geschwistern zusammen bei meinen Eltern and NOT: ich wohne mit meiner Mutter, which is a
direct translation from their mother tongue. Einkaufszentrum is the beautiful German word for Mall.
