      Paper 2



Key Message:
Learners should ensure that they understand that Question 5 requires them to summarise both texts in their own words,
whereby problems and solutions are to be covered regarding pollution and environmental issues.

1   GENERAL COMMENTS

Candidates in general performed less successfully than in the previous year, where they wrote the NSSCAS level
examinations for the second time in Foreign Language German. This shows, that teachers should receive advice from
a training workshop again to prepare their learners more thoroughly.

Most candidates tried to use their own words for answering the questions and it rarely happened that random sections
from the text were copied. However, some candidates just reshuffled the words from the text to create an answer which
resulted in sentences which did not make sense at all.

Learners should be made aware, that due to the fixed time of 1 hour 45 minutes, learners have no time to write their
answers in pencil first. The instructions are clear on the front page to write in dark blue or black pen.

Questions 3 and 4 require structured sentences, not abbreviated bullet point type of answers.

Question 5 requires a short piece of writing to be structured as an essay. Again, abbreviated bullet points do not give
credit to essay expectations.

2   COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS
    Question 1

    In this part of the paper, learners are given five synonyms for words from the text and then have to find matching
    words from that text. All words can be found in the first paragraph of the first text and have to fit into the text
    appropriately. The words are in sequence in that paragraph and can be identified according to their parts of speech
    (Wortarten).

    In this year, many candidates could not master this question well especially because they disregarded that the
    parts of speech of the given word can guide them, e.g., a noun requires a synonym noun again.

    Where candidates copied the word incorrectly, when they wrote “verursacht” for “gemacht “with a capital “V”, that
    answer was not credited.

    Learners often can be guided by the ending of a word as in “akutes” which shows that this adjective ends with “es”
    and the answer “drängendes” also ends with “es”. A plural noun must have a plural noun as a synonym again.

    Question 2

    In this part of the paper, learners are required to rephrase sentences from text 1 to test their grammatical knowledge.
    More candidates compared to the previous year found this exercise very challenging and about 80 % of the
    candidates could not obtain any marks. A few learners could obtain full marks, but it was obvious that they were
    of German Mother tongue background. A few learners knew how to convert the direct speech “meine Tomaten”
    to indirect speech “ihre Tomaten”, while some did not know the female possessive pronoun and used the male
    pronoun “seine”. Learners should be reminded only to write the answers in the open spaces instead of copying
    the whole sentence. They are not awarded any marks, if they make a spelling mistake anywhere in the copied
    sentence even if the requested answer phrase would have been correct.

    Question 3

    In this part of the paper, learners have to answer comprehension questions based on the first text. 15 points are
    awarded for content, while 5 extra marks are available for the quality of language used. If learners lift information
    directly from the text, they cannot obtain language marks and they may lose marks for not demonstrating full
    understanding of the text. Learners should not randomly reshuffle the words, which may lead to sentences which
    do not make sense, such as “Musst jeder verwendet ein Baum nachgepflanzt werden” or “Durch die Einnahme

                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                  269
und Verdauung des Menschen in die Abwässer.” By taking in and devouring of people into the sewerage waters.

(a) Many candidates obtained full marks, while some candidates did not understand that household
    appliances are made from plastic, glass or metal or could not understand that these materials are not
    easily utilised for bio degradable purposes.

(b) Only a few candidates could not find the examples for using natural resources: “Holz für Möbel”
    and “Pflanzenfasern für Kleidung”. Some candidates, however, forgot, that questions are asked in
    sequence within the text and they interchanged the answers of 3b with 3c. In that case, the answers
    were not credited.

(c) Many candidates obtained all 3 marks. The information of the reason as to why trees should be
    replanted was added to the mark scheme, because many candidates wrote about that explanation,
    instead of “umweltbewusst vorgehen”. Only one of those two pieces of information was credited,
    however, to add to the other two pieces of information: “Bäume nachpflanzen” and “Ackergebiete
    nicht einseitig bepflanzen”. With mother tongue background it was possible for one candidate to
    replace “einseitig” with “Man sollte Ackergebiete mehrseitig bepflanzen”. Again, when two questions
    relate to one longer paragraph, then the two questions which relate to it are in sequence.

(d) Many candidates obtained full marks. Some candidates did not clarify clearly, that due to population
    explosion “humans” or their living areas “Wohngebiete” take over areas that were once inhabited
    by plants and animals resulting in random reshuffling. For example, “Es ist ihre Wohngebiete
    übernehmen die Gegenden.”

(e) Some candidates reshuffled the sentences to write sentences that do not make sense. In that case,
    instead of “bei der Herstellung von Medikamenten“, they wrote „Bei der Herstellung und Verdauung
    des Menschen“. By the construction and devouring of humans...

(f)   Many candidates only gave an example of how harmful chemicals can enter the human body, namely
      through the pores when playing football on a pitch which has been watered with contaminated water.
      Few candidates identified the two other facts, namely that tomatoes can become contaminated
      with chemicals when watered with semi-purified water and people then eat the tomatoes containing
      harmful chemicals.
Question 4

In this part of the paper, learners have to answer comprehension questions based on the second text. 15 points
are awarded for content, while 5 extra marks are available for the quality of language use. Again, if learners lift
information directly from the text, they cannot obtain language marks and they may lose marks for not demonstrating
full understanding of the text.

Many candidates struggled to rephrase the answers to relate to the expectation of the questions. Some candidates
randomly copied phrases from the text and reshuffled the words to write a piece of writing which did not make
sense at all. As such, they lost content marks and language marks.

Some candidates wrote abbreviated bullet points where the meaning was not conveyed properly. Short but
complete sentences assist in structuring a clear message in the answer.

(a) Many candidates obtained the full 2 marks for this question. A few candidates reshuffled the
    sentences randomly. Examples are: “Man kann bepflastert ganze Flächen mit Solarkollektoren
    oder Windrädern, als man kann Wasserturbinen gebrauchen um Elektizität zu erzeugen und auf
    Solaranlagen setzen.“ „Die Menschen können alle Dächer auf Solaranlagen setzen.“ The people can
    put all roofs on solar panels.

(b) The majority of candidates scored both possible marks, but again the same candidates reshuffled
    sentences randomly or used abbreviated bullet points.

(c) This question required 4 possible facts to be identified and many candidates gained all four marks.
    By using compound sentences and pronouns, some candidates gave ambiguous answers where it
    was not clear whether they were referring to insects or birds. An example of reshuffling randomly is:
    “Auf natürliche Weise bekämpfen man muss Insekten bei der Bestäubung und außerdem Nahrung für
    unterschiedliche Vögel sind. “By natural means you must fight against insects which are pollinating
    plants and at the same time are food for different birds.


                                        NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
270
    Some candidates did not pay attention to spelling, which could change the meaning of the word
    completely and instead of “Man soll verschiedene Blumen wachsen lassen” You should let different
    flowers grow, they wrote “Man soll verschiedene Blumen waschen lassen” which means You should
    let different flowers be washed.

(d) 3 answers were expected. Many candidates did not realise that to use “Pfandflaschen” was part of
    the answer. They also were not credited if they did not clarify why people should carry containers
    with them, namely that they would use them for shopping, as in “Man soll eigene Behälter für Waren
    mitnehmen.” The third information related to “unverpacktes Obst kaufen” oder zumindest “unverpackte
    Waren kaufen“. Many candidates wrote „Man soll unverpackt kaufen“, which means one should buy
    unwrapped, which implies that people might have to appear unwrapped. That information could not
    be credited.

(e) This question required 4 answers. Most candidates could obtain at least 3 out of 4 marks.

Question 5

This question required an argumentative essay approach, whereby the arguments for the problems of pollution and
possible solutions to the situations should be taken from both texts.

More candidates than last year wrote an introduction to the text. However, those introductions were too long.
A suitable short introduction could be adapted from the instruction: “Es gibt viele Umweltprobleme, aber auch
Lösungen dazu.”

Very few candidates wrote paragraphs for the problems and solutions to rectify or combat environmental issues.
Many candidates did not relate to the texts but randomly wrote their own version without stating that it was their own
opinion. Own opinions must be clearly stated as, “Meiner Meinung nach… - Ich denke, dass …,”

To gain marks for their own opinion, the candidates could easily relate to the advice given, that they should clarify
which solutions to environmental issues could be applied to the situation in Namibia.

Two candidates did not write anything at all. Learners can be guided by some informational details, which they
have covered in the questions 3 and 4 at least to attempt to answer question 5. Any answer beyond the word limit
cannot be credited, thus, it is advisable for learners to include that own opinions within the written text.

Candidates who copied and reshuffled random phrases in Question 4 did the same in Question 5 and their answers
made no sense so could not be credited.

Some candidates gave their shortened answers in the form of bullet points, which cannot be evaluated as an
argumentative essay approach. Random copying of text phrases can also not be credited.

Many candidates ended their argumentative essay with their personal response to give a clear indication that they
had taken note of section (b) in the question, but many candidates did not elaborate on their opinion to be credited
with 5 marks. Most candidates’ own opinions, however, were clearly stated and gave the impression of a clear
stance to the theme.
A few candidates constructed their whole essay around the situation of Namibia, thus ignored Section A of
the question, which counted 10 marks. That also affected the language mark, which takes both sections into
consideration.

General Teaching Advice:

Learners should be made familiar with the words “der Vorteil und der Nachteil” for argumentative Essays.

It is advisable to teach the learners fixed phrases, such as
•     Der erste Vorteil…
•     Ein weiterer Vorteil ...,        Ein weiterer Aspekt ...
•     Zusätzlich kann man sagen, dass ...,            dazu kann man ergänzen, dass ...
•     Dagegen spricht, dass ... ,           Als Gegenargument sagen viele / manche, dass ...
•     Nicht nur ...., aber auch ...
•     Zum Schluss kann man sagen, dass ...              Zusammenfassend kann man sagen, dass ...
•     Meiner Meinung nach ...            Ich denke, dass ...       Ich finde, dass ...
•     Learners should be taught once more the difference between :
      “für” und “vor”           “wenn“ und „als“ und „anstatt“       „weil“ und „wann“


                                         NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                             271
    •      In German you use articles for sentences, unlike English, where you do write, “People believe that meat is
           unhealthy.” In German: “Die Menschen sollten natürliche Düngemittel einsetzen.”
    •      Umlaute have a function in German, because they change the sound of a vocal. It must be “sparen” not
           “spären”, “bedroht” not “bedröht”. Many candidates used single words from the text to then spell them with
           or without Umlaut to either end up with a changed meaning or no meaning at all.
    •      The comma is in front of the conjunction, which is the same sentence structure in English, Afrikaans or then
           German.
    •      The word “or” is written without the “r” in German as “oder”.
    •      Learners should be able to conjugate “haben”, “sein” und “werden” and Modal verbs at this stage, as well as
           be able to know how to detect singular and plural nouns to be able to conjugate the verbs accordingly.

GENERAL COMMENTS

This was the third written external examination under the new syllabus. 82 candidates wrote this examination; thus 82
essays were marked. To mark the essays, the same marking scheme as the previous year was used.

Candidates coped well with all five topics, although it must be emphasised that candidates should discuss the specific
topic, and not just the general one.

COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

In the Writing Paper, all the topics are either discursive or argumentative. During the year in which the Foreign Language
German AS level is taught, the teachers are presented with five topics, as can be seen below. For the essays however,
a specific aspect under each topic needs to be addressed. This is the title of each essay that is to be written on.
Learners should write the specific title of the topic on top of the page, NOT the GENERAL TOPIC. Therefore, it can be
said, that some candidates wrote about the topic instead of on the specific title, or only ever so slightly touched on the
title. If a candidate did not at all write about what is asked in the title, then no marks can be awarded for Content and
only some marks for Language. As a teacher the adequate row in the Mark Scheme still must reflect authentic German.
If the essay contains other European grammatical structures or vocabulary, it definitely influences both the Content and
the Language mark.

Writing an essay consisting of 250 – 400 words needs to be practised. The availability of more lines to write the essay
on helped the candidates to produce better argumentative or discursive essays this year as well. Blank pages may be
used for planning. Candidates who do their planning, deliver a better-quality essay. It is essential that candidates do
that in their final examination, as the mark scheme awards marks for a clear structure: introduction, paragraphs and a
conclusion. In the introduction candidates should mention the title. The conclusion should contain a clear point of view.

Foreign Language German AS learners may give their opinion in the introduction, but still need to write a proper
conclusion.

The following topics were given to the candidates, of which one had to be answered.

Umweltverschmutzung

     die Zerstörung unserer Umwelt.“
     Diskutieren Sie diese Aussage.

     Setzen Sie sich mit dieser Behauptung kritisch auseinander.

     Geschäftsführer.
     Nehmen Sie zu dieser Aussage Stellung.

Wissenschaftlicher und medizinischer Fortschritt

     Äußern Sie sich kritisch zu dieser Fragestellung.

Gleichberechtigung

Topic 1 was the most popular topic. 31 of the 82 candidates wrote about Umweltverschmutzung. The reading texts of
paper 2 covered this topic, thus candidates used vocabulary, information and arguments from the reading texts in their
essays. This, however, caused the candidates occasionally to ignore the specific topic.

Topic 3 was the second most popular topic. 22 of the 82 candidates wrote about Arbeit und Freizeit. Candidates
covered the general topic more often than writing about the specific topic. The specific topic required a discussion on a
four-day workweek. Only single essays were successful at this discussion.

Topic 5 was the third most popular topic. 15 of the 82 candidates wrote about Gleichberechtigung. Generally, candidates
discussed the general topic, and not the specific one. The latter required a discussion on separating boys and girls into
different schools. It would have been pleasing to see what the advantages and disadvantages of separate schools are,
as well as for mixed-gender schools.

Topic 2 was chosen by 13 of the 82 candidates. Although the general topic is very close to topic 1, the specific topic
required a different avenue. The specific topic mentioned water shortages because of climate change. This should
have been explored as well as other factors contributing to climate change. Generally, only the second part of the
specific topic was focused on, thus resulting in only satisfactory essays.

Topic 4, about scientific and medical progress, specifically questioning whether gene manipulation is ethical and moral,
was chosen by one candidate. The candidate produced a well-argued essay. It must be mentioned that it was clear
that this was a candidate with German as mother tongue background.

Some vocabulary and grammar to which the teachers should pay more attention to:
•    Only nouns are written with a capital letter in German.
•    Relativsätze, as in die Schüler, die … NOT die Schüler, was …
•    Negation, as in kein or keine NOT mit ohne
•    Steigerungen, as in klüger NOT mehr klug; which is a direct, wrong translation from English.
•    In “das größte Problem” – problem takes on the neutral definite article das, and then learners should be taught the
     correct endings of adjectives when combining definite articles, adjectives and nouns, which could be a topic for a
     workshop.
•    The position of verbs in sentences and subclauses as well that Modalverben always go together with the Infinitiv
     form of the second verb, as in kann verursachen.
•    After linking words in German there is NO comma as in Außerdem ist der Mensch …
•    Adjectives are written in small, and nouns are written with a capital letter as in sauberes Wasser, stabile
     Temperaturen, fossile Ressourcen.
•    „man“ conjugates the same way as “er, sie, es”, therefore it should also read “es hilft einem” (NOT es hilft man)
•    “false friends” should be avoided, as in Zeit spandieren, correct: verbringen, affektieren, correct: beeinflussen,
     Faktoren vs. Fabriken (factories in English), wohnen vs. bleiben, wees (Afrikaans) is NOT wissen in German, Gase
     vs Gasse, alley in German, arbeiten NOT werken from Afrikaans, fokusieren correct: sich auf etwas konzentrieren
•    “ich” is written small in the middle of a sentence.
•    the difference between wenn and als
•    Sentence structures need to be practised more:
     -    …., weil ……. Verb
     -    …, dass …….. Verb
     -    how to construct a proper German sentence in general
•    Learners “helped themselves” by translating some expressions directly into German. By using these direct
     translations, they do not write authentic German, as in Skills Fähigkeiten, Futur Zukunft, in meine Meinung instead
     of meiner Meinung nach
•    Learners should be confident in changing verbs into nouns and adjectives or vice versa. Maybe this could also be
     addressed at a workshop, for example zerstören – Zerstörung – zerstörend
•    Learners need to be trained to copy correctly. Umwelt is written with a capital letter and learners just ignored that.
     This issue also counts for Paper 2.
•    Müll (rubbish) has an Umlaut. Luft does not have an Umlaut. Learners did not copy correctly.
•    Humans “essen” and animals “fressen”
•    “zum Beispiel” are two words, as the first word is a contraction of a preposition (zu) and a declinated article (dem)
     which then follows the noun Beispiel


                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
     274
•   Sport treiben but Fußball spielen, Basketball spielen refers to the fact that any sport where a ball is involved, “wird
    gespielt”. In all the others the corresponding verb has to be used.
•   “Zusammenfassend kann man sagen” is the correct way to conclude
•   die Deutschen NOT: die deutschen Menschen, die Namibier NOT: Namibibianer, namibische Leute

Some issues raised here should be taught in the lower grades already.

The subject was again written fairly early at the beginning of the examination session. Languages are practical subjects
and with all the other subjects being written in English, the later learners write German the greater are the chances of
them demonstrating “weaker” language skills. Learners definitely showcased their language skills more effectively by
writing German Foreign Language more at the beginning of the examinations.

AOA: The majority of candidates have demonstrated a good knowledge of Geographical aspects and concepts.

AOB: A major challenge identified in the assessment is the candidates’ inability to respond correctly to the questions
that use the command word “Explain” the candidates provided single sentences with no reasoning, which led to low
marks for the question. Teacher should teach the learners the correct command word since the word explain requires
cause and effect reasoning.
AOC: The majority of candidates demonstrated poor skills in interpreting sources to assist them in responding to the
demand of the question. Some candidates totally ignored the sources provided and struggled to connect the sources
to theoretical knowledge, with some only describing but failing to explain, which was also the demand of the question.

GENERAL COMMENTS
•   Candidates often read sections of the questions, instead of the whole question. They could therefore not score
    full marks in the AOC questions with the two command words: describe and explain.

•   When presented with numerical data, candidates often struggle to identify whether values are increasing,
    decreasing, fluctuating or remain constant.
•   Candidates overlook scale, perspective and context. As a result their answers were descriptive rather than
    analytical.

         Correct answer
         Batholiths: Batholiths are large, dome-shaped intrusive igneous rock formations that cover an area of more
         than 100 square kilometres. They are formed when large volumes of magma solidify deep within the Earth’s
         crust. Over time, the overlying rocks erode, exposing the batholiths at the surface.

         Sills:  Sills are horizontal sheet-like intrusions of igneous rock that are injected between existing rock layers.
         They are formed when magma is injected along parallel layers of country rock and solidifies.
         Dykes:  Dykes are vertical or near-vertical sheet-like intrusions of igneous rock that cut across existing rock
         layers. They are formed when magma rises through fractures or cracks in the Earth’s crust and solidifies. [3]

    Soil erosion:  Flow mass movements, such as landslides or mudflows, can remove layers of soil from
    slopes, modifying their shape and gradient.

    Sediment deposition: Conversely, flow mass movements can deposit large amounts of sediment at the base
    of slopes, leading to the formation of new slopes or altering the existing ones.
    Scarp formation:  Flow mass movements can create scarps, which are steep cliffs or slopes formed by the
    removal of material from a slope, causing a modification in its overall shape.

    Slope flattening:  The accumulation of sediment or debris at the base of a slope due to flow mass movements
    can cause the slope to flatten out or become less steep.
    Slope steepening: On the other hand, flow mass movements can steepen slopes by removing material
    from the upper part of the slope, making it more inclined.

    Slope widening:  Flow mass movements can cause the widening of slopes by removing material from the
    sides of the slope, resulting in a broader slope profile.

          Frequent Channel Shifts:  Braided rivers are characterized by the constant shifting and changing of their

          Sandbars and Islands:  The large amount of sediment carried by braided rivers leads to the formation of
          sandbars and islands within the river channels. These features can change and shift as the river’s channels
          constantly adjust.
          Wide and Shallow Channels:  Braided rivers typically have wide and shallow channels due to the high

          river.

          formation of the river channels. The coarse sediment is easily transported and deposited by the flowing water.
          High Sediment Load: Braided rivers are known for their high sediment load, which is the result of erosion
          and deposition processes occurring upstream. This sediment load contributes to the formation of sandbars,
          islands and the shifting nature of the channels.

          Variable Water Discharge:  The water flows in braided rivers can vary significantly, especially during periods
          of high precipitation or snowmelt. This variability in water discharge can result in increased sediment transport
          and channel shifting.

        Hydraulic action:  This process occurs when the force of flowing water dislodges and removes rock
        fragments from the river bed and banks. The fast-moving water in a river can exert significant pressure
        against the sides of the channel, causing erosion and widening of the river channel, eventually leading to the
        formation of a gorge.

        Abrasion/Corrasion:  Abrasion is the process by which the river’s load such as sediment, rocks or boulders
        is repeatedly carried along the river bed and banks. As these materials are transported downstream, they
        scrape against the river channel, wearing it away over time. The continuous abrasion by the moving load
        helps deepen and widen the river channel, creating a gorge.
        Corrosion/solution: This process involves the chemical dissolution of rock material in the river water.
        Certain rocks, such as limestone or chalk, are particularly susceptible to dissolution due to the presence of
        weak acids in the water, like carbonic acid. Over time, the dissolution weakens the rock and causes it to erode,
        contributing to the formation of a gorge.                                                                    [6]

SECTION B:  ECONOMIC ACTIVITIES AND THE USE OF RESOURCES

4   (a) AOA:  Give a reason why areas of water supply and areas of water demand are often different.
        Wrong Answers:
        Some areas experience higher rainfall while some experience lower rainfall.
        Areas of water surplus and areas of water demand have water deficit.

        Correct Answers:
        Geographic location:  areas of water supply are often located in regions that have abundant water resources,
        such as near rivers, lakes or underground aquifers. On the other hand, areas of water demand can be situated
        far away from these sources, particularly in arid or drought-prone regions.

        Population density:  areas of high population density tend to have high water demand due to the concentration
        of residential, commercial and industrial activities. However, they may not necessarily have a sufficient local
        water supply to meet this demand.
        Economic activities:   areas with intensive agricultural, industrial or commercial activities often have high
        water demand. These areas may not coincide with areas that have ample water supply, especially if the
        economic activities are located in water-stressed regions.

        Climate variations: areas with high water supply availability, such as regions with heavy rainfall or rivers
        with significant flows, may not align with areas of high water demand. For example, water-rich areas may
        experience seasonal or periodic water surplus, while areas of demand may experience water scarcity due to
        drought or other climatic factors.
        Water infrastructure:  areas of water supply are often where water infrastructure, such as reservoirs, dams
        or water treatment plants, are located. These infrastructures are typically built in areas that can efficiently
        harness and manage water resources, rather than being determined solely by areas of high water demand.

        Environmental constraints: areas of high water supply may be determined by environmental factors such
        as topography, soil type and vegetation, which may not necessarily align with areas of high water demand.
        Water rights and ownership: in some cases, areas of water supply may be owned or controlled by different
        entities other than areas of water demand. This can result in water being transported over long distances to
        meet demand, further exacerbating the mismatch between supply and demand areas. Any one                  [1]

        Accept other relevant responses.
        Recommendation:
        Teachers should teach learners what causes the difference between areas of water supply and water
        demand.

      major river systems.
      Climate patterns: some areas experience specific climate patterns that contribute to water surplus. For

      Melting snow and ice:  regions with significant snowfall or glaciers can experience surplus water during the

      Poor drainage infrastructure:  in some cases, areas may have a surplus of water due to inadequate

      different communities, regions or social groups. It means that some people or areas have limited or no access
      to sufficient and good quality water, while others have more than enough. This inequality can be caused
      by various factors, including geographical location, socioeconomic status, political factors and infrastructure
      development.

      Displacement of communities:  refers to the forced relocation of people from their homes and land due to
      the construction of dams, reservoirs, canals or other water infrastructure projects. This displacement often
      occurs when these projects require the flooding of large areas, resulting in the loss of homes, agricultural
      lands, and livelihoods for affected communities. The displaced communities are then relocated to other
      areas, sometimes with inadequate compensation or support, leading to social, economic and environmental
      challenges for those affected.
      Conflict and competition: conflict and competition by water sharing projects refers to the disputes and
      rivalries that arise between different individuals, communities or countries over the allocation and distribution
      of water resources. Water is a limited and essential resource and as populations grow or demand increases,
      the competition for water resources becomes more intense. Water sharing projects are initiatives aimed at
      managing and distributing water fairly among different users or regions. However, these projects can often
      lead to conflicts and competition between stakeholders such as farmers, industries and urban populations who
      compete for limited water resources.

      Environmental degradation:   environmental degradation caused by water sharing projects refers to the
      negative impacts on the natural environment resulting from the construction, operation and management of
      water infrastructure projects, such as dams, reservoirs, canals and pipelines, which are intended to facilitate
      the sharing of water resources among different regions or communities. The construction of dams and
      reservoirs often leads to the flooding of large areas, resulting in the destruction of natural habitats, including

                                           NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
282
        forests, wetlands and riverine ecosystems. This can lead to the loss of biodiversity and have negative impacts
        on wildlife.                                                                                               [6]

    (b) AOB:  Explain three spatial characteristics of factories in High Income Countries (HICs).
        Wrong Answers:
        They employ many people.
        They operate in many countries and headquarters in HIC.
        They are located in the CBD.

        Correct Answers:
        Concentration in industrial zones: factories in HICs are often located in designated industrial zones or
        industrial parks. These areas are specifically designated for manufacturing and industrial activities, providing
        a concentrated space for factories to operate. This spatial concentration allows for efficient infrastructure
        development and access to necessary resources.

        Proximity to transportation networks: factories in HICs are typically located in close proximity to
        transportation networks such as highways, railways and ports which ensures easy access to transportation
        routes, allowing for efficient movement of raw materials, finished goods as well as workforce.
        Accessibility to skilled labor: HICs generally have a skilled workforce and factories locate in areas where
        there is easy access to these skilled labour pools. This often involves being in close proximity to urban centers
        or areas with high levels of education and training facilities.

        Availability of supportive infrastructure:  factories in HICs are typically located in areas with robust
        infrastructure, including reliable electricity, water supply, telecommunications and waste management
        systems. These infrastructural provisions are essential for smooth factory operations.
        Proximity to suppliers and markets: factories in HICs often prioritize locating near their suppliers and
        target markets. This reduces transportation costs, lead times and allows for quick response to changing
        demands. Being close to suppliers also facilitates just-in-time inventory management.

          Soil Quality: Intensive farming areas require fertile soil with high nutrient content in order to support the
          rapid growth of crops. Soil fertility is often maintained through the use of various techniques such as chemical
          fertilizers, crop rotation and organic matter amendments.




                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025

    Topography:  the physical features of the land, including its slope and drainage patterns, can significantly
    influence the suitability of an area for intensive farming. Flat areas with good water drainage are preferred as
    they allow for efficient irrigation and mechanized farming practices.
    Climate: intensive farming areas usually have a favourable climate with adequate rainfall or access to irrigation
    systems. The availability of water throughout the growing season is crucial for crop growth and productivity.

    Access to Water: intensive farming requires a reliable and sufficient water supply for irrigation purposes.
    Proximity to water sources such as rivers, lakes or underground aquifers is essential for maintaining optimal
    moisture levels in the soil.
    Temperature:  the temperature range in an intensive farming area should be suitable for the crops being
    grown. Different crops have specific temperature requirements for growth and the area should fall within
    these optimal ranges.

    Pest and Disease Pressure:  intensive farming areas often face higher risks of pests and diseases due to the
    concentration and monoculture of crops. Factors such as the prevalence of specific pests and diseases in an
    area, as well as the ability to implement effective pest management strategies, can determine the viability of
    intensive farming operations.                                  Any three                                   [3]

(c) AOA and AOC:  Using Fig. 6 only, describe and explain how two of these factors positively
    influence pastoral farming systems.
    Wrong Answers:
    Technology can be used to fertilise crops for higher yield.
    Using an incubator to make eggs hatch.

    Correct Answers:
    Population density: In areas with high population density, this can provide a larger local market for livestock
    products. This encourages pastoral farmers to produce more and earn more income. A higher population also
    means greater pressure on land, so farmers often shift to a more efficient system such as controlled grazing,
    reduced herd sizes with improved breeds or buying of supplementary feed. This leads to higher productivity
    per animal. More people also provide labour for herding and caring of animals, which makes farms operate
    efficiently.

    Technology:   has had a significant impact on pastoral farming systems, revolutionizing the way these
    systems are managed and improving their overall efficiency by monitoring and data collection: Technology
    allows farmers to gather real-time data on various parameters like weather conditions, soil moisture levels and
    pasture growth. Remote sensing technologies, such as satellite imagery and drones, can provide valuable
    information for making informed decisions about grazing management.
    Transport:   good transportation networks ensure easy access to markets, veterinary services and other
    necessary inputs for pastoral farmers. This allows them to bring their products to the market efficiently,
    reducing post-harvest losses and ensuring timely delivery of perishable items like milk or meat to enable
    pastoral farmers to reach a wider customer base, both domestically and internationally. This not only helps
    them increase their sales but also provides opportunities to diversify their products and specialize in high-
    value market demands.

    Physical environment:   Pastoral farming relies heavily on access to ample grazing land. The physical
    environment, such as natural grasslands and open spaces, provides the necessary resources for livestock
    to graze and forage. A diverse range of vegetation in the environment ensures a balanced diet for animals,
    promoting their health and productivity. The physical environment’s climate characteristics, including
    temperature, rainfall and sunlight directly impact pastoral farming systems. Certain types of livestock thrive
    in specific climate conditions and favorable weather patterns support healthier animals as well as abundant
    forage availability. Adequate rainfall ensures the growth of nutritious grasses and vegetation, essential for
    animal nutrition.                                                                                          [6]

         that comes with living in a new and unfamiliar environment. They may be drawn to the natural beauty, diverse

         LIC can challenge individuals to adapt to new circumstances, learn new skills and overcome obstacles that
         they may not have encountered in a HIC. This can lead to personal growth and development, as individuals
         learn to navigate unfamiliar situations and expand their worldview.                                      [6]

         Accept other relevant responses Any two developed Only descriptions ‒ maximum 2 marks                           [10]

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS

AOA
•   Provide at least two triggers in definitions.
•   Provide at least two definitions of terms.
•   Teach learners how to describe scaffolds provided.

AOB
•   Provide detailed descriptions and explanations of geographical terms.
•   Provide examples (case studies) so learners understand from a practical point of view.

AOC
•   Provide learners with scaffolds (maps, graphs, tables or photographs) when dealing with specific objectives under
    AOA, AOB, AOC and AOD where possible.
•   Teach learners how to interpret and manipulate scaffolds.
•   AOC can be done by AOA, AOB or by AOC itself.

1   (a) (i)      AOA: Distinguish between soil moisture and river discharge.
                        Comment on question
                        Fairly well answered as the majority of learners were able to score at least two to four marks.
                        Wrong answers
                        Soil moisture refers to water available for the plants, whereas river discharge refers to when the
                        water leaves the river through the mouth.
                        Correct answers
                        Soil moisture refers to the amount of water contained within the soil.
                        River discharge refers to the volume of water flowing through a river or stream over a specific
                        period of time.
                        Soil moisture is localized and relates to water availability for plants while river discharge
                        encompasses the movement and availability of water within a larger river basin.

                        Accept other relevant answers

                        Any two triggers for both (definition/description or example provided)
                        Comparative word not regarded                                                                   [4]

                        Suggested improvement:
                        Teachers should emphasize the definitions of geographic concepts under each topic.
          (ii)   AOA: Describe the concept of water balance.
                 Comment on question
                 Fairly well answered as candidates showed knowledge of the concept though a few were giving the
                 importance of water balance and not describing the concept.
                 Candidates were aware of the formula to work out water balance, but could not recall it correctly.
                 Wrong answers
                 Water balance is used to identify areas of water surplus and water deficit.

                 Correct answers
                 Water balance: refers to the inflows to any water system or area is equal to its outflows plus the change
                 in storage during a time interval.
                 It involves analyzing the various processes that affect the availability and distribution of water.
                 Precipitation: determines the amount of water that flows into a geographic area. Precipitation should be
                 equal to evaporation to maintain water balance.
                 Runoff: determines the amount of water available for processes in the geographic area. The amount of
                 water infiltrating and percolating should be equal to the amount of water evaporating to maintain water
                 balance.
                 Groundwater recharge or soil moisture: the amount of water infiltrating and percolating should be
                 equal to the amount of ground water flow into rivers and aquifers to maintain water balance.
                 Evaporation: determines the amount of water leaving the geographic area. The amount of evaporation
                 should be equal to the amount of precipitation to maintain water balance.                              [5]
                 Accept other relevant answers

                 Candidate can take two examples of contrasting water balance situations and describe the
                 concept in more detail like that.
                 1 mark – description of water balance.
                 1 mark – description of input.
                 1 mark – description of flow.
                 1 mark – description of store.
                 1 mark – description of outflow

                 AOA by definition – 2 triggers
                 AOA by explanation and comparison which triggers impact
                 AOA by equation – 2 marks

        Suggested improvement
        Teachers should emphasis the processes of water balance with regard to the input, flow, store and output.

(b) AOB: Explain the components of the hydrological cycle in tropical deserts during summer.
    Comment on question
    Fairly well answered as candidates showed knowledge of the processes of a hydrological cycle, but could
    not explain how it changes in summer as well as in tropical deserts.
    Wrong answers
    Rainfall is less in summer than in winter.
    Desert rainfall is more than 1000mm in summer
    The lag time is shorter and the rising limb is gentle
    Correct answers
    Evaporation: the intense heat in tropical deserts during summer leads to high evaporation rates. The sun’s
    energy causes the water on the surface, such as rivers, lakes or even soil moisture, to evaporate and transform
    into water vapor.
    Transpiration: vegetation in tropical deserts, although sparse, undergoes transpiration, wherein plants
    release water vapor through their leaves. This contributes to the overall moisture in the atmosphere.
    Condensation: as the water vapour rises in the atmosphere, it cools down, leading to condensation. This
    process forms clouds, especially during the late afternoon or evening when the temperatures drop.
    Precipitation: in tropical deserts during summer, precipitation is relatively low. However, occasional rain
    showers or thunderstorms may occur due to the convective activity generated by the intense heat and rapid
    heating of the land surface. These rain showers are typically short-lived but can provide temporary relief to
    the arid environment.
    Infiltration: when precipitation occurs, a portion of it penetrates the ground, a process known as infiltration.
    The sandy soils found in tropical deserts have good drainage capacity, which allows water to percolate into
    the underground aquifers.
    Runoff: due to the limited vegetation cover and the porous nature of desert soils, the rate of surface runoff is
    high in tropical deserts. This means that a significant portion of the precipitation quickly flows over the surface,
    rather than being absorbed by the ground.
    Groundwater recharge: in tropical deserts, where water availability is limited, groundwater plays a crucial
    role. The infiltration of water into the ground helps recharge the underground water reserves, sustaining the
    oasis and providing water for plants, animals and human communities.
    Evapotranspiration: The combination of evaporation and transpiration, known as evapotranspiration, is
    a vital stage in the hydrological cycle. In tropical deserts during summer, with high temperatures and low
    humidity, evapotranspiration rates can be quite significant, resulting in the loss of water from the surface back
    into the atmosphere.                                                                                             [6]

    Accept other relevant answers
    3 marks reserved for just descriptions
    1 description well developed = 5 marks
    Any 3/6 explanations – 1 explanation developed well can gain an extra mark for development.
    Words and phrases that do not bear explanations – 0 marks

    Suggested improvement
    Teachers should emphasis the processes of hydrological cycles of each tropical region and how they are
    influenced in each season. Teachers should also clearly explain the differences between the hydrological
    cycle and the hydrographs.

(c) AOB (3) AOD (7): To what extent do you agree that the modification of the hydrological cycle
    is caused by human activities?
    Comment on question
    Well answered
    Candidates could make decisions, as they could evaluate how human activities or physical factors modify
    the hydrological cycle. Many learners could score at least seven marks.

    Correct answers
    Ideas such as

    Agree to a large extent/agrees
    Dam construction: humans modify the hydrological cycle by building dams across rivers, which can control
    the flow of water, store water in reservoirs and release water when needed for various purposes such as
    irrigation, drinking water supply or hydroelectric power generation.
    Deforestation: the removal of trees and vegetation alters the hydrological cycle by reducing evapotranspiration,
    which is the process of water vapour being released into the atmosphere through both plant transpiration and

                                         NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                              293
      evaporation from the soil. This results in decreased rainfall, disrupted precipitation patterns and changes in
      runoff dynamics.
      Urbanization: the expansion of urban areas and construction of impervious surfaces, such as roads, buildings
      and parking lots modify the hydrological cycle by reducing the amount of water that infiltrates into the ground.
      This leads to increased surface runoff, decreased groundwater recharge and increased likelihood of flooding.
      Irrigation: humans modify the hydrological cycle by using water from freshwater sources, such as rivers
      or underground aquifers, to irrigate crops. This increases the amount of water evaporated from agricultural
      fields, resulting in altered evapotranspiration rates and potentially affecting regional rainfall patterns.
      Climate change: human-induced climate change is altering the hydrological cycle on a global scale.
      Increased greenhouse gas emissions from human activities are leading to rising global temperatures, which
      in turn affect precipitation patterns, evaporation rates and the overall water cycle. This can result in changes
      in rainfall intensity, shifts in the timing and distribution of rainfall, as well as increased frequency of extreme
      weather events such as droughts and floods.
      Agrees to a low extent/disagrees
      Natural Climate change: rising global temperatures due to climate change can lead to changes in precipitation
      patterns and the melting of glaciers as well as ice sheets. These changes can modify the hydrological cycle
      by altering the timing and amount of water availability.
      Natural disasters: events such as hurricanes, floods and droughts can significantly impact the hydrological
      cycle. For example, hurricanes can cause heavy rainfall and flooding, whereas droughts can lead to water
      scarcity and decreased river flow.
      Volcanic eruptions: volcanic eruptions can release large amounts of ash and gases into the atmosphere,
      which can affect rainfall patterns. The ash particles can act as cloud condensation nuclei, potentially leading
      to increased rainfall, while volcanic gases like sulfur dioxide can form aerosols that reflect sunlight and lead to
      cooling, impacting evaporation rates.
      Earthquakes and landslides: these natural phenomena can alter the flow of water by changing the
      topography of the land, creating new pathways for water or blocking existing ones. This can result in increased
      or decreased runoff, affecting the overall balance of the hydrological cycle.
      Erosion and sedimentation: natural processes like erosion and sedimentation can modify watercourses or
      river channels. The movement of sediments can alter river flow patterns and affect the distribution as well as
      the availability of water, thus impacting the hydrological cycle.

      Agrees to a certain extent/ agrees and disagrees
      Humans modify the hydrological cycle by building dams across rivers, which can control the flow of water,
      store water in reservoirs and release water when needed for various purposes such as irrigation, drinking
      water supply, or hydroelectric power generation, BUT natural processes like erosion and sedimentation can
      also modify watercourses and river channels. The movement of sediments can alter river flow patterns and
      affect the distribution and availability of water, thus impacting the hydrological cycle, suggesting that the
      modification of the hydrological cycle is modified by both human activities and natural processes or
      suggests that human activities are not the only factors modifying the hydrological cycle.

      Accept other relevant answers
      Answer based on learner’s evaluation and decision made.

      Level 3 (8-10 marks)
      Knowledge and understanding of the modification of the hydrological cycle by human activities and/or
      nature has been shown to a full extent.
      Evaluation of the modification of the hydrological cycle by human activities and/or by nature has been done
      clearly and thoroughly.
      A decision on whether the modification of the hydrological cycle is caused by humans and/or nature has
      been made clearly.

      Level 2 (4-7marks)
      Knowledge and understanding of the modification of the hydrological cycle by human activities and/or
      nature has been shown to a certain extent.
      Evaluation of the modification of the hydrological cycle by human activities and/or by nature has been done,
      although not clearly and thoroughly.
      A decision on whether the modification of the hydrological cycle is caused by humans and/or nature has
      been made.

      Level 1 (1-3 marks)
      Limited knowledge and understanding of the modification of the hydrological cycle by human activities and/
      or nature has been shown to a full extent

               Correct answers
               Stratosphere:
               -   located directly above the troposphere the lowest layer of the atmosphere and extends from about
                   10 to 50 kilometers above the Earth’s surface.
               -   temperatures generally increase with altitude due to the absorption of solar radiation by ozone
                   molecules.
               -   contains the ozone layer, which absorbs and filters out a significant portion of the sun’s harmful
                   ultraviolet or UV radiation.

               -   stable, less turbulent conditions.

               Mesosphere:
               -   positioned above the stratosphere, reaching from about 50 to 85 kilometers above the Earth’s
                   surface.
               -   temperatures in the mesosphere decrease with altitude, reaching their lowest point around -90 to
                   -100 degrees Celsius.
               -   contains a layer called the mesopause, which is the coldest part of the Earth’s atmosphere.
               -   due to its low density and high altitude

               Any two differences                                                                                       [4]

        (ii)   AOA: Describe how the atmosphere is heated during the night.
               Comment on question
               Well answered.
               Most candidates could describe how the atmosphere is heated during the night. They started with
               insolation during the day, terrestrial radiations at night and how cloud cover may act as a blanket to
               keep the atmosphere warm at night.
               Wrong answers
               The atmosphere is heated by the sun directly
               There is no sun at night, therefore, the atmosphere is cold at night.




                                              NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
                                                                                                                 295
          Correct answers
          Radiation:
          As the Earth’s surface cools down at night, it emits long wave radiation, also known as infrared radiation.
          This outgoing radiation is absorbed by the greenhouse gases present in the atmosphere, such as
          carbon dioxide and water vapour.
          These greenhouse gases then re-emit some of the absorbed energy in all directions, including back
          towards the Earth’s surface. This process is known as the greenhouse effect.
          Conduction:
          As the Earth’s surface cools down, it loses heat through direct contact with the cooler air in its
          immediate vicinity.
          The molecules in the lowest layer of the atmosphere, called the boundary layer, gain thermal energy
          from the Earth’s surface through conduction, thus leading to heating of the atmosphere.

          Accept other relevant answers

          1 mark – radiation emitted by earth
          1 mark – radiation absorbed by greenhouse gases
          1 mark – re-emitting of absorbed energy by greenhouse gases
          1 mark – losing of heat by conduction
          1 mark – how conduction occurs

          AOA by description
          AOA by explanation
                                                                                                                [5]
          Suggested on improvement
          Teachers should help learners understand that although the primary source of energy is the sun, incoming
          solar radiation does not directly warm up the atmosphere. Teachers should also explain other processes
          that transfer heat to the atmosphere apart from terrestrial radiation.

(b) AOB: Explain the local daytime energy budget in terms of input and output analysis.
      Comment on question
      Poorly answered; many candidates could explain insolation as input and terrestrial radiations as output, but
      could not explain other processes. Candidates were able to score at least two marks.

      Correct answers

      The input of energy in the daytime energy budget can come from several sources:
      Incoming solar radiation: the primary source of energy input during the daytime is the Sun. Solar
      radiation provides the Earth with heat and light energy.
      Human activities: human activities can also contribute to the input of energy in the form of artificial light
      sources, such as streetlights and buildings.
      Latent heat transfers: when a substance changes from one phase to another, such as from solid to
      liquid or liquid to gas, energy is released in the form of latent heat adding energy to the daytime budget. An
      example would be when water condenses and changes from a gas to a liquid, it releases latent heat into its
      surroundings, causing the surrounding area to warm up.
      The output of energy refers to the ways in which energy is released or transferred from the local
      area:
      Terrestrial radiation: the Earth’s surface absorbs a portion of the incoming solar radiation and re-emits it
      as long wave radiation or infrared radiation. This terrestrial radiation is an important output of energy, as it
      helps to cool the Earth’s surface.
      Evaporation: energy is also transferred from the local area through the process of evaporation. When
      water evaporates, it takes energy from the surroundings, causing a cooling effect.
      Convection: heat is transported vertically in the atmosphere through convection. Warm air rises, carrying
      energy away from the surface, while cooler air sinks, transferring energy back to the surface.
      Reflection and scattering: some of the incoming solar radiation is reflected or scattered back to space
      without being absorbed by the Earth’s surface. This reflects a loss of energy from the local area.

      Accept other relevant answers
      3 marks reserved for just descriptions
      1 description well developed = 5 marks
      Any 3/6 explanations – 1 explanation developed well can given an extra mark for development.
      Words and phrases that do not bear explanations – 0 marks                                                     [6]




                                          NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025
296
    Suggested improvement
    Teachers should help learners to understand the local energy budget in terms of input and output analysis
    with reference to daytime and night time energy model. Teachers should also emphasize the role of other
    processes in addition to insolation and terrestrial radiations.

(c) AOB (3) AOD (7): To what extent do you agree that climate change has a positive effect on the
    local context?
    Comment on question
    Fairly well answered; candidates were able to make a decision and evaluate the positive or negative effects
    of climate change on the local context. Many candidates were able to score at least five marks.

    Correct answers:
    Ideas such as.
    Agree to a large extent/agrees
    Longer growing seasons: a warmer climate and extended periods of frost-free days may result in longer
    growing seasons. This allows farmers to cultivate a broader range of crops and potentially increase
    agricultural productivity.
    Increased tourism: some regions may experience a boost in tourism due to milder winters, longer
    summers or the emergence of new ecosystems. This can potentially lead to economic growth and job
    opportunities.
    Improved energy production: certain areas may benefit from increased wind or solar energy production
    due to changes in wind patterns or increased sunlight hours. This can contribute to a more sustainable and
    cleaner energy supply.
    Access to new resources: melting glaciers and changes in precipitation patterns may lead to increased
    water availability in some regions. This can provide communities with access to alternative water sources
    for drinking, agriculture and industrial purposes.
    Expanded biodiversity: climate change may result in shifts in ecosystems, leading to the introduction
    of new plant and animal species to an area. This can enhance biodiversity and provide opportunities for
    ecological research and conservation efforts.
    Reduced heating costs: in colder regions, warmer temperatures can lead to reduced heating requirements
    for households and businesses. This can potentially lower energy consumption and heating costs, freeing
    up resources for other uses.
    Enhanced water transport: rising sea levels may increase water transport accessibility in coastal regions,
    potentially improving trade routes and economic connections between communities.

    Agrees to a low extent/disagrees
    Increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events: climate change can result in more
    frequent and intense heatwaves, droughts, storms, floods and hurricanes. These events can cause
    significant damage to infrastructure, homes and livelihoods in the local context.
    Decline in agricultural productivity: climate change affects temperature, rainfall patterns and the
    availability of water resources, which can lead to reduced crop yields and livestock productivity. This, in turn,
    impacts food security and the local economy.
    Rising sea levels and coastal erosion: global warming leads to the melting of polar ice caps and glaciers,
    causing sea levels to rise. Coastal areas and low-lying regions are particularly vulnerable to flooding and
    erosion. This poses a threat to coastal communities, infrastructure and ecosystems.
    Loss of biodiversity and ecosystem disruption: climate change can disrupt ecosystems and result in
    the loss of biodiversity. Changes in temperature and precipitation can alter habitats and disrupt the natural
    balance of ecosystems, affecting local flora as well as fauna.
    Spread of diseases: climate change can influence the geographical distribution and prevalence of
    diseases. Warmer temperatures and altered rainfall patterns can create favourable conditions for disease-
    carrying organisms such as mosquitoes, leading to increased transmission of vector-borne diseases like
    malaria and dengue fever.
    Water scarcity and reduced water quality: climate change can impact on water availability and quality.
    Droughts, increased evaporation rates and changes in precipitation patterns can lead to water scarcity,
    affecting agriculture, industries and households. Additionally, higher temperatures can contribute to water
    pollution and the spread of waterborne diseases.
    Economic impacts and displacement: the negative effects of climate change can have significant
    economic consequences on the local context. Losses in agriculture, infrastructure damage, increased
    healthcare costs and the displacement of populations due to extreme weather events can strain local
    economies as well as lead to long-term socio-economic challenges.

    Accept other relevant answers
    Other relevant answers to be discussed at standardisation.
    Answer based on learner’s evaluation and decision made.

    Solar energy is a renewable and abundant source of energy. The sun provides an unlimited supply
    of energy that can be converted into electricity through solar panels. Unlike fossil fuels, which are finite
    resources, solar energy can be harnessed for generations to come.
    Solar energy helps in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The production of electricity from solar
    energy is a clean process that does not release any harmful pollutants or greenhouse gases into the
    atmosphere. This helps in mitigating climate change and reducing air pollution.
    Solar energy can be deployed in various scales and locations. Solar panels can be installed on
    rooftops, open fields, or even floating on water bodies. This flexibility in deployment allows for the
    production of electricity at the point of use, reducing transmission losses and the need for extensive
    infrastructure.
    Solar energy reduces reliance on fossil fuels. By producing electricity from solar energy, we reduce our
    dependence on fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas. This helps in diversifying our energy sources
    and enhancing energy security.
    Solar energy has become increasingly affordable. The cost of solar panels and related technologies has
    significantly decreased over the years, making solar energy more accessible and economically viable. This
    has led to a rapid increase in the deployment of solar power plants as well as the adoption of solar panels by
    individuals and businesses alike.
    Agree to a low extent/disagrees
    Intermittent Power Generation: solar energy is reliant on sunlight, so power production fluctuates with
    weather conditions and time of day. This intermittency can lead to inconsistent power output and reliability
    issues.
    High Initial Costs: the cost of solar panels and associated equipment can be prohibitive of expensive
    for some, making it difficult to implement solar energy on a large scale. This can hinder the widespread
    adoption of solar power.
    Land Requirements: solar farms require significant land space to install large arrays of solar panels. This
    can be challenging in densely populated areas or regions with limited available land, restricting the potential
    for solar energy production.
    Environmental Impact: the production of solar panels involves the use of toxic chemicals, such as silicon
    tetrachloride, which can be harmful if not handled and disposed of properly. Additionally, the manufacturing
    process contributes to greenhouse gas emissions. Furthermore, large-scale solar farms can disrupt local
    ecosystems and habitats.
    Limited Energy Storage: solar energy production is subject to the availability of sunlight, meaning
    excess energy generated during peak periods may go to waste if not captured and stored efficiently. The
    development of cost-effective and efficient energy storage systems is crucial for maximizing the use of solar
    power.

    Agrees to a certain extent/agrees and disagrees

    Solar panels can be installed on rooftops, open fields or even floating on water bodies. This flexibility in
    deployment allows for the production of electricity at the point of use, reducing transmission losses and the
    need for extensive infrastructure, BUT the production of solar panels involves the use of toxic chemicals,
    such as silicon tetrachloride, which can be harmful if not handled and disposed of properly and the
    manufacturing process contributes to greenhouse gas emissions. Farms can also disrupt local ecosystems
    and habitats, which makes people reluctant to use it, suggesting that it is not entirely gaining importance.

    Accept other relevant answers

    Answer based on learner’s evaluation and decision made.

    Evaluation of why the production of electricity through solar energy is gaining and/or not gaining importance

    Correct answers

    Economic growth: industrial change often leads to increased productivity and innovation, which can
    contribute to overall economic growth in HICs. It can result in higher GDP, higher incomes and improved living
    standards for the people.
    Job creation: industrial change creates new industries and sectors, leading to job creation. As traditional
    industries may decline, new opportunities emerge in areas such as technology, renewable energy and
    advanced manufacturing. This can help reduce unemployment rates and provide more diverse employment
    opportunities for people.
    Technological advancements: industrial change fosters technological advancements as companies invest
    in research and development. This can lead to the development of new products, services and processes that
    improve efficiency and quality of life. Technological advancements can also have positive spill-over effects
    across various sectors, leading to further innovation.
    Environmental sustainability: industrial change can drive the adoptation of sustainable practices and
    technologies. With growing concerns about climate change and environmental degradation, industries are
    increasingly transitioning towards cleaner and greener alternatives. This includes the use of renewable
    energy, waste reduction, recycling and sustainable production methods which improves people’s quality of life.
    Improved infrastructure: industrial change often necessitates investments in infrastructure. This can include
    the development of transportation networks, communication systems, energy grids and urban planning.
    Improved infrastructure can enhance connectivity, efficiency, and quality of life for people.
    Human capital development: industrial change leads to a shift in the skill sets demanded by the job
    market. This encourages investment in human capital development through education and training

(c) AOB (3) AOD (7): To what extent do you agree that the structural characteristics of a small
    scale cottage industry are beneficial to the local people?
      Comment on question
      Moderately answered, as many candidates demonstrated good knowledge of the small scale cottage
      industry, however, the evaluations brought forth are limited. The majority could score at least six marks.

      Correct answers
      Ideas such as:

      Agree to a large extent/agrees
      Flexibility and autonomy: the small scale cottage industry allows local people to have more control over
      their work and schedule. They can work from their own homes or small workshops, giving them the freedom
      to set their own hours and maintain a better work-life balance.
      Low start-up costs: small scale cottages often require minimal investment in terms of infrastructure and
      equipment. This makes it more accessible for local people to start their own businesses, as they do not
      need to take on significant financial burdens.
      Utilization of local skills and resources: small scale cottage industry relies on local skills and resources,
      which can help preserve traditional craftsmanship and knowledge. This can be particularly beneficial in rural
      areas, where people have specialized skills that may not be easily transferred to other industries.
      Employment opportunities: small scale cottage industry can generate employment opportunities for local
      people, especially in areas where formal job opportunities may be limited. By providing income-generating
      activities, the cottage industry can contribute to poverty reduction and economic development at the local
      level.
      Promotion of cultural heritage and tourism: small scale cottage industries often produce unique and
      handmade goods that are representative of a particular region’s culture and heritage. This can attract
      tourists and create opportunities for cultural exchange, leading to increased local pride and economic
      benefits through tourism.
      Agrees to a low extent/disagrees
      Limited job opportunities: the small scale cottages industry is often characterized by small-scale
      production units, which means it offers limited job opportunities for local people. This can lead to
      unemployment or underemployment in the community.
      Low wages: due to the small scale of production and lack of bargaining power, small scale cottage industry
      workers often receive low wages, which may not be sufficient to meet their basic needs or improve their
      standard of living.
      Lack of access to resources and technology: small scale cottage industries typically operate on a small
      scale and lack access to resources, such as capital, raw materials and modern technology. This can hinder
      productivity and prevent local people from fully harnessing their skills and potential.
      Vulnerability to market fluctuations: small scale cottage industries are often highly dependent on external
      markets for their products. As a result, they are vulnerable to fluctuations in demand and prices, which can
      negatively impact the income and stability of local people involved in the industry.
      Limited scope for growth and development: due to their small scale and limited resources, small scale
      cottage industries often face challenges in expanding their operations, diversifying their products or adopting
      new technologies. This can prevent local people from benefiting from economies of scale and hinder their
      prospects for growth and development.
